items.stem: Shown below is how ln(V / V) falls linearly with time t during discharge through a 50 kΩ resistor, passing through (0 s, 2.351) and (50 s, 0.351).
items.workedSolution: (a) Taking natural logarithms gives a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the reciprocal of the time constant and a vertical intercept equal to the natural logarithm of the initial potential difference. (b) Calculating the slope gives gradient m = -0.04000 s⁻¹, so τ = −1/m = 25.00 s ≈ 25.0 s. (c) C = τ/R = 500 μF. (d) Uses all measured data points along a straight line of best fit rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.

markScheme.criterion: Shows taking natural logs produces a linear relation between ln(V) and t.
Identifies gradient = −1/τ and vertical intercept = ln(V₀).
Evaluates negative gradient m = -0.0400 s⁻¹ and uses τ = −1/m.
Correct time constant τ = 25.0 s.
Correct capacitance C = τ / R = 500 μF.
States that it uses all measured data points along a straight line of best fit rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.

parts.prompt: Explain why plotting the natural logarithm of potential difference against time yields a straight line, identifying the physical meaning of its gradient and vertical intercept.
parts.expectedAnswer: From the exponential discharge equation, taking natural logarithms gives a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the reciprocal of the time constant and a vertical intercept equal to the natural logarithm of the initial potential difference.
workingSteps: Take natural logarithms of both sides of the exponential decay equation.
Compare with a linear equation to identify the negative gradient and the vertical intercept.

parts.prompt: Determine the time constant τ of the RC circuit from the gradient of the graph.
workingSteps: Time constant τ = −1 / m = 25.00 s ≈ 25.0 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the capacitance of the capacitor in μF given R = 50 kΩ.
State why determining τ from the gradient of a ln(V) against t graph is more reliable than drawing an initial tangent to a V against t curve.
parts.expectedAnswer: The logarithmic gradient method is more reliable because it uses all measured data points along a straight line of best fit rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.
workingSteps: Drawing a tangent to a curve by eye is subjective and sensitive to noise at a single point, whereas a linear best-fit averages random errors over all readings.

items.stem: From an initial offset of 22.0 m past the base marker, a small rover travels for 8.0 s as shown on the graph. What is its mean speed for this motion?
items.workedSolution: Distance travelled Δx = ½(8 + 4)(12) = 72.0 m (independent of the 22 m starting offset). Mean speed = 72.0 / 8 = 9.00 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Divides trapezium distance (72.0 m) by 8 s to obtain 9.00 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: In a lab test on a nylon thread, the limit of proportionality occurs at strain 0.2 on the plotted curve. Find the initial Young's modulus of the material.
items.workedSolution: Reading the end of the linear section at ε = 0.2 gives a stress of 150 MPa. Hence E = σ / ε = 150 / 0.2 = 750 MPa.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates initial linear gradient E = 150 / 0.2 = 750 MPa (C).

items.stem: Determine k|Q₁Q₂| from the straight line of F against r⁻² up to 100.0 m⁻² using two small charged metal spheres on a digital balance.
items.workedSolution: At r⁻² = 0.0 m⁻², tare offset F₀ = 0.1 N; at r⁻² = 100 m⁻², F = 1.2 N. Gradient = (1.2 − 0.1) / 100 = 0.0110 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts tare offset F₀ = 0.1 N to get (1.2 − 0.1) / 100 = 0.0110 N m² (A).

items.stem: The graph shows the non-linear V–I characteristic for a metal filament lamp. Calculate the electrical resistance of the component at a current of 2.0 A.
items.workedSolution: Electrical resistance at an operating point is defined by R = V / I (not the local slope ΔV / ΔI). At I = 2 A, V = 11 V, so R = 11 / 2 = 5.50 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses static ratio R = V / I = 11 / 2 = 5.50 Ω (B).

items.stem: In a photodiode experiment, the graph shows the steepest line of worst fit drawn from 1.5 mW to 7.5 mW. Calculate the gradient of this worst-fit line.
items.workedSolution: At x₁ = 1.5 mW, y₁ = 3 μA; at x₂ = 7.5 mW, y₂ = 24 μA. Worst-fit gradient m_worst = (24 − 3) / (7.5 − 1.5) = 3.50 μA mW⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δy / Δx = (24 − 3) / (7.5 − 1.5) = 3.50 μA mW⁻¹ (B).

options.distractorRationale: Computes the secant y₂ / x₂ as though the worst-fit line passed through the origin (0, 0) rather than (x₁, y₁).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inverts Δx / Δy instead of evaluating Δy / Δx.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts y₁ in the numerator but divides by x₂ instead of the horizontal span (x₂ − x₁).

items.stem: Data for a sealed glass flask of dry air are plotted with ±1.4 kPa vertical error bars on suppressed-origin axes. Given a best-fit gradient of 0.3650 kPa K⁻¹ and a shallowest acceptable worst-fit gradient of 0.3125 kPa K⁻¹, determine the absolute uncertainty in the gradient.
items.workedSolution: Comparing worst-fit and best-fit slopes gives Δm = |m_worst − m_best| = |0.3125 − 0.3650| = 0.05250 kPa K⁻¹ ≈ 0.0525 kPa K⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δm = |m_worst − m_best| = 0.0525 kPa K⁻¹.

items.stem: Slope measurements on a tilted air track give sin θ = 0.3. Using g = 9.8 m s⁻², v² is plotted against s from s = 0.0 m to s = 2.5 m for a small puck. Passing the first gate with speed u₀ > 0, it obeys v² = u₀² + 2as. Determine the slope Δ(v²) / Δs from the graph.
items.workedSolution: From v² = u₀² + (2g sin θ)s, the vertical intercept is u₀² = 3.5 m² s⁻² and at s = 2.5 m, v² = 18.2 m² s⁻². Gradient = (18.2 − 3.5) / 2.5 = 2(9.8)(0.3) = 5.88 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept u₀² = 3.5 m² s⁻² (or evaluates 2 × 9.8 × 0.3) to get 5.88 m s⁻² (A).

items.stem: Five data points with error bars are plotted for the potential difference across a heating coil in a Paper 3A practical. The best-fit line passes through $(1.00, 3.90)$ and $(5.00, 17.5)$. Steepest and shallowest worst-fit lines have gradients 3.99 Ω and 2.86 Ω and intercepts -0.718 V and 1.58 V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Using the large gradient triangle: $m = (17.5 - 3.90) / (5.00 - 1.00) = 3.40 Ω$. (b) $\Delta m = \frac{1}{2}(3.99 - 2.86) = 0.565 Ω$, giving percentage uncertainty $= 16.6\%$. (c) $\Delta c = \frac{1}{2}(1.58 - -0.718) = 1.15 V$. (d) Vertical error bars grow proportionally with the dependent variable because percentage uncertainty is constant; a non-zero intercept indicates a systematic error.

markScheme.criterion: Uses large gradient triangle spanning >50% of line.
Best-fit gradient $m = 3.40 Ω$.
Calculates half-spread $\Delta m = 0.565 Ω$.
Percentage uncertainty $= 16.6\%$.
Applies $\Delta c = \frac{1}{2}(c_{\max} - c_{\min})$.
Absolute intercept uncertainty $\Delta c = 1.15 V$.
Vertical error bars grow proportionally with the dependent variable because percentage uncertainty is constant
Identifies non-zero vertical intercept as a systematic error (reject random error).

parts.prompt: Determine the gradient $m$ of the line of best fit, showing your working clearly.
workingSteps: Triangle spans more than 50% of the plotted line.

parts.prompt: Use the steepest and shallowest worst-fit gradients to calculate the percentage uncertainty in $m$.
workingSteps: Percentage uncertainty $= (0.565 / 3.40) \times 100\% = 16.6\%$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the absolute uncertainty $\Delta c$ in the vertical intercept.
Explain how the lengths of the vertical error bars change across the plotted range and state what a non-zero vertical intercept indicates.
parts.expectedAnswer: Vertical error bars grow proportionally with the dependent variable because percentage uncertainty is constant; a non-zero intercept indicates a systematic zero offset.
workingSteps: Identify constant absolute vs constant percentage uncertainty scaling.
Link non-zero intercept when theory predicts direct proportionality to a systematic error.

items.stem: Driven by a 2400 Hz clock signal, a 4-stage binary ripple counter (modulus 16) uses rising-edge D-type flip-flops. Its waveforms appear in the timing diagram.
items.workedSolution: (a) $f_{\mathrm{out}} = 150 Hz$. (b) Count after 53 pulses is 5. (c) Connecting not-Q back to the D input toggles Q on every rising clock edge dividing frequency by two.

markScheme.criterion: Divides clock frequency by modulus 16.
Obtains 150 Hz.
Finds remainder of 53 divided by 16.
Obtains decimal state 5.
States $\bar{Q}$ is wired back to $D$.
Explains output toggles on each rising edge, halving frequency.

parts.prompt: Calculate the repetition frequency of the counter's full output cycle in Hz.
workingSteps: $f_{\mathrm{out}} = \frac{f_{\mathrm{clk}}}{16} = \frac{2400}{16} = 150 Hz$.

parts.prompt: Starting from zero, determine the decimal count stored after 53 rising clock pulses.
workingSteps: Take remainder modulo 16: 53 mod 16 = 5.

parts.prompt: Explain how each individual D-type flip-flop stage divides the frequency of its incoming clock signal by two.
parts.expectedAnswer: Connecting not-Q back to the D input toggles Q on every rising clock edge dividing frequency by two.
workingSteps: With $\bar{Q}$ wired to $D$, each rising clock edge copies the complement of $Q$ to the output.
Two input clock periods are therefore needed for one complete output cycle at $Q$.

items.stem: The displacement–time graph shows the motion of a toy train moving along a straight track from t = 0.0 s to t = 12.0 s. Calculate its velocity during the initial stage from t = 0.0 s to t = 4.0 s.
items.workedSolution: At t = 0.0 s, s₀ = 6 m; at t = 4 s, s₁ = 26 m. Velocity v = Δs / Δt = (26 − 6) / 4 = 5.00 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts initial position s₀ = 6 m to obtain v = (26 − 6) / 4 = 5.00 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: Shown below is a straight line from the origin to (10.0 V, 0.500 A) on an I (y-axis) versus V (x-axis) plot. For a uniform metal wire of area 6.60 × 10⁻⁸ m² and length 1.20 m, find the resistivity of the metal.
items.workedSolution: Calculating the slope gives gradient m = ΔI / ΔV = 0.5000 A / 10.00 V = 0.05000 A V⁻¹. Since gradient = 1/R, R = 1/m = 20.00 Ω. Therefore ρ = R A / L = 1.100 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m ≈ 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses R = 1 / gradient and ρ = R A / L to obtain 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m.

items.stem: The graph shows how the force on a steel spring varies with compression up to 0.8 m. The compressed spring is released from rest on a smooth horizontal track to launch a 0.6 kg glider.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies k as the gradient ΔF / Δx.
Obtains k = 90.0 N m⁻¹.
Uses triangular area ½Fx.
Obtains E_p = 28.8 J.
Equates ½(0.6)v² to stored elastic energy from (b).
Obtains v = 9.80 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A resting adult's ECG trace shows an R–R interval of $0.72\text{ s}$ and an R-wave peak of $1.25\text{ mV}$ at the skin surface. The signal passes through an amplifier of voltage gain $800$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\text{HR} = \frac{60}{0.72} = 83.3 beats min⁻¹$. (b) $V_{\text{out}} = 800 \times 1.25 \times 10^{-3} = 1.00 V$. (c) The QRS complex is produced by ventricular depolarisation; because ventricular walls are far thicker than atrial walls, the resulting potential spike is much larger than the P wave.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $\text{HR} = 60 / T_{\text{RR}}$.
Correct heart rate 83.3 beats min⁻¹.
Converts $1.25\text{ mV}$ to volts and multiplies by gain $800$.
Correct output peak voltage 1.00 V.
States QRS arises from ventricular depolarisation.
Explains greater ventricular muscle mass produces a larger surface potential change.

parts.prompt: Calculate the patient's heart rate in beats per minute.
workingSteps: Use $\text{heart rate} = \frac{60}{T_{\text{RR}}}$.
Substitute $T_{\text{RR}} = 0.72\text{ s}$ to obtain 83.3 beats min⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the peak output voltage from the ECG amplifier.
workingSteps: Convert $V_{\text{in}} = 1.25\text{ mV} = 1.25 \times 10^{-3}\text{ V}$.
Multiply by gain $800$: $V_{\text{out}} = 1.00 V$.

parts.prompt: State the electrical event responsible for the QRS complex and explain why its peak exceeds the P wave.
parts.expectedAnswer: Rapid ventricular depolarisation across the much thicker ventricular muscle walls generates a larger potential difference than atrial depolarisation.
workingSteps: Identify the QRS complex with ventricular depolarisation.
Link the larger amplitude to the greater muscle mass of the ventricles compared with the atria.

items.stem: A student logs the velocity of a trolley along a straight track on the graph below. Determine the net displacement over 10.0 s.
items.workedSolution: Motion reverses at t = 7 s. Positive area = 54.0 m and area below the axis has magnitude 10.0 m. Net displacement = 54.0 − 10.0 = 44.0 m.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts reverse area (10.0 m) from forward area (54.0 m) to obtain 44.0 m (B).

items.stem: With starting momentum 15.0 kg m s⁻¹, a puck (mass 5.0 kg) experiences the 4.0 s forward force pulse shown on the graph. Deduce the average resultant force for the 4.0 s duration.
items.workedSolution: From the shaded F–t trapezium, J = ½(4 + 2)(35) = 105 N s; hence F_mean = J / Δt = 105 / 4 = 26.3 N.

markScheme.criterion: Divides impulse (105 N s) by 4 s to obtain 26.3 N (C).

items.stem: Plotted below is the I–V characteristic of a light-dependent resistor (LDR), with current on the vertical axis and potential difference on the horizontal axis. The marked operating point is at V = 6.00 V, I = 0.750 A.
items.workedSolution: (a) R = V / I = 8.000 Ω ≈ 8.00 Ω. (b) Connect a potential divider with a series protective resistor, an ammeter in series, and a voltmeter in parallel across the component, and reverse the supply connections for negative readings. (c) Resistance decreases as light intensity increases because more charge carriers are released so the curve becomes steeper.

Correct static resistance 8.00 Ω.

Correctly describes how resistance changes across the graph.
Correct microscopic explanation: resistance decreases as light intensity increases because more charge carriers are released so the curve becomes steeper.

parts.prompt: Calculate the static resistance of the component at the highlighted operating point.
workingSteps: Recall that static resistance at a point is R = V / I (not the inverse of the local tangent).
Substitute V = 6.000 V and I = 0.7500 A to obtain R = 8.000 Ω ≈ 8.00 Ω.

parts.prompt: Describe the circuit arrangement and experimental procedure used to obtain a complete I–V characteristic safely across positive and negative potential differences.
parts.expectedAnswer: To obtain the full characteristic safely, connect a potential divider with a series protective resistor, an ammeter in series, and a voltmeter in parallel across the component, and reverse the supply connections for negative readings.
workingSteps: Use a potential divider to vary potential difference smoothly from zero while limiting excessive current with a protective resistor.
Measure current with a series ammeter, potential difference with a parallel voltmeter, and reverse the supply leads for negative polarity.

parts.prompt: Explain the physical shape of the I–V characteristic in terms of charge carriers and resistance.
parts.expectedAnswer: The curve shows that the component resistance decreases as light intensity increases because more charge carriers are released so the curve becomes steeper.
workingSteps: Link the changing ratio of potential difference to current directly to the microscopic conduction mechanism.

items.stem: The Q–V graph records a capacitor charged evenly from zero. Its final state is Q = 3.50 mC at a potential difference of V = 14.0 V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Capacitance is the charge stored per unit potential difference across the plates. (b) C = Q / V = 250 μF. (c) Triangular area E = ½ Q V = 0.02450 J ≈ 0.0245 J.

markScheme.criterion: States charge stored per unit potential difference across the plates.
Correct capacitance 250 μF.
Recognises triangular area E = ½ Q V and converts mC to C.
Correct stored energy 0.0245 J.

items.stem: A thick rubber cord is stretched to twice its original length. It is then allowed to contract back to its original length, giving the loading and unloading curves shown.
items.workedSolution: (a) Polymeric rubber shows large non linear elastic strain and an unloading hysteresis loop dissipating thermal energy. (b) Area enclosed by the hysteresis loop equals thermal energy dissipated per unit volume.

markScheme.criterion: Rubber returns to original length (zero strain) when stress is removed.
Non-linear elastic behaviour due to tangled polymer chains uncoiling and recoiling.
Enclosed hysteresis loop area equals thermal energy dissipated per unit volume.
Repeated loading/unloading cycles heat the tyre continuously.

parts.prompt: Explain why the deformation is still classified as elastic even though the unloading curve does not retrace the loading curve.
parts.expectedAnswer: The unloading curve returns to zero strain at zero stress (no permanent extension): polymeric rubber shows large non linear elastic strain and an unloading hysteresis loop dissipating thermal energy.
workingSteps: Zero residual strain on unloading defines elastic deformation; tangled polymer chains recoil.

parts.prompt: State what the shaded area enclosed between the two curves represents and explain why a car tyre warms up as it rolls.
parts.expectedAnswer: The area enclosed by the hysteresis loop equals thermal energy dissipated per unit volume, so repeated flexing cycles convert mechanical work into internal thermal energy inside the rubber tyre.
workingSteps: Area = thermal energy dissipated per unit volume per cycle.

items.stem: Starting at 18.0 m s⁻¹ upward, a test lift follows the acceleration–time curve below for 12.0 s. Determine the velocity of the object when t = 12.0 s.
items.workedSolution: Positive a–t area (0 to 6 s) = 36.0 m s⁻¹; negative area magnitude (6 s to 12 s) = 18.0 m s⁻¹. Net Δv = 36.0 − 18.0 = 18.0 m s⁻¹. Final velocity = 18 + (18.0) = 36.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Combines net signed area (18.0 m s⁻¹) with u₀ = 18 m s⁻¹ to obtain 36.0 m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: Graphing v² against distance s from s = 0.0 m to s = 2.0 m produces a straight line for a trolley on a smooth inclined ramp. Here sin θ = 0.3 and g = 9.81 m s⁻². It enters the timed section with non-zero speed u₀. Determine the slope of this v²–s graph.
items.workedSolution: From v² = u₀² + (2g sin θ)s, the vertical intercept is u₀² = 1.5 m² s⁻² and at s = 2 m, v² = 13.272 m² s⁻². Gradient = (13.272 − 1.5) / 2 = 2(9.81)(0.3) = 5.89 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept u₀² = 1.5 m² s⁻² (or evaluates 2 × 9.81 × 0.3) to get 5.89 m s⁻² (B).

items.stem: Over a 10.0 m distance, the plotted resultant force acts on a glider (mass 2.0 kg) moving forward at 5.0 m s⁻¹. Determine the speed of the object when x = 10.0 m.
items.workedSolution: Summing signed areas: positive work (0 to 8 m) = ½(8 + 4)(12) = 72.0 J. Resistive work (8 m to 10 m) = −½(2)(4) = −4.00 J. Net work W = 68.0 J. From ½mv² = ½mu₀² + W, v = √(5² + 2 × 68.0 / 2) = 9.64 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds net work W = 68.0 J and v = √(5² + 2W/2) = 9.64 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: The momentum–time curve below tracks a 0.8 kg glider on a horizontal air track. A steady net force acts from t = 1.0 s to t = 5.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Reading rise over run on the plot: F = Δp / Δt = (7.2 − 1.6) / (5 − 1) = 1.40 N. (b) Calculating kinetic energy gain: W = ΔE_k = (7.2² − 1.6²) / (2 × 0.8) = 30.8 J.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies resultant force as gradient Δp / Δt of the p–t graph.
Obtains F = 1.40 N.
Relates net work to ΔE_k = (p₂² − p₁²) / (2m).
Substitutes p₁ = 1.6 kg m s⁻¹, p₂ = 7.2 kg m s⁻¹, and m = 0.8 kg.
Obtains W = 30.8 J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resultant force acting between t = 1.0 s and t = 5.0 s.
Calculate the net work done on the 0.8 kg object between t = 1.0 s and t = 5.0 s.
workingSteps: Use E_k = p² / (2m) before and after the force acts.

items.stem: Graphing total resistance R versus L / A reaching 500.0 m⁻¹ gives the straight line below for a conducting plastic strip. With constant lead resistance R₀, the line obeys R = ρ(L / A) + R₀. Allowing for the intercept, calculate resistivity ρ.
items.workedSolution: In R = ρ(L / A) + R₀, the vertical intercept is the contact offset and resistivity ρ is ΔR / Δ(L / A) = (36 − 7) / 500 = 0.0580 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept R₀ = 7 Ω to obtain ρ = (36 − 7) / 500 = 0.0580 Ω m (C).

items.stem: Over current I from 0.0 A to 1.0 A, a laboratory power supply produces the plotted terminal potential difference V. Use the linear graph to calculate the mean terminal potential difference.
items.workedSolution: Since the V–I plot is linear from 4.5 V at I = 0.0 A down to 1.5 V at I = 1 A, V_mean = ½(4.5 + 1.5) = 3.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Averages endpoint voltages ½(4.5 + 1.5) = 3.00 V (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Halves the EMF as if terminal voltage dropped to zero at I_max.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Reads the minimum terminal potential difference at maximum current rather than averaging across the current interval.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Reads the open-circuit EMF intercept and ignores internal voltage drop.

items.stem: An IB Paper 1B V–I graph spans from (0.20 A, 2.00 ± 0.30 V) to (1.00 A, 8.40 ± 0.30 V). The dashed maximum and minimum gradient lines pass through all uncertainty bars from the endpoint bars. Calculate the absolute uncertainty Δm in the gradient.

markScheme.criterion: Computes Δm = (m_max − m_min)/2 = 0.750 Ω.

items.stem: Two neutrons inside an oxygen nucleus briefly approach each other to the separation marked on the graph.
items.workedSolution: (a) Below $0.5\text{ fm}$ it is strongly repulsive preventing nuclear collapse. (b) It acts equally between all nucleons and has no effect on leptons.

markScheme.criterion: State that the force is repulsive below 0.5 fm.
Explain that this prevents the nucleus from collapsing.
State that the strong force is identical between n–n, p–n, and p–p pairs.
State that electrons are leptons and do not experience the strong nuclear force.

parts.prompt: State whether the strong nuclear force between the two neutrons is attractive or repulsive at this separation and explain its significance.
parts.expectedAnswer: The strong nuclear force is strongly repulsive preventing nuclear collapse at separations below 0.5 fm.
workingSteps: Identify that separation is below 0.5 fm where force is positive (repulsive).
Link short-range repulsion to preventing nucleon collapse.

parts.prompt: State how the strong nuclear force between two neutrons compares with that between two protons at the same separation, and explain why atomic electrons are unaffected.
parts.expectedAnswer: The strong nuclear force is identical in magnitude and range because it acts equally between all nucleons and has no effect on leptons such as electrons.
workingSteps: State charge-independence of strong nuclear force for all nucleon pairs.
Identify electrons as leptons that do not interact via the strong force.

items.stem: A niobium–titanium superconducting magnet coil ($T_{\text{c}} = 9.20\text{ K}$) operates in liquid helium at $4.20\text{ K}$ carrying $120\text{ A}$. Just above $T_{\text{c}}$, its normal resistance is $0.300\,\Omega$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Zero electrical resistance at or below the critical temperature; operates in superconducting state with zero resistance and zero heating loss. (b) $P = I^2R = 4.32 × 10³ W$. (c) Expensive low-temperature cooling is required to stay below the critical temperature.

markScheme.criterion: Zero electrical resistance / resistivity at or below critical temperature $T_{\text{c}}$.
Correctly identify superconducting state with zero resistance and zero heating loss.
Substitute current and normal resistance into $P = I^2R$.
Expensive / technically difficult low-temperature cooling required below $T_{\text{c}}$.

parts.expectedAnswer: Critical temperature is the transition temperature at or below which a superconductor has zero electrical resistance; at $4.2\text{ K}$ it is in the superconducting state with zero resistance and zero heating loss.
workingSteps: Define Tc as transition to exact zero resistance (at or below Tc).
Compare operating temperature 4.2 K against Tc = 9.2 K.

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal power that would be dissipated if the coil accidentally warmed just above $T_{\text{c}}$ while still carrying the same current.
State one major practical limitation preventing widespread room-temperature use of superconducting power cables.
parts.expectedAnswer: A major limitation is that expensive low-temperature cooling is required to stay below the critical temperature.
workingSteps: State cost and difficulty of maintaining low-temperature cooling below Tc.

items.stem: The graph compares a spreadsheet Euler model of ΔN/Δt = −λN (using steps Δt) with the exact curve N = N₀e^(−λt). Why do the Euler points always lie slightly below the exact exponential curve?
items.workedSolution: Because |ΔN/Δt| decreases continuously as N drops, applying the steeper initial slope for the whole interval Δt subtracts slightly too many nuclei. Therefore the correct statement is: Across each finite interval, the iterative step method underestimates the remaining quantity because it applies the steeper starting gradient across the whole finite time interval.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: the iterative step method underestimates the remaining quantity because it applies the steeper starting gradient across the whole finite time interval.

options.text: The iterative step method overestimates the decay constant λ automatically at every second spreadsheet row.
options.distractorRationale: λ stays constant in the spreadsheet; the error arises from holding the gradient fixed over Δt.

options.label: B
options.text: Exponential decay curves are concave downward, so any straight-line tangent segment drops beneath the true curve.
options.distractorRationale: An exponential decay curve is concave upward (gradient becomes less negative with time), which is why tangent steps drop below it.

options.label: C
options.text: Random statistical fluctuations inside the spreadsheet always force negative rounding bias below the analytical solution.
options.distractorRationale: Euler stepping is fully deterministic; the systematic underestimate is numerical truncation error.

options.text: Across each finite interval, the iterative step method underestimates the remaining quantity because it applies the steeper starting gradient across the entire finite time interval.

items.stem: In a damping practical, a pendulum's amplitude $x$ follows $x = A e^{-\lambda t}$. With a false origin at $t = 10$ s, the best-fit line of ln(x / mm) against t / s passes through $(15, 2.90)$ and $(65, 1.15)$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Taking natural logarithms gives ln y = ln A − λt, and the false origin means a point on the line must be substituted rather than reading the vertical axis crossing. (b) $\lambda = -(1.15 - 2.9) / (65 - 15) = 0.0350 s⁻¹$. (c) $\ln A = 3.42$, so $A = 30.7$. (d) $T_{1/2} = \ln 2 / \lambda = 19.8 s$.

markScheme.criterion: States $\ln y = \ln A - \lambda t$ with gradient $-\lambda$.
Uses point substitution instead of reading vertical axis at false origin.
Calculates magnitude of negative gradient.
Decay constant $\lambda = 0.0350 s⁻¹$.
Computes $\ln A = y_1 + \lambda t_1$ and applies $e^{\ln A}$.
Initial value $A = 30.7$.
Applies $T_{1/2} = \ln 2 / \lambda$.
Half-time $T_{1/2} = 19.8 s$.

items.stem: The oscillation period $T$ of a clamped vibrating metre rule of length $L$ obeys $T = k L^n$. Plotting lg(T / ms) against lg(L / cm) with a false origin at 0.60 gives a best-fit line through $(0.70, 0.35)$ and $(1.50, 1.55)$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Taking base ten logarithms gives lg y = n lg x + lg k, and a false origin means a point on the line must be substituted to find the intercept. (b) $n = (1.55 - 0.35) / (1.5 - 0.7) = 1.50$. (c) $\lg k = 0.35 - (1.50)(0.7) = -0.700$. (d) $k = 10^{-0.700} = 0.200$.

markScheme.criterion: Writes $\lg y = n \lg x + \lg k$ (reject $\lg x^n$ unexpanded).
Explains false origin requires substituting a point $(x_1, y_1)$ on the line.
Computes gradient from wide pair of points on the line.
Exponent $n = 1.50$.
Substitutes $(x_1, y_1)$ and $n$ into $\lg k = y_1 - n x_1$.
True intercept $\lg k = -0.700$.
Evaluates base-10 antilogarithm $k = 10^{\lg k}$.
Constant $k = 0.200$.

items.stem: During Required Practical 7 on a vertical mass-spring system, four timings for 20 oscillations are 17.8 s, 18.1 s, 14.3 s, and 17.9 s, each with reaction-time uncertainty $\pm 0.2$ s. Plotting $T^2$ against mass $m$ across six masses gives a straight line of gradient 1.58 s² kg⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Discard 14.3 s; $T = 0.897 s$. (b) $\%\Delta T = 1.12\%$. (c) $k$ $= 4\pi^2 / 1.58 = 25.0 N m⁻¹$. (d) Place the fiducial marker at the equilibrium position where speed is maximum, discard anomalous timings before averaging, and time many oscillations to reduce reaction-time uncertainty.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies and discards anomaly (14.3 s) before averaging.
Mean period $T = 0.897 s$.
Uses $\Delta T_{20} / T_{20} \times 100\%$.
Percentage uncertainty in $T = 1.12\%$.
Equates gradient to $4\pi^2 / k$.
Fiducial marker at equilibrium where oscillator moves fastest (minimising transit-time uncertainty).
Timing 20 oscillations divides fixed human reaction-time error by 20.

items.stem: The graph shows a spreadsheet iterative model of radioactive decay (ΔN/Δt = −λN). It also shows the exact exponential curve N = N₀e^(−λt) and a tangent drawn to the curve.
items.workedSolution: Constant fractional decay per unit time leads to exponential decay, which can be modelled step by step on a spreadsheet so smaller time steps improve agreement with the analytical curve. Because radioactive decay is spontaneous and random, every undecayed nucleus has the same constant decay probability λ per second, so the rate of decay ΔN/Δt is proportional to N. A spreadsheet fixes a small step Δt, computes ΔN = −λNΔt from the current row, and sets N_next = N + ΔN. Because the gradient becomes shallower during Δt, holding the steeper initial rate constant over Δt subtracts too many nuclei. Reducing Δt updates the rate more frequently and reduces truncation error. Graphically, drawing a tangent at any point (t, N) gives λ = |gradient| / N or subtangent 1/λ.

markScheme.criterion: L1: States that decay is spontaneous and random with constant decay probability λ per second per undecayed nucleus.
L1: Links proportionality ΔN/Δt = −λN (and capacitor analogy ΔQ/Δt = −Q/(RC)) to exponential decay with constant half-life.
L2: Clearly states the spreadsheet iteration rule: compute ΔN = −λNΔt from current N, then update N_next = N + ΔN at t + Δt.
L2: Explains why the Euler model systematically underestimates exact N(t) by assuming the steeper initial rate holds across the whole interval Δt.
L3: Explains that decreasing Δt recalculates the rate more frequently, converging smoothly toward N₀e^(−λt).
L3: Describes extracting λ from the gradient of a tangent at a chosen point via λ = |gradient| / N (or subtangent = 1/λ).

parts.prompt: Explain how constant decay probability per unit time leads to exponential decay, describe how a spreadsheet iteratively solves ΔN/Δt = −λN step by step, explain why the iterative curve systematically underestimates the exact curve, and explain how to improve accuracy and extract λ graphically from a tangent. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Constant fractional decay per unit time leads to exponential decay, which can be modelled step by step on a spreadsheet so smaller time steps improve agreement with the analytical curve. Because radioactive decay is spontaneous and random, every undecayed nucleus has the same constant decay probability λ per second, so the rate of decay ΔN/Δt is proportional to N. A spreadsheet fixes a small step Δt, computes ΔN = −λNΔt from the current row, and sets N_next = N + ΔN. Because the gradient becomes shallower during Δt, holding the steeper initial rate constant over Δt subtracts too many nuclei. Reducing Δt updates the rate more frequently and reduces truncation error. Graphically, drawing a tangent at any point (t, N) gives λ = |gradient| / N or subtangent 1/λ.
workingSteps: Link constant decay probability λ to ΔN/Δt = −λN and constant half-life exponential decay.
Write exact spreadsheet recursion ΔN_k = −λ N_k Δt and N_{k+1} = N_k + ΔN_k.
Explain why finite Δt systematically underestimates convex exponential N(t) and improves as Δt decreases.
Show tangent extraction λ = |ΔN/Δt| / N (or capacitor RC subtangent analogy).

items.stem: A student investigates the simple harmonic motion of a vertical steel spring loaded with slotted masses. The aim is to determine the spring constant $k$ and effective spring mass.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 Model Response: Place the fiducial marker at the equilibrium position where speed is maximum, discard anomalous timings before averaging, and time many oscillations to reduce reaction-time uncertainty. In addition, clamp the retort stand firmly with a G-clamp/counterweight and wear safety goggles, restrict oscillations to small vertical amplitudes within the elastic limit, plot T² against slotted mass m, obtain k = 4π² / gradient, and interpret the non-zero intercept as the effective mass of the spring and hanger.

markScheme.criterion: Secures retort stand with a G-clamp/counterweight, places a sand tray/pad underneath, and wears safety goggles in case the spring detaches.
Keeps oscillations vertical with small amplitude within the elastic limit so coils never collide or go slack.
Positions a horizontal fiducial marker at the equilibrium position where mass speed is maximum.
Times 10–20 complete oscillations (starting count at zero), repeats >= 3 times per mass, and discards anomalies before averaging T.
Repeats for at least six different total slotted masses m and plots T² against m.
Extracts k = 4π² / gradient from a > 50% gradient triangle and identifies the small vertical/negative horizontal intercept with effective spring/hanger mass.

parts.prompt: Plan a safe, high-precision practical investigation to determine $k$ using a graphical method, covering setup, timing technique, safety, error reduction, and interpretation of the graph's gradient and intercept. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Place the fiducial marker at the equilibrium position where speed is maximum, discard anomalous timings before averaging, and time many oscillations to reduce reaction-time uncertainty; clamp the retort stand firmly with a G-clamp/counterweight and wear safety goggles, restrict oscillations to small vertical amplitudes within the elastic limit, plot T² against slotted mass m, obtain k = 4π² / gradient, and interpret the non-zero intercept as the effective mass of the spring and hanger.
workingSteps: Level 1: Rigid setup, safety/small-angle controls, and correct independent/dependent variables.
Level 2: Equilibrium fiducial marker (max speed), timing 20 oscillations with zero start, repeats & anomaly rejection.
Level 3: Wide range (>= 6 points), T² linearization, 4π²/gradient extraction, and systematic offset interpretation.

items.stem: A Year 13 student plans to determine the acceleration of free fall $g$ using a simple pendulum held in a split-cork clamp.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 Model Response: Place the fiducial marker at the equilibrium position where speed is maximum, discard anomalous timings before averaging, and time many oscillations to reduce reaction-time uncertainty. In addition, measure length L from the underside of the split cork to the centre of mass of the bob, keep angular displacement below 10°–15°, repeat timings for at least six lengths, plot T² against L, and obtain g = 4π² / gradient.

markScheme.criterion: Suspends dense small bob via non-stretching string clamped tightly in a split cork and measures L from pivot to centre of mass of bob.
Keeps oscillation angle small (< 10°–15°) in a single vertical plane so SHM approximation sin θ ≈ θ holds.
Places a fiducial marker directly behind the equilibrium position where bob speed is maximum (reject 'zero acceleration' alone).
Counts 'zero' at start, times 10–20 complete oscillations, takes >= 3 repeat timings per length, and discards anomalies before averaging.
Repeats for at least six different lengths L across a wide range and records L, mean T, and T² in a table.
Plots T² against L (best-fit straight line through origin), measures gradient using a > 50% triangle, and computes g = 4π² / gradient.

parts.prompt: Describe a complete experimental procedure to determine $g$ graphically from simple harmonic oscillations, detailing apparatus setup, timing precision, control of assumptions, and graphical analysis. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Place the fiducial marker at the equilibrium position where speed is maximum, discard anomalous timings before averaging, and time many oscillations to reduce reaction-time uncertainty; measure length L from the underside of the split cork to the centre of mass of the bob, keep angular displacement below 10°–15°, repeat timings for at least six lengths, plot T² against L, and obtain g = 4π² / gradient.
workingSteps: Level 1: Rigid setup, safety/small-angle controls, and correct independent/dependent variables.
Level 2: Equilibrium fiducial marker (max speed), timing 20 oscillations with zero start, repeats & anomaly rejection.
Level 3: Wide range (>= 6 points), T² linearization, 4π²/gradient extraction, and systematic offset interpretation.

items.stem: Shown below is a linear RC discharge plot of ln(V / V) against t passing through (0 s, 1.609) and (16 s, -0.391). Given R = 20 kΩ, calculate the capacitance.
items.workedSolution: Calculating the slope gives gradient m = (-0.391 − 1.609) / (16 − 0) = -0.1250 s⁻¹. Time constant τ = −1/m = 8.000 s. Capacitance C = τ / R = 8.000 s / (20 × 10³ Ω) = 400 μF.

markScheme.criterion: Extracts linearized graph parameters accurately to obtain 400 μF.

items.stem: Shown below is a 15.0 s velocity–time curve for a lift cage (at rest 50.0 m ahead of the reference mark at t = 0.0 s). Uniform braking starts at t = 9.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Area under the v–t trapezium is Δx = ½(15 + 6)(22) = 231 m. (b) Final distance from the reference mark = 50 + 231 = 281 m. (c) Mean speed = 231 / 15 = 15.4 m s⁻¹. (d) Braking acceleration = (0 − 22) / (15 − 9) = -3.67 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Identifies distance travelled as the area under the v–t trapezium.
Obtains Δx = 231 m.
Adds 50 m offset to obtain 281 m.
Divides distance travelled from (a) by 15 s.
Obtains mean speed = 15.4 m s⁻¹.
Obtains braking acceleration = -3.67 m s⁻².

items.stem: A plastic strip obeys Hooke's law from strain 0.0 to 0.4 and is stretched up to 0.8. The curve is shown below.
items.workedSolution: (a) Over the initial linear stretch, Young's modulus E = 140 / 0.4 = 350 MPa. (b) Energy per unit volume = ½(0.4)(140) + ½(140 + 200)(0.4) = 96.0 MJ m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates initial gradient σ / ε up to ε = 0.4.
Obtains E = 350 MPa.
Identifies work per unit volume as total area under the σ–ε graph.
Splits area into initial triangle plus upper trapezium.
Obtains 96.0 MJ m⁻³.

items.stem: To test the inverse-square law with two small charged metal spheres on a digital balance, a student graphs force F against r⁻² up to 80.0 m⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) At r⁻² = 0, systematic tare offset F₀ = 0.200 N. (b) Gradient = (2.2 − 0.2) / 80 = 0.0250 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Reads intercept F₀ = 0.200 N.
Evaluates ΔF = 2.2 − 0.2 using intercept from (a).
Divides ΔF by 80 m⁻² and states correct unit N m².
Obtains 0.0250 N m².

items.stem: A student measures the potential difference V across a small filament bulb as the current I increases from 0.0 A to 1.2 A. The graph shows the resulting non-linear V–I characteristic.
items.workedSolution: (a) At I = 1.2 A, V = 8.40 V. (b) Static resistance R = V / I = 8.4 / 1.2 = 7.00 Ω (the upper segment gradient 12.0 Ω is ΔV / ΔI, not R).

markScheme.criterion: Reads V = 8.40 V at I = 1.2 A.
Selects R = V / I rather than local segment gradient ΔV / ΔI.
Substitutes V = 8.4 V and I = 1.2 A.
Obtains R = 7.00 Ω.

items.stem: In a force-sensor experiment, a student plots data with vertical error bars from 0.5 N to 2.5 N. The graph shows the steepest acceptable line of worst fit through the error bars.
items.workedSolution: (a) At 2.5 N, y₂ = 12.4 mV. (b) Worst-fit gradient = (12.4 − 1.2) / (2.5 − 0.5) = 5.60 mV N⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Reads y₂ = 12.4 mV.
Reads y₁ = 1.2 mV at x₁ = 0.5 N and forms Δy / Δx.
Subtracts x₁ = 0.5 N in the denominator (2.5 − 0.5).
Obtains 5.60 mV N⁻¹.

items.stem: In a lab test on a steel spring, data points carry vertical error bars of ±0.01 m on a suppressed-origin graph. Two widely spaced best-fit points are (7.0 N, 0.3118 m) and (23.0 N, 0.4942 m). The shallowest acceptable line through all error bars has gradient 9.900 × 10⁻³ m N⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) From the large gradient triangle, m_best = (0.4942 − 0.3118) / (23.0 − 7.0) = 0.01140 m N⁻¹ ≈ 0.0114 m N⁻¹. (b) Δm = |9.900 × 10⁻³ − 0.01140| = 1.50 × 10⁻³ m N⁻¹. (c) A suppressed origin expands the plotted data to fill more than half of the grid improving reading precision.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly substitutes large-triangle coordinates (0.4942 − 0.3118) / (23.0 − 7.0).
Obtains best-fit gradient = 0.0114 m N⁻¹ with correct compound SI unit.
Calculates Δm = |m_worst − m_best| = 1.50 × 10⁻³ m N⁻¹.
States that a false origin expands the plotted data to fill more than half of the grid improving reading precision.

items.stem: While heating an insulated aluminium block at steady power, a student draws steepest and shallowest worst-fit lines through all error bars. The best-fit gradient is 2.80 °C min⁻¹, and the worst-fit lines cross the vertical axis at -0.971 °C and 3.52 °C. Calculate the absolute uncertainty in the vertical intercept.
items.workedSolution: Using half the spread between extreme intercepts, $\Delta c = \frac{1}{2}(c_{\max} - c_{\min}) = \frac{1}{2}(3.52 - -0.971) = 2.24 °C$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly applies half-spread rule to obtain 2.24 °C (3 sf).

items.stem: A modulo-10 BCD counter uses an AND gate to detect binary 1010 ($Q_3 \cdot Q_1$) and reset to 0000 on every 10th pulse. The input clock frequency is 600 Hz. Calculate the frequency of the reset pulse.
items.workedSolution: Because the counter recycles every 10 clock pulses (states 0 to 9), the reset repetition frequency is $f_{\mathrm{out}} = \frac{600}{10} = 60.0 Hz$.

markScheme.criterion: Reset repetition frequency equals 60.0 Hz.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides by $16$ as if no reset decoding gate were connected.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides by maximum state $9$ instead of modulus $10$.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Divides by $2^3 = 8$ instead of $10$.

items.stem: The displacement–time graph shows the motion of a toy train moving along a straight track from t = 0.0 s to t = 20.0 s. It stops briefly and then returns between t = 12.0 s and t = 20.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Maximum displacement at the plateau = 56.0 m. (b) Return-stage velocity = (24 − 56) / (20 − 12) = -4.00 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Reads plateau displacement = 56.0 m.
Uses gradient formula Δs / Δt = (24 − 56) / (20 − 12).
Retains negative sign for motion back toward the origin.
Obtains -4.00 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A 1.25 m piece of uniform metal wire has cross-sectional area 6.00 × 10⁻⁸ m². Its best-fit I–V line goes through the origin and reaches I = 0.500 A at V = 6.00 V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area. (b) Gradient = 0.08333 A V⁻¹, so R = 1 / gradient = 12.0 Ω. (c) ρ = RA/L = 5.760 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 5.76 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: States resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area.
Correctly specifies all quantities (or notes constant temperature / material property).
Computes large-triangle gradient m = ΔI/ΔV = 0.0833 A V⁻¹ and takes its reciprocal R = 1/m.
Correct wire resistance R = 12.0 Ω.
Substitutes R, A, and L correctly into ρ = RA/L.
Correct resistivity 5.76 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m with unit Ω m.

parts.prompt: Define the electrical resistivity of a material.
parts.expectedAnswer: Electrical resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area, where resistance, cross-sectional area, and length are measured for a uniform sample at constant temperature.
workingSteps: State the definition in terms of a conductor of unit length and unit cross-sectional area.
Identify that resistivity is an intrinsic property of the material at constant temperature.

parts.prompt: Determine the resistance of the wire from the gradient of the I–V line of best fit using a large triangle.
workingSteps: Because I is on the vertical axis, R = 1 / m = 12.00 Ω ≈ 12.0 Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resistivity of the alloy, stating the appropriate SI unit.
workingSteps: Evaluate ρ = 5.760 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 5.76 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

items.stem: A 0.22 kg glider rests against a metal spring compressed by 0.4 m on a smooth horizontal bench. The graph shows how the force varies with compression. Calculate the launch speed of the glider when the spring is released.
items.workedSolution: Elastic energy stored E_p = ½(44)(0.4) = 8.80 J. Equating ½mv² = E_p gives v = √(2 × 8.80 / 0.22) = 8.94 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Sets ½(0.22)v² = 8.80 J to obtain v = 8.94 m s⁻¹ (D).

items.workedSolution: (a) Vertical intercept at t = 0 is ln(C₀ / s⁻¹) = 8.40. (b) Gradient = (3.6 − 8.4) / 60 = -0.0800 s⁻¹ (which equals −λ).

items.stem: An endurance athlete's resting ECG shows an R–R period of $0.92\text{ s}$ with an R-wave amplitude of $1.50\text{ mV}$. Determine the athlete's resting pulse rate.
items.workedSolution: Resting pulse rate $= \frac{60}{0.92\text{ s}} = 65.2 beats min⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 65.2 beats min⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies sixty by the period instead of dividing.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Leaves the answer in hertz rather than beats per minute.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Assumes two beats occur per R–R interval.

items.stem: Tracking a trolley along a straight track over 12.0 s gives the plotted velocity–time line below. Positive values represent forward motion. Braking reverses its motion between t = 6.0 s and t = 10.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) The curve crosses the time axis at t = 9 s. Positive area = 54.0 m and unsigned negative area = 7.50 m, giving total distance = 61.5 m. (b) Net displacement = 54.0 − 7.50 = 46.5 m; average velocity = 46.5 / 12 = 3.88 m s⁻¹. (c) Acceleration = (−3 − 9) / (10 − 6) = -3.00 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Finds zero-crossing t = 9 s and evaluates both unsigned areas (54.0 m and 7.50 m).
Obtains total distance = 61.5 m.
Subtracts areas for net displacement (46.5 m) and divides by 12 s.
Obtains average velocity = 3.88 m s⁻¹.
Obtains acceleration = -3.00 m s⁻² including negative sign.

workingSteps: Velocity crosses zero at t = 9 s; forward area = 54.0 m.
Unsigned reverse area = 7.50 m, so total distance = 54.0 + 7.50 = 61.5 m.

parts.prompt: Determine the net displacement and hence calculate the average velocity over the 12.0 s interval.
workingSteps: Net displacement Δs = 54.0 − 7.50 = 46.5 m.
Average velocity = Δs / Δt = 46.5 / 12 = 3.88 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the acceleration between t = 6.0 s and t = 10.0 s.

items.stem: With initial momentum 9.0 kg m s⁻¹ at t = 0.0 s, a trolley of mass 3.0 kg experiences a forward force lasting 2.5 s, as shown on the graph.
items.workedSolution: (a) Area under the F–t trapezium gives impulse J = ½(2.5 + 1.5)(46) = 92.0 N s. (b) Final momentum p_f = 9 + 92.0 = 101 kg m s⁻¹. (c) Speed increase Δv = 92.0 / 3 = 30.7 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes impulse from the trapezium area under the F–t curve.
Obtains J = 92.0 N s.
Adds 9 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 101 kg m s⁻¹.
Divides impulse from (a) by 3 kg.
Obtains Δv = 30.7 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A metal rod of length $L = 2.00\text{ m}$ and cross-sectional area $A = 0.600\text{ mm}^2$ obeys Hooke's law. It extends by $4.00\text{ mm}$ under a tensile load of $96.0\text{ N}$. Calculate the elastic strain energy stored per unit volume ($\text{J m}^{-3}$).
items.workedSolution: $\sigma = 96.0 / (0.600 \times 10^{-6}) = 1.60 \times 10^8\text{ Pa}$; $\varepsilon = 4.00 \times 10^{-3} / 2.00 = 2.00 \times 10^{-3}$; energy density $= \frac{1}{2}\sigma\varepsilon = 1.60 × 10⁵ J m⁻³$. Option B (1.60 × 10⁵ J m⁻³) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Strain energy density $= 1.60 × 10⁵ J m⁻³$ (1.60 × 10⁵ J m⁻³, option B).

items.stem: During a 15.0 s journey, a lift starts at t = 0.0 s moving upward at 15.0 m s⁻¹, with acceleration shown on the graph.
items.workedSolution: (a) Speed peaks where a crosses zero at t = 8.00 s. (b) Positive area = 52.0 m s⁻¹, giving v_max = 15 + 52.0 = 67.0 m s⁻¹. (c) Negative area magnitude = 24.0 m s⁻¹, so v_final = 67.0 − 24.0 = 43.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: States t = 8.00 s.
Evaluates positive area up to 8 s (52.0 m s⁻¹) and adds u₀ = 15 m s⁻¹.
Obtains v_max = 67.0 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts negative area (24.0 m s⁻¹) from v_max.
Obtains final velocity = 43.0 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Data below track the resultant force over 8.0 m on a small sled of mass 1.6 kg, which has speed 4.5 m s⁻¹ at x = 0.0 m.
items.workedSolution: (a) Evaluating the net F–x area yields W = 54.0 − 4.00 = 50.0 J. (b) v = √(4.5² + 2(50.0)/1.6) = 9.10 m s⁻¹. (c) Mean force = 50.0 / 8 = 6.25 N.

Divides net work by 8 m to get 6.25 N.

items.stem: Shown below is how measured resistance R of a ceramic heating rod increases with L / A from 0.0 m⁻¹ to 50.0 m⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Lead resistance is the vertical axis crossing, R₀ = 4.00 Ω. (b) Taking the gradient gives ρ = (20 − 4) / 50 = 0.320 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: States R₀ = 4.00 Ω.
Identifies ρ with the gradient ΔR / Δ(L / A).
Subtracts R₀ = 4 Ω from 20 Ω before dividing by 50 m⁻¹.
Obtains ρ = 0.320 Ω m.

items.stem: Using a variable resistor across a rechargeable battery, a student records terminal potential difference V for current I from zero to 5.0 A.
items.workedSolution: (a) Open-circuit intercept gives ε = 25.0 V. (b) Gradient = (10 − 25) / 5 = -3.00 V A⁻¹. (c) Mean terminal p.d. = ½(25 + 10) = 17.5 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reads ε = 25.0 V at I = 0.
Evaluates (10 − 25) / 5 including negative sign.
Obtains -3.00 V A⁻¹.
Uses ½(25 + 10) or area divided by 5 A.
Obtains 17.5 V.

items.stem: In an IB Paper 1B investigation of a spring, force F is plotted against extension x with ±0.25 N uncertainty bars from (0.040 m, 1.50 N) to (0.240 m, 7.50 N). Point 4 at (0.160 m, 6.40 N) is circled as an anomalous data point.
items.workedSolution: (a) k = 30.0 N m⁻¹. (b) Δk = 2.50 N m⁻¹, 8.33%. (c) Δc = 0.350 N; a non-zero vertical intercept on a linear graph expected to pass through the origin indicates a constant systematic zero error that shifts every reading equally without changing the gradient. (d) An anomalous data point whose uncertainty bar lies clearly outside the linear trend of the remaining points should be circled and excluded from the best-fit gradient with an experimental justification rather than silently deleted.

markScheme.criterion: Uses wide triangle along best-fit line excluding the circled outlier.
Obtains best-fit gradient k = 30.0 N m⁻¹.
Evaluates m_max = 32.5 N m⁻¹ and m_min = 27.5 N m⁻¹.
Obtains Δk = 2.50 N m⁻¹.
Computes percentage uncertainty = 8.33%.
Obtains intercept uncertainty Δc = 0.350 N.
Identifies a positive vertical intercept as evidence of a constant systematic zero offset.
States outlier lies well outside uncertainty bars of the trend and is circled/excluded from best-fit line.
Notes the raw data point must remain documented with experimental justification rather than silently deleted.

items.stem: Two protons lie on opposite sides of a heavy nucleus at the separation shown by the purple marker. Which statement correctly describes the strong nuclear force between them?
items.workedSolution: Beyond about $3\text{ fm}$ the strong nuclear force becomes negligible, while infinite-range electrostatic repulsion still acts across large nuclei. Therefore option B is correct: negligible beyond the short range of three femtometres.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: negligible beyond the short range of three femtometres.

options.label: A
options.text: At this separation the strong nuclear force is strongly attractive and dominates electrostatic repulsion
options.distractorRationale: Fails to recognise the short ~3 fm cut-off of the strong nuclear force.

options.label: B
options.text: At this separation the strong nuclear force is negligible beyond the short range of three femtometres

options.label: C
options.text: At this separation the strong nuclear force is strongly repulsive pushing the nucleus apart
options.distractorRationale: Repulsion occurs only below 0.5 fm; long-range repulsion in large nuclei is electrostatic.

options.label: D
options.text: At this separation the strong nuclear force follows an inverse-square law like Coulomb's law
options.distractorRationale: Only electromagnetic and gravitational forces have infinite inverse-square range.

items.stem: The resistance–temperature graph shows dashed grey Curve Y and solid blue Curve X. Which feature identifies Curve Y as a normal metal such as copper?
items.workedSolution: A normal metal's resistance decreases smoothly with falling temperature to a non-zero residual value and never drops suddenly to zero at a finite $T_{\text{c}}$. Therefore option D is correct: normal metal resistance decreases smoothly with temperature but never drops suddenly to zero.

markScheme.criterion: Select option D: normal metal resistance decreases smoothly with temperature but never drops suddenly to zero.

options.label: A
options.text: Unlike a superconductor, a normal metal exhibits a sharp vertical cliff down to zero ohms at a finite critical temperature
options.distractorRationale: That abrupt drop at Tc is the defining signature of a superconductor (Curve X), not a normal metal.

options.label: B
options.text: Unlike a superconductor, a normal metal increases in resistance as it is cooled toward absolute zero
options.distractorRationale: Cooling reduces lattice vibration amplitude so metallic resistance falls smoothly (NTC semiconductors rise when cooled).

options.label: C
options.text: Unlike a superconductor, a normal metal has constant resistance completely independent of temperature
options.distractorRationale: Metallic resistance decreases as temperature falls, levelling off at finite residual impurity resistance.

options.label: D
options.text: Unlike a superconductor, a normal metal resistance decreases smoothly with temperature but never drops suddenly to zero

items.stem: A sample initially contains N₀ = 2000 undecayed nuclei with decay constant λ = 0.10 s⁻¹. A spreadsheet models the decay iteratively using ΔN = −λNΔt with fixed time step Δt = 2.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) 1600. (b) 1020. (c) 1100. (d) The iterative step method underestimates the remaining quantity because it applies the steeper starting gradient across the whole finite time interval.

items.stem: For a clamped vibrating metre rule obeying $T = k L^n$, a plot of lg(T / ms) against lg(L / cm) uses a false origin at 0.60. Its best-fit line passes through $(0.70, 0.35)$ and $(1.50, 1.55)$. Find the exponent $n$.
items.workedSolution: Gradient $n = (1.55 - 0.35) / (1.5 - 0.7) = 1.50$. Because the horizontal axis has a false origin, substitute $(0.7, 0.35)$ into $\lg y = n \lg x + \lg k$: $\lg k = -0.700$, giving $k = 10^{\lg k} = 0.200$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly evaluates the exponent $n = 1.50$ without falling for the false-origin intercept trap.

items.stem: Four repeat timings of 20 oscillations for a mass-spring system in Required Practical 7 are 17.8 s, 18.1 s, 14.3 s, and 17.9 s. Discard any anomalous timing and determine the best estimate of the period $T$.
items.workedSolution: Discard the anomalous trial (14.3 s). Mean $T_{20} = (17.8 + 18.1 + 17.9)/3 = 17.9 s$, giving $T = 0.897 s$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines period $T = 0.897 s$.

items.stem: Four repeat timings of 20 oscillations of a simple pendulum in Required Practical 7 are 32.1 s, 31.8 s, 36.8 s, and 32.4 s. Rejecting any anomalous reading, determine the best estimate of the period $T$.
items.workedSolution: Discard the anomalous trial (36.8 s). Mean $T_{20} = (32.1 + 31.8 + 32.4)/3 = 32.1 s$, giving $T = 1.60 s$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines period $T = 1.60 s$.

items.stem: Two metre-rule readings, each with an absolute uncertainty of ±1.0 mm, are used to find extension e = L₂ − L₁. Calculate the absolute uncertainty Δe.
items.workedSolution: When subtracting two measurements, absolute uncertainties add: Δe = ΔL₁ + ΔL₂ = 1.0 + 1.0 = 2.00 mm (whereas percentage uncertainty in the graph gradient is 16.3%).

markScheme.criterion: Adds absolute uncertainties of both scale readings to obtain 2.00 mm.

items.stem: Coordinates (0 s, 2.485) and (48 s, 0.485) lie on a straight-line plot of ln(V / V) against time t. The capacitor discharges across a 40 kΩ resistor.
items.workedSolution: (a) Taking natural logarithms gives a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the reciprocal of the time constant and a vertical intercept equal to the natural logarithm of the initial potential difference. (b) Using the two plotted points, slope m = -0.04167 s⁻¹, so τ = −1/m = 24.00 s ≈ 24.0 s. (c) C = τ/R = 600 μF. (d) Uses all measured data points along a straight line of best fit rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.

markScheme.criterion: Shows taking natural logs produces a linear relation between ln(V) and t.
Identifies gradient = −1/τ and vertical intercept = ln(V₀).
Evaluates negative gradient m = -0.0417 s⁻¹ and uses τ = −1/m.
Correct time constant τ = 24.0 s.
Correct capacitance C = τ / R = 600 μF.
States that it uses all measured data points along a straight line of best fit rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.

parts.prompt: Explain why plotting the natural logarithm of potential difference against time yields a straight line, identifying the physical meaning of its gradient and vertical intercept.
parts.expectedAnswer: From the exponential discharge equation, taking natural logarithms gives a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the reciprocal of the time constant and a vertical intercept equal to the natural logarithm of the initial potential difference.
workingSteps: Take natural logarithms of both sides of the exponential decay equation.
Compare with a linear equation to identify the negative gradient and the vertical intercept.

parts.prompt: Determine the time constant τ of the RC circuit from the gradient of the graph.
workingSteps: Time constant τ = −1 / m = 24.00 s ≈ 24.0 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the capacitance of the capacitor in μF given R = 40 kΩ.
State why determining τ from the gradient of a ln(V) against t graph is more reliable than drawing an initial tangent to a V against t curve.
parts.expectedAnswer: The logarithmic gradient method is more reliable because it uses all measured data points along a straight line of best fit rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.
workingSteps: Drawing a tangent to a curve by eye is subjective and sensitive to noise at a single point, whereas a linear best-fit averages random errors over all readings.

items.stem: Initially 30.0 m from the starting mark, a trolley follows the velocity–time plot below, braking evenly from t = 8.0 s until stopping at t = 12.0 s. Determine its acceleration while braking.
items.workedSolution: Reading the braking slope between t = 8 s and t = 12 s gives a = (0 − 14) / (12 − 8) = -3.50 m s⁻².

items.stem: Shown below is tensile stress versus strain for a rubber strip stretched to 0.4 (linear up to 0.2). Determine the Young's modulus of the material.
items.workedSolution: Over the initial straight line up to ε = 0.2, tensile stress rises to 150 MPa, so E = σ / ε = 150 / 0.2 = 750 MPa.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates initial linear gradient E = 150 / 0.2 = 750 MPa (D).

options.distractorRationale: Evaluates the secant ratio σ_max / ε_max beyond the limit of proportionality rather than the initial linear gradient.

options.label: B

items.stem: For two charged conducting spheres on a top-pan balance, the linear graph records electrostatic force F versus r⁻² up to 100.0 m⁻². The readings follow F = k|Q₁Q₂|r⁻² + F₀, where F₀ is a constant zero offset. Deduce k|Q₁Q₂| from the gradient of the straight line.
items.workedSolution: At r⁻² = 0.0 m⁻², tare offset F₀ = 0.2 N; at r⁻² = 100 m⁻², F = 1.8 N. Gradient = (1.8 − 0.2) / 100 = 0.0160 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts tare offset F₀ = 0.2 N to get (1.8 − 0.2) / 100 = 0.0160 N m² (B).

items.stem: The graph shows the non-linear V–I characteristic for a small filament bulb. Calculate the electrical resistance of the component at a current of 2.0 A.
items.workedSolution: Electrical resistance at an operating point is defined by R = V / I (not the local slope ΔV / ΔI). At I = 2 A, V = 16.5 V, so R = 16.5 / 2 = 8.25 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses static ratio R = V / I = 16.5 / 2 = 8.25 Ω (C).

items.stem: In a fluid-flow experiment, the graph shows the shallowest line of worst fit drawn from 4.0 kPa to 20.0 kPa. Calculate the gradient of this worst-fit line.
items.workedSolution: At x₁ = 4 kPa, y₁ = 12 mL s⁻¹; at x₂ = 20 kPa, y₂ = 56 mL s⁻¹. Worst-fit gradient m_worst = (56 − 12) / (20 − 4) = 2.75 mL s⁻¹ kPa⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δy / Δx = (56 − 12) / (20 − 4) = 2.75 mL s⁻¹ kPa⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: A student plots measurements for a steel spring on a suppressed-origin grid. The line of best fit passes through (3.0 N, 0.2585 m) and (11.0 N, 0.4065 m). Determine the best-fit gradient.
items.workedSolution: Taking the two widely spaced points on the best-fit line gives gradient = (0.4065 − 0.2585) / (11.0 − 3.0) = 0.01850 m N⁻¹ ≈ 0.0185 m N⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates best-fit gradient = 0.0185 m N⁻¹ from Δy / Δx.

items.stem: During a lab run with g = 9.8 m s⁻², a small block moves down a smooth slope (sin θ = 0.4), yielding a v² against s graph between 0.0 m and 1.6 m. Use the graph to calculate its gradient.
items.workedSolution: From v² = u₀² + (2g sin θ)s, the vertical intercept is u₀² = 2.4 m² s⁻² and at s = 1.6 m, v² = 14.944 m² s⁻². Gradient = (14.944 − 2.4) / 1.6 = 2(9.8)(0.4) = 7.84 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept u₀² = 2.4 m² s⁻² (or evaluates 2 × 9.8 × 0.4) to get 7.84 m s⁻² (B).

items.stem: Heating an insulated aluminium block at steady power in Paper 3A yields five points with error bars. The best-fit line links $(2.00, 7.00)$ to $(10.0, 29.4)$, while the steepest and shallowest worst-fit lines give gradients 3.38 °C min⁻¹ and 2.26 °C min⁻¹ and vertical intercepts -0.971 °C and 3.52 °C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Using the large gradient triangle: $m = (29.4 - 7.00) / (10.0 - 2.00) = 2.80 °C min⁻¹$. (b) $\Delta m = \frac{1}{2}(3.38 - 2.26) = 0.561 °C min⁻¹$, giving percentage uncertainty $= 20.0\%$. (c) $\Delta c = \frac{1}{2}(3.52 - -0.971) = 2.24 °C$. (d) Vertical error bars grow proportionally with the dependent variable because percentage uncertainty is constant; a non-zero intercept indicates a systematic error.

markScheme.criterion: Uses large gradient triangle spanning >50% of line.
Best-fit gradient $m = 2.80 °C min⁻¹$.
Calculates half-spread $\Delta m = 0.561 °C min⁻¹$.
Percentage uncertainty $= 20.0\%$.
Applies $\Delta c = \frac{1}{2}(c_{\max} - c_{\min})$.
Absolute intercept uncertainty $\Delta c = 2.24 °C$.
Vertical error bars grow proportionally with the dependent variable because percentage uncertainty is constant
Identifies non-zero vertical intercept as a systematic error (reject random error).

items.stem: A student designs a portable control circuit using the decade-counter timing diagram below. They compare a Johnson decade counter with a 4-bit binary ripple BCD counter.
items.workedSolution: A Johnson decade counter activates one decoded output at a time without extra decoding gates whereas a BCD counter outputs binary weights needing a decoder. Edge triggering prevents race-around during HIGH clock pulses; synchronous Johnson counters avoid asynchronous ripple glitches when driving sequential loads, whereas BCD counters remain compact for binary/7-segment decoding.

markScheme.criterion: Contrasts binary ripple waveforms ($f/2, f/4, f/8$) with sequential single-HIGH decoded pulses of a Johnson decade counter.
Explains that rising/falling edge triggering samples inputs only at clock transitions, preventing uncontrolled race-around toggling.
States that a BCD counter emits compact 4-bit binary-weighted codes suited to numeric decoders.
States that a Johnson counter directly drives ten sequential outputs without external decoding gates.
Identifies asynchronous ripple propagation delay / brief decoding glitches as a limitation of binary ripple counters.
Identifies higher pin count or unsuitability for direct binary arithmetic as a trade-off of Johnson counters.

parts.prompt: Describe how the timing waveforms of a Johnson decade counter differ from those of a 4-bit binary ripple counter, explain why edge triggering is essential in sequential logic, and evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of both counter architectures.
parts.expectedAnswer: In a 4-bit binary ripple counter, $Q_0$ toggles at half the clock frequency, $Q_1$ at one quarter, $Q_2$ at one eighth, and multiple bits switch at the same time on carries, whereas a Johnson decade counter activates one decoded output at a time without extra decoding gates whereas a BCD counter outputs binary weights needing a decoder. Edge triggering ensures each flip-flop samples its D input only at the precise rising (or falling) clock transition rather than transparently throughout a HIGH level, preventing race-around oscillations where the output flips uncontrollably within a single pulse. While a BCD ripple counter needs only four flip-flops and interfaces naturally with arithmetic or numeric display decoders, its asynchronous ripple propagation delay can cause brief decoding glitches; a synchronous Johnson counter eliminates ripple glitches and directly drives ten sequential loads, at the cost of extra pins and needing a separate encoder if binary arithmetic is desired.
workingSteps: L1: Contrast waveforms: binary ripple outputs divide by $2, 4, 8, 16$ with multiple HIGH bits at the same time vs Johnson single-active sequential pulses.
L1: State that both divide a decade cycle frequency by ten.
L2: Explain why edge triggering is vital: prevents continuous toggling/race-around during a wide clock HIGH pulse.
L2: Explain BCD advantages: compact 4-bit binary-weighted format for 7-segment decoders and numerical processing.
L3: Explain Johnson advantages: glitch-free synchronous transitions and direct 1-of-10 decoded outputs without external AND gates.
L3: Note trade-offs (asynchronous ripple propagation delay glitches in ripple BCD vs extra output pins/lack of binary weights in Johnson).

items.stem: The displacement–time graph shows the motion of a remote-controlled car moving in a straight line. Calculate its signed velocity during the return stage between t = 8.0 s and t = 16.0 s.
items.workedSolution: From t = 8 s to t = 16 s, displacement changes from 46 m to 22 m. Velocity v = (22 − 46) / (16 − 8) = -3.00 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: What is the resistivity of the metal? Its I–V line (I on y-axis, V on x-axis) runs from the origin through (8.00 V, 0.800 A) for a uniform metal wire (1.60 m long, area 8.00 × 10⁻⁸ m²).
items.workedSolution: The line has gradient m = ΔI / ΔV = 0.8000 A / 8.000 V = 0.1000 A V⁻¹. Since gradient = 1/R, R = 1/m = 10.00 Ω. Therefore ρ = R A / L = 5.000 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses R = 1 / gradient and ρ = R A / L to obtain 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

items.stem: The graph shows how the force on a light spring varies with compression up to 0.8 m. The compressed spring is released from rest on a frictionless horizontal rail to launch a 0.6 kg glider.
items.workedSolution: (a) k = 92 / 0.8 = 115 N m⁻¹. (b) Elastic energy E_p = ½(92)(0.8) = 36.8 J. (c) Launch speed v = √(2(36.8)/0.6) = 11.1 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies k as the gradient ΔF / Δx.
Obtains k = 115 N m⁻¹.
Uses triangular area ½Fx.
Obtains E_p = 36.8 J.
Equates ½(0.6)v² to stored elastic energy from (b).
Obtains v = 11.1 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: An electrocardiogram (ECG) records tiny millivolt potential changes at the skin surface during each heartbeat. The trace shows the characteristic P, Q, R, S, and T waveform.
items.workedSolution: Reliable ECG acquisition cleans/abrades the skin, applies conducting gel beneath Ag/AgCl electrodes to minimise contact resistance, keeps the patient still to avoid skeletal EMG artefacts, and feeds shielded leads into a high-input-resistance differential amplifier to reject 50 Hz interference and amplify the $\approx 1\text{ mV}$ signal. Physiologically, the trace shows atrial depolarisation (P wave), ventricular depolarisation (QRS complex), and ventricular repolarisation (T wave): the small P wave corresponds to atrial depolarisation, the large sharp QRS spike reflects rapid depolarisation across the thick ventricular walls, and the wider T wave marks gradual ventricular repolarisation.

markScheme.criterion: L1: Describes attaching surface electrodes to cleaned skin with conducting gel to lower contact resistance.
L1: States the patient remains still and relaxed to minimise competing skeletal-muscle (EMG) electrical signals.
L2: Explains use of shielded leads and a high-input-resistance differential amplifier to amplify the ~1 mV signal without loading or 50 Hz mains interference.
L2: Correctly links the P wave to atrial depolarisation spreading from the sinoatrial node prior to atrial contraction.
L3: Links the sharp, high-amplitude QRS complex to rapid ventricular depolarisation through the much larger ventricular muscle mass (following AV delay).
L3: Links the broader T wave to slower ventricular repolarisation restoring resting potential and notes heart rate follows from the R–R time interval.

parts.prompt: Describe the practical principles used to obtain a reliable surface ECG trace and explain the physical origin of each major feature (P wave, QRS complex, and T wave) of a normal waveform.
parts.expectedAnswer: A clean ECG uses cleaned skin, conducting gel, non-polarising electrodes, shielded leads, a relaxed stationary patient, and a high-input-resistance differential amplifier (~1000 gain) to detect millivolt cardiac potentials while rejecting mains and muscle noise. The waveform reflects atrial depolarisation (P wave), ventricular depolarisation (QRS complex), and ventricular repolarisation (T wave), with the large QRS amplitude caused by thick ventricular walls and the broader T wave by slower recovery.
workingSteps: Detail skin preparation, conducting gel, electrode attachment, patient stillness, shielded cables, and high-input-resistance differential amplification.
Explain P wave as atrial depolarisation triggered by the sinoatrial node.
Explain QRS complex as rapid ventricular depolarisation across thick ventricular muscle (large ~1 mV spike) after AV-node delay.
Explain T wave as slower ventricular repolarisation returning cells to resting potential, and note heart rate equals $60 / T_{\text{RR}}$.

items.stem: For a cable car along a straight slope, velocity against time is plotted below. Take uphill motion as positive. What total distance does it travel over 10.0 s?
items.workedSolution: Splitting the graph at the zero crossing at t = 7 s. Forward area (0 to 7 s) = ½(2)(6) + (2)(6) + ½(3)(6) = 27.0 m. Reverse area magnitude (7 s to 10 s) = ½(1)(2) + (2)(2) = 5.00 m. Total distance = 27.0 + 5.00 = 32.0 m.

markScheme.criterion: Sums unsigned positive (27.0 m) and negative (5.00 m) velocity–time areas to obtain 32.0 m (A).

items.stem: What is the momentum at t = 1.6 s of a 1.5 kg glider starting at 4.5 kg m s⁻¹ under the 1.6 s forward F–t graph shown?
items.workedSolution: Impulse Δp = ½(1.6 + 0.8)(40) = 48.0 N s. Final momentum p_f = p₀ + Δp = 4.5 + 48.0 = 52.5 kg m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Adds impulse (48.0 N s) to p₀ = 4.5 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 52.5 kg m s⁻¹ (C).

workingSteps: Recall that static resistance at a point is R = V / I (not the inverse of the local tangent).
Substitute V = 8.000 V and I = 0.8000 A to obtain R = 10.00 Ω ≈ 10.0 Ω.

parts.prompt: Describe the circuit arrangement and experimental procedure used to obtain a complete I–V characteristic safely across positive and negative potential differences.
parts.expectedAnswer: To obtain the full characteristic safely, connect a potential divider with a series protective resistor, an ammeter in series, and a voltmeter in parallel across the component, and reverse the supply connections for negative readings.
workingSteps: Use a potential divider to vary potential difference smoothly from zero while limiting excessive current with a protective resistor.
Measure current with a series ammeter, potential difference with a parallel voltmeter, and reverse the supply leads for negative polarity.

parts.prompt: Explain the physical shape of the I–V characteristic in terms of charge carriers and resistance.
parts.expectedAnswer: The curve shows that the component resistance decreases as temperature increases because more charge carriers are released so the curve becomes steeper.
workingSteps: Link the changing ratio of potential difference to current directly to the microscopic conduction mechanism.

items.stem: Plotted below is the charge Q against potential difference V as a capacitor is charged from zero to Q = 7.50 mC and V = 15.0 V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Capacitance is the charge stored per unit potential difference across the plates. (b) C = Q / V = 500 μF. (c) Triangular area E = ½ Q V = 0.05625 J ≈ 0.0562 J.

markScheme.criterion: States charge stored per unit potential difference across the plates.
Correct capacitance 500 μF.
Recognises triangular area E = ½ Q V and converts mC to C.
Correct stored energy 0.0562 J.

items.stem: Data below give the eastward acceleration of a glider for 10.0 s. Its eastward velocity starts at 8.0 m s⁻¹. Deduce the final eastward velocity at t = 10.0 s.
items.workedSolution: Positive a–t area (0 to 5 s) = 28.0 m s⁻¹; negative area magnitude (5 s to 10 s) = 16.0 m s⁻¹. Net Δv = 28.0 − 16.0 = 12.0 m s⁻¹. Final velocity = 8 + (12.0) = 20.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Combines net signed area (12.0 m s⁻¹) with u₀ = 8 m s⁻¹ to obtain 20.0 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: With sin θ = 0.2 and g = 9.81 m s⁻², a steel ball accelerates along a smooth inclined track. Speed v is logged to plot v² against s between 0.0 m and 2.0 m. Find the gradient of the plotted line.
items.workedSolution: From v² = u₀² + (2g sin θ)s, the vertical intercept is u₀² = 2.2 m² s⁻² and at s = 2 m, v² = 10.048 m² s⁻². Gradient = (10.048 − 2.2) / 2 = 2(9.81)(0.2) = 3.92 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept u₀² = 2.2 m² s⁻² (or evaluates 2 × 9.81 × 0.2) to get 3.92 m s⁻² (D).

items.stem: Force readings over 14.0 m are graphed below for a toy car of mass 3.2 kg, moving forward at 4.0 m s⁻¹ at x = 0.0 m. Determine the speed of the object when x = 14.0 m.
items.workedSolution: The positive area (0 to 11 m) = ½(11 + 6)(16) = 136 J. Resistive work (11 m to 14 m) = −½(3)(4) = −6.00 J. Net work W = 130 J. From ½mv² = ½mu₀² + W, v = √(4² + 2 × 130 / 3.2) = 9.86 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds net work W = 130 J and v = √(4² + 2W/3.2) = 9.86 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: A 0.8 kg block sliding on a frictionless table has its linear momentum graphed below. A steady force acts from t = 1.0 s to t = 5.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Force is the momentum gradient: F = Δp / Δt = (7.2 − 1.6) / (5 − 1) = 1.40 N. (b) Work done equals ΔE_k, so W = ΔE_k = (7.2² − 1.6²) / (2 × 0.8) = 30.8 J.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies resultant force as gradient Δp / Δt of the p–t graph.
Obtains F = 1.40 N.
Relates net work to ΔE_k = (p₂² − p₁²) / (2m).
Substitutes p₁ = 1.6 kg m s⁻¹, p₂ = 7.2 kg m s⁻¹, and m = 0.8 kg.
Obtains W = 30.8 J.

items.stem: Over L / A up to 80.0 m⁻¹, calculate resistivity ρ for a ceramic heating rod using the straight line shown.
items.workedSolution: Matching R = ρ(L / A) + R₀ with y = mx + c shows that resistivity ρ equals ΔR / Δ(L / A) = (25 − 5) / 80 = 0.250 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept R₀ = 5 Ω to obtain ρ = (25 − 5) / 80 = 0.250 Ω m (A).

items.stem: A dry cell is tested over current I from zero to 2.0 A, giving the downward linear V–I graph below. The line obeys V = ε − Ir. Determine the signed slope of the V–I line.
items.workedSolution: At I = 0.0 A, V = ε = 7 V; at I = 2 A, V = 3.4 V. Gradient = (3.4 − 7) / 2 = -1.80 V A⁻¹ (equal to −r).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates (3.4 − 7) / 2 = -1.80 V A⁻¹ (A).
