items.stem: A helium-4 nucleus contains two protons and two neutrons within a radius of about $2\text{ fm}$. The graph shows how the strong nuclear force varies with nucleon separation.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 (5–6 marks): Names electrostatic repulsion between protons and strong nuclear force between all nucleons (gravity negligible); states that the strong nuclear force is repulsive below zero point five fm and attractive up to three fm balancing electrostatic proton repulsion; identifies virtual photons (EM) and pions/gluons (strong) as exchange particles (reject 'force mediator') and explains equilibrium separation where net force balances.

markScheme.criterion: L1 (Area 1): Identifies repulsive electromagnetic/electrostatic force acting between protons and attractive strong nuclear force acting between nucleons (p–p, p–n, n–n).
L1 (Area 1): Notes that gravitational attraction between nucleons is negligible on nuclear scales.
L2 (Area 2): States the strong nuclear force is strongly repulsive at very short separations below ~0.5 fm, preventing the nucleus from collapsing.
L2 (Area 2): States the strong nuclear force is attractive between ~0.5 fm and ~3 fm (short range, negligible beyond ~3 fm), overcoming electrostatic repulsion.
L3 (Area 3): Names the exchange particles correctly: virtual photon for electromagnetic interaction and pion (condone gluon) for the strong interaction (reject 'force mediator').
L3 (Area 3): Logically links all three areas to explain equilibrium nucleon separation where resultant force balances so the nucleus neither collapses nor flies apart.

parts.prompt: Explain how the fundamental forces acting between nucleons keep a stable nucleus together without collapsing or flying apart. In your answer you should: identify the forces acting, describe how the strong nuclear force varies with separation, and name the exchange particles responsible.
parts.expectedAnswer: Inside a nucleus, protons experience long-range repulsive electromagnetic (electrostatic) forces mediated by virtual photons, while gravitational attraction between nucleons is negligible. All nucleons (protons and neutrons) experience the strong nuclear force, mediated by pions between nucleons (condone gluons between quarks). The strong nuclear force is repulsive below zero point five fm and attractive up to three fm balancing electrostatic proton repulsion: below 0.5 fm repulsion prevents nuclear collapse, between 0.5 fm and 3 fm strong attraction overcomes electrostatic repulsion, and at equilibrium separation the net force on nucleons is zero so the nucleus stays stable.
workingSteps: Area 1 (L1): Identify electrostatic proton repulsion, strong nuclear force between nucleons, and negligible gravity.
Area 2 (L2): Specify SNF profile: repulsive below 0.5 fm (prevents collapse), attractive from 0.5 fm to ~3 fm (overcomes EM repulsion), negligible beyond ~3 fm.
Area 3 (L3): Name exchange particles (virtual photon for EM; pion — condone gluon — for strong) and link balance of forces at equilibrium separation to nuclear stability.

items.stem: A mercury wire has critical temperature $T_{\text{c}} = 4.20\text{ K}$ and normal resistance $0.150\,\Omega$ above $T_{\text{c}}$. The cooling vessel warms to $5.00\text{ K}$ while a constant $40.0\text{ A}$ current flows through it.
items.workedSolution: (a) Zero electrical resistance at or below the critical temperature; operates in normal resistive state above the critical temperature. (b) $P = I^2R = 240 W$. (c) Expensive low-temperature cooling is required to stay below the critical temperature.

markScheme.criterion: Zero electrical resistance / resistivity at or below critical temperature $T_{\text{c}}$.
Correctly identify normal resistive state above the critical temperature.
Substitute current and normal resistance into $P = I^2R$.
Power $= 240 W$.
Expensive / technically difficult low-temperature cooling required below $T_{\text{c}}$.

parts.prompt: Define the critical temperature $T_{\text{c}}$ of a superconductor and state whether this conductor is superconducting at its operating temperature.
parts.expectedAnswer: Critical temperature is the transition temperature at or below which a superconductor has zero electrical resistance; at $5\text{ K}$ it is in the normal resistive state above the critical temperature.
workingSteps: Define Tc as transition to exact zero resistance (at or below Tc).
Compare operating temperature 5 K against Tc = 4.2 K.

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal power dissipated in the filament at $5.00\text{ K}$ and explain why cooling below $4.20\text{ K}$ eliminates this loss.
workingSteps: Apply $P = I^2R = 40^2 \times 0.15 = 240 W$.

parts.prompt: State one major practical limitation preventing widespread room-temperature use of superconducting power cables.
parts.expectedAnswer: A major limitation is that expensive low-temperature cooling is required to stay below the critical temperature.
workingSteps: State cost and difficulty of maintaining low-temperature cooling below Tc.

items.stem: The excess temperature $\Delta\theta$ of a cooling copper sphere obeys $\Delta\theta = A e^{-\lambda t}$. Plotting ln(Δθ / °C) against t / s with a false origin at $t = 20$ s gives a best-fit line through $(30, 3.60)$ and $(110, 2.00)$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Taking natural logarithms gives ln y = ln A − λt, and the false origin means a point on the line must be substituted rather than reading the vertical axis crossing. (b) $\lambda = -(2 - 3.6) / (110 - 30) = 0.0200 s⁻¹$. (c) $\ln A = 4.20$, so $A = 66.7$. (d) $T_{1/2} = \ln 2 / \lambda = 34.7 s$.

markScheme.criterion: States $\ln y = \ln A - \lambda t$ with gradient $-\lambda$.
Uses point substitution instead of reading vertical axis at false origin.
Calculates magnitude of negative gradient.
Decay constant $\lambda = 0.0200 s⁻¹$.
Computes $\ln A = y_1 + \lambda t_1$ and applies $e^{\ln A}$.
Initial value $A = 66.7$.
Applies $T_{1/2} = \ln 2 / \lambda$.
Half-time $T_{1/2} = 34.7 s$.

items.stem: Drag force $F$ and terminal speed $v$ of falling paper cones satisfy $F = k v^n$. With a false origin at 0.40, a graph of lg(F / mN) against lg(v / m s⁻¹) has a best-fit line through $(0.50, 0.60)$ and $(1.30, 2.04)$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Taking base ten logarithms gives lg y = n lg x + lg k, and a false origin means a point on the line must be substituted to find the intercept. (b) $n = (2.04 - 0.6) / (1.3 - 0.5) = 1.80$. (c) $\lg k = 0.6 - (1.80)(0.5) = -0.300$. (d) $k = 10^{-0.300} = 0.501$.

markScheme.criterion: Writes $\lg y = n \lg x + \lg k$ (reject $\lg x^n$ unexpanded).
Explains false origin requires substituting a point $(x_1, y_1)$ on the line.
Computes gradient from wide pair of points on the line.
Exponent $n = 1.80$.
Substitutes $(x_1, y_1)$ and $n$ into $\lg k = y_1 - n x_1$.
True intercept $\lg k = -0.300$.
Evaluates base-10 antilogarithm $k = 10^{\lg k}$.
Constant $k = 0.501$.

items.stem: For a vertical mass-spring oscillator in Required Practical 7, a graph of $T^2$ against mass $m$ over six masses has gradient 1.94 s² kg⁻¹. Four repeat timings of 20 oscillations are 21.4 s, 21.1 s, 25.2 s, and 21.6 s (reaction-time uncertainty $\pm 0.2$ s per timing).
items.workedSolution: (a) Discard 25.2 s; $T = 1.07 s$. (b) $\%\Delta T = 0.936\%$. (c) $k$ $= 4\pi^2 / 1.94 = 20.3 N m⁻¹$. (d) Place the fiducial marker at the equilibrium position where speed is maximum, discard anomalous timings before averaging, and time many oscillations to reduce reaction-time uncertainty.

Mean period $T = 1.07 s$.
Uses $\Delta T_{20} / T_{20} \times 100\%$.

Equates gradient to $4\pi^2 / k$.
Fiducial marker at equilibrium where oscillator moves fastest (minimising transit-time uncertainty).
Timing 20 oscillations divides fixed human reaction-time error by 20.

items.stem: Coordinates (0 s, 2.303) and (40 s, 0.303) lie on the straight-line ln(V / V) against t graph of an RC discharge circuit with R = 40 kΩ. Find the capacitance.
items.workedSolution: The line has gradient m = (0.303 − 2.303) / (40 − 0) = -0.05000 s⁻¹. Time constant τ = −1/m = 20.00 s. Capacitance C = τ / R = 20.00 s / (40 × 10³ Ω) = 500 μF.

markScheme.criterion: Extracts linearized graph parameters accurately to obtain 500 μF.

items.stem: Beginning at rest 50.0 m past the base marker at t = 0.0 s, a small rover completes the 15.0 s velocity–time graph below, braking evenly from t = 9.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Using the area of a trapezium: Δx = ½(15 + 6)(22) = 231 m. (b) Final distance from the reference mark = 50 + 231 = 281 m. (c) Mean speed = 231 / 15 = 15.4 m s⁻¹. (d) Braking acceleration = (0 − 22) / (15 − 9) = -3.67 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Identifies distance travelled as the area under the v–t trapezium.
Obtains Δx = 231 m.
Adds 50 m offset to obtain 281 m.
Divides distance travelled from (a) by 15 s.
Obtains mean speed = 15.4 m s⁻¹.
Obtains braking acceleration = -3.67 m s⁻².

parts.prompt: Calculate the distance travelled during the 15.0 s journey.
workingSteps: Distance equals the trapezium area under the v–t curve.

parts.prompt: Hence state its final distance from the base marker at t = 15.0 s.
Determine the mean speed over the 15.0 s run.
workingSteps: v_mean = Δx / t_total = 231 / 15 = 15.4 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the acceleration between t = 9.0 s and t = 15.0 s.

items.stem: From zero up to strain 0.4, the stress–strain curve for a plastic strip is linear. The full loading curve extends to tensile strain 0.8.
items.workedSolution: (a) Over the initial linear stretch, Young's modulus E = 170 / 0.4 = 425 MPa. (b) Energy per unit volume = ½(0.4)(170) + ½(170 + 240)(0.4) = 116 MJ m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates initial gradient σ / ε up to ε = 0.4.
Obtains E = 425 MPa.
Identifies work per unit volume as total area under the σ–ε graph.
Splits area into initial triangle plus upper trapezium.
Obtains 116 MJ m⁻³.

parts.prompt: Determine the Young's modulus of the sample over the proportional region (0.0 to 0.4).
workingSteps: Read σ = 170 MPa at ε = 0.4.

parts.prompt: Calculate the work done per unit volume in stretching the sample from zero strain to 0.8.
workingSteps: Area from 0 to 0.4 = ½(0.4)(170) = 34.0 MJ m⁻³.
Area from 0.4 to 0.8 = ½(170 + 240)(0.4) = 82.0 MJ m⁻³; total = 116 MJ m⁻³.

items.stem: For two light charged spheres above an electronic balance, measurements of electrostatic force F are plotted against r⁻² up to 80.0 m⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) At r⁻² = 0, systematic tare offset F₀ = 0.400 N. (b) Gradient = (2.4 − 0.4) / 80 = 0.0250 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Reads intercept F₀ = 0.400 N.
Evaluates ΔF = 2.4 − 0.4 using intercept from (a).
Divides ΔF by 80 m⁻² and states correct unit N m².
Obtains 0.0250 N m².

parts.prompt: State the systematic tare offset F₀ of the balance as separation r approaches infinity.
workingSteps: As r → ∞, r⁻² → 0, where the vertical intercept gives F₀ = 0.400 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the gradient k|Q₁Q₂| of the linearized plot over 0.0 m⁻² to 80.0 m⁻².
workingSteps: Read F = 2.4 N at r⁻² = 80 m⁻².

items.stem: A student uses a variable DC supply, an ammeter, and a voltmeter to test an NTC thermistor. The graph shows the potential difference V against current I up to 1.2 A.
items.workedSolution: (a) At I = 1.2 A, V = 8.40 V. (b) Static resistance R = V / I = 8.4 / 1.2 = 7.00 Ω (the upper segment gradient 9.50 Ω is ΔV / ΔI, not R).

markScheme.criterion: Reads V = 8.40 V at I = 1.2 A.
Selects R = V / I rather than local segment gradient ΔV / ΔI.
Substitutes V = 8.4 V and I = 1.2 A.
Obtains R = 7.00 Ω.

items.stem: Shown below is a suppressed-origin graph for a steel spring with ±0.014 m vertical error bars. The best-fit line connects (9.0 N, 0.4802 m) and (27.0 N, 0.7106 m). The shallowest acceptable line through all error bars has gradient 0.01105 m N⁻¹. Micrometer readings give a wire diameter of d = 0.92 ± 0.024 mm.
items.workedSolution: (a) Best-fit gradient m_best = (0.7106 − 0.4802) / (27.0 − 9.0) = 0.01280 m N⁻¹ ≈ 0.0128 m N⁻¹. (b) Δm = |0.01105 − 0.01280| = 1.75 × 10⁻³ m N⁻¹. (c) A suppressed origin expands the plotted data to fill more than half of the grid improving reading precision. (d) %Δm = 13.67%, %ΔA = 2 × %Δd = 5.217%, total = 18.89% ≈ 18.9%.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly substitutes large-triangle coordinates (0.7106 − 0.4802) / (27.0 − 9.0).
Obtains best-fit gradient = 0.0128 m N⁻¹ with correct compound SI unit.
Calculates Δm = |m_worst − m_best| = 1.75 × 10⁻³ m N⁻¹.
States that a false origin expands the plotted data to fill more than half of the grid improving reading precision.
Evaluates %Δm = 13.7% and %ΔA = 2 × %Δd = 5.22%.
Sums percentage uncertainties to obtain 18.9%.

items.stem: Stretching a metal spring with slotted masses in Paper 3A gives a best-fit gradient of 18.5 N m⁻¹. Across all error bars, the steepest and shallowest worst-fit gradients are 21.8 N m⁻¹ and 15.5 N m⁻¹. Find the percentage uncertainty in the gradient.
items.workedSolution: First calculate the half-spread $\Delta m = \frac{1}{2}(m_{\max} - m_{\min}) = \frac{1}{2}(21.8 - 15.5) = 3.18 N m⁻¹$. Then percentage uncertainty $= (\Delta m / m_{\mathrm{best}}) \times 100\% = 17.2\%$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly applies half-spread rule to obtain 17.2% (3 sf).

items.stem: A 4-stage binary ripple counter uses rising-edge D-type flip-flops clocked at 3200 Hz. Calculate the output frequency at the most significant bit $Q_3$.
items.workedSolution: Each D-type stage halves the frequency: $f_{\mathrm{out}} = \frac{f_{\mathrm{clk}}}{2^n} = \frac{3200}{2^4} = \frac{3200}{16} = 200 Hz$.

markScheme.criterion: Output frequency at $Q_3$ equals 200 Hz.

items.stem: The displacement–time graph shows the motion of a trolley moving along a straight track over 16.0 s. It moves back toward the start between t = 10.0 s and t = 16.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Maximum displacement at the plateau = 56.0 m. (b) Return-stage velocity = (28 − 56) / (16 − 10) = -4.67 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Reads plateau displacement = 56.0 m.
Uses gradient formula Δs / Δt = (28 − 56) / (16 − 10).
Retains negative sign for motion back toward the origin.
Obtains -4.67 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: In a resistivity practical, a uniform metal wire gives a straight I–V graph through the origin up to V = 8.00 V, I = 1.00 A. The sample measures 1.60 m with area 6.40 × 10⁻⁸ m².
items.workedSolution: (a) Resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area. (b) Gradient = 0.1250 A V⁻¹, so R = 1 / gradient = 8.00 Ω. (c) ρ = RA/L = 3.200 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 3.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: States resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area.
Correctly specifies all quantities (or notes constant temperature / material property).
Computes large-triangle gradient m = ΔI/ΔV = 0.125 A V⁻¹ and takes its reciprocal R = 1/m.
Correct wire resistance R = 8.00 Ω.
Substitutes R, A, and L correctly into ρ = RA/L.
Correct resistivity 3.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m with unit Ω m.

parts.prompt: Define the electrical resistivity of a material.
parts.expectedAnswer: Electrical resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area, where resistance, cross-sectional area, and length are measured for a uniform sample at constant temperature.
workingSteps: State the definition in terms of a conductor of unit length and unit cross-sectional area.
Identify that resistivity is an intrinsic property of the material at constant temperature.

parts.prompt: Determine the resistance of the wire from the gradient of the I–V line of best fit using a large triangle.
workingSteps: Because I is on the vertical axis, R = 1 / m = 8.000 Ω ≈ 8.00 Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resistivity of the alloy, stating the appropriate SI unit.
workingSteps: Evaluate ρ = 3.200 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 3.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

items.stem: The graph shows how the applied force on a steel spring varies with extension up to 0.5 m. The spring obeys Hooke's law. Determine the spring constant k.
items.workedSolution: Spring constant k = gradient ΔF / Δx = 30 / 0.5 = 60.0 N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gradient k = 30 / 0.5 = 60.0 N m⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: A student uses a Geiger–Müller tube to measure the background-corrected count rate C of a radioactive sample over 80.0 s. The graph shows ln(C / s⁻¹) plotted against time t.
items.workedSolution: (a) Vertical intercept at t = 0 is ln(C₀ / s⁻¹) = 8.80. (b) Gradient = (2.4 − 8.8) / 80 = -0.0800 s⁻¹ (which equals −λ).

markScheme.criterion: Reads vertical intercept = 8.80.

Obtains gradient = -0.0800 s⁻¹.

items.stem: During light exercise on a clinical treadmill, a volunteer's ECG trace records an R–R interval of $0.625\text{ s}$. Calculate the cardiac beat frequency in hertz.
items.workedSolution: Frequency $f = \frac{1}{T_{\text{RR}}} = \frac{1}{0.625\text{ s}} = 1.60 Hz$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 1.60 Hz.

options.distractorRationale: Divides by twice the R–R period.

items.stem: A trolley along a straight track travels between t = 0.0 s and t = 12.0 s according to the velocity–time graph below. Forward velocity is positive. Reversal occurs during braking from t = 6.0 s to t = 10.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Direction reverses at t = 9 s. Positive area = 108 m and unsigned negative area = 15.0 m, giving total distance = 123 m. (b) Net displacement = 108 − 15.0 = 93.0 m; average velocity = 93.0 / 12 = 7.75 m s⁻¹. (c) Acceleration = (−6 − 18) / (10 − 6) = -6.00 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Finds zero-crossing t = 9 s and evaluates both unsigned areas (108 m and 15.0 m).
Obtains total distance = 123 m.
Subtracts areas for net displacement (93.0 m) and divides by 12 s.
Obtains average velocity = 7.75 m s⁻¹.
Obtains acceleration = -6.00 m s⁻² including negative sign.

items.stem: Over a 2.5 s interval, a forward force pushes a glider of mass 3.0 kg along a straight path. Its momentum at t = 0.0 s starts at 9.0 kg m s⁻¹, as graphed below.
items.workedSolution: (a) Area under the F–t trapezium gives impulse J = ½(2.5 + 1.5)(46) = 92.0 N s. (b) Final momentum p_f = 9 + 92.0 = 101 kg m s⁻¹. (c) Speed increase Δv = 92.0 / 3 = 30.7 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes impulse from the trapezium area under the F–t curve.
Obtains J = 92.0 N s.
Adds 9 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 101 kg m s⁻¹.
Divides impulse from (a) by 3 kg.
Obtains Δv = 30.7 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Passing through the origin, the straight Q–V graph for a capacitor ends at Q = 8.00 mC when V = 20.0 V. Find the capacitance.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly converts mC to C and obtains 400 μF.

items.stem: How are stiffness and strength distinguished on a tensile stress–strain graph?
items.workedSolution: Gradient measures stiffness (Young modulus $E$), peak stress measures ultimate tensile strength (UTS), and total area to fracture measures toughness. Therefore option C is correct: gradient measures stiffness Young modulus whereas peak stress measures ultimate tensile strength.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: gradient measures stiffness Young modulus whereas peak stress measures ultimate tensile strength.

options.label: A
options.text: On a stress–strain graph, the total area to fracture measures stiffness whereas the initial gradient measures strength
options.distractorRationale: Total area to fracture measures toughness (energy absorbed per unit volume), not stiffness.

options.label: B
options.text: On a stress–strain graph, thicker wires of the same metal show a steeper gradient and higher Young modulus
options.distractorRationale: Classic AQA trap! Stress and strain normalise for area and length, so Young modulus E is an intrinsic material constant independent of dimensions.

options.label: C
options.text: On a stress–strain graph, the gradient measures stiffness Young modulus whereas peak stress measures ultimate tensile strength

options.label: D
options.text: On a stress–strain graph, the strain at fracture measures stiffness while the elastic limit measures toughness
options.distractorRationale: Fracture strain indicates ductility, not stiffness.

items.stem: An accelerometer records the forward acceleration of a small cart for 20.0 s. Starting at t = 0.0 s, its velocity is 17.0 m s⁻¹ forward.
items.workedSolution: (a) Maximum speed is reached as acceleration drops through zero at t = 10.0 s. (b) Positive area = 48.0 m s⁻¹, giving v_max = 17 + 48.0 = 65.0 m s⁻¹. (c) Negative area magnitude = 15.0 m s⁻¹, so v_final = 65.0 − 15.0 = 50.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: States t = 10.0 s.
Evaluates positive area up to 10 s (48.0 m s⁻¹) and adds u₀ = 17 m s⁻¹.
Obtains v_max = 65.0 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts negative area (15.0 m s⁻¹) from v_max.
Obtains final velocity = 50.0 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Over an 8.0 m distance, a variable resultant force acts on a toy car of mass 1.6 kg, whose speed at x = 0.0 m is 4.5 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Combining forward and resistive areas gives W = 54.0 − 4.00 = 50.0 J. (b) v = √(4.5² + 2(50.0)/1.6) = 9.10 m s⁻¹. (c) Mean force = 50.0 / 8 = 6.25 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates positive (54.0 J) and negative (−4.00 J) areas.
Obtains net work W = 50.0 J.
Uses ½mv² = ½(1.6)(4.5²) + W.
Obtains v = 9.10 m s⁻¹.
Divides net work by 8 m to get 6.25 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the net work done on the 1.6 kg object between x = 0.0 m and x = 8.0 m.
workingSteps: Positive area (0 to 6 m) = ½(6 + 3)(12) = 54.0 J; negative area (6 m to 8 m) = −½(2)(4) = −4.00 J.

parts.prompt: Calculate its speed at x = 8.0 m.
State the mean resultant force over the 8.0 m displacement.

items.stem: For a small cart of mass 4.0 kg on a smooth level track, linear momentum varies with time as plotted below. Calculate the total work done on the object between t = 4.0 s and t = 8.0 s.
items.workedSolution: Since kinetic energy satisfies E_k = p² / (2m), net work equals W = ΔE_k = (28² − 8²) / (2 × 4) = 90.0 J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies W = (p₂² − p₁²) / (2m) = (28² − 8²) / (8) = 90.0 J (C).

items.stem: A class measures resistance R of a column of salt solution for varying L / A between 0.0 m⁻¹ and 400.0 m⁻¹, obtaining the graph below.
items.workedSolution: (a) The y-intercept equals lead resistance R₀ = 10.0 Ω. (b) Computing rise over run yields ρ = (46 − 10) / 400 = 0.0900 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: States R₀ = 10.0 Ω.
Identifies ρ with the gradient ΔR / Δ(L / A).
Subtracts R₀ = 10 Ω from 46 Ω before dividing by 400 m⁻¹.
Obtains ρ = 0.0900 Ω m.

workingSteps: At L / A = 0.0 m⁻¹, the vertical intercept gives R₀ = 10.0 Ω.

parts.prompt: Determine the resistivity ρ of a column of salt solution from the graph.
workingSteps: From R = ρ(L / A) + R₀, ρ equals the gradient ΔR / Δ(L / A).

items.stem: For a rechargeable battery connected to a variable load, the graph tracks terminal potential difference V versus current I over the current range 0.0 A to 5.0 A.
items.workedSolution: (a) Open-circuit intercept gives ε = 16.0 V. (b) Gradient = (7 − 16) / 5 = -1.80 V A⁻¹. (c) Mean terminal p.d. = ½(16 + 7) = 11.5 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reads ε = 16.0 V at I = 0.
Evaluates (7 − 16) / 5 including negative sign.
Obtains -1.80 V A⁻¹.
Uses ½(16 + 7) or area divided by 5 A.
Obtains 11.5 V.

Determine the signed gradient of the V–I graph between 0.0 A and 5.0 A.
workingSteps: At I = 5 A, V = 7 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the mean terminal potential difference across the 0.0 A to 5.0 A interval.

items.stem: A temperature sensor records the excess temperature Δθ of cooling water above room temperature, following Δθ = Δθ₀ e^(−λt). The graph plots ln(Δθ / K) against time t from (0 s, 3.60 ± 0.10) to (80 s, 2.00 ± 0.10).
items.workedSolution: (a) λ = 0.0200 s⁻¹. (b) Δλ = 2.50 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. (c) Δθ₀ = 36.6 K. (d) Only the independent variable is changed while all other variables are kept constant as control variables so changes in the dependent variable are valid. Using a calibrated digital sensor or high-frame-rate video tracker reduces human reaction-time random uncertainty and allows rapid sampling, while calibration removes any constant systematic zero offset.

markScheme.criterion: Takes natural log: ln(Δθ) = −λt + ln(Δθ₀), so λ = −gradient.
Obtains λ = 0.0200 s⁻¹.
Determines extreme slopes −0.0175 s⁻¹ and −0.0225 s⁻¹.
Obtains Δλ = 2.50 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹.
Evaluates Δθ₀ = e^(3.60) = 36.6 K.
Identifies time as IV, excess temperature as DV, and room temperature/water mass as control variables.
Notes digital logging removes parallax/reaction timing scatter and supports rapid sampling.
Notes sensor calibration is essential to eliminate systematic zero offset.

parts.prompt: Determine the cooling decay constant λ from the gradient of the semi-log best-fit line.
Calculate the absolute uncertainty Δλ in the decay constant using the extreme gradient lines.
workingSteps: Δλ = |m_max − m_min| / 2 = 2.50 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹

parts.prompt: Determine the initial excess temperature Δθ₀ at t = 0 s from the vertical intercept.
Explain the experimental role of independent, dependent, and control variables (such as water mass and draughts) and outline why a calibrated digital sensor improves data quality.
parts.expectedAnswer: Only the independent variable is changed while all other variables are kept constant as control variables so changes in the dependent variable are valid. In addition, using a calibrated digital sensor or high-frame-rate video tracker reduces human reaction-time random uncertainty and allows rapid sampling, while calibration removes any constant systematic zero offset.

items.stem: The graph shows how the strong nuclear force varies with nucleon separation. At what approximate separation $r_0$ does the force change from repulsive to attractive?
items.workedSolution: The strong nuclear force curve crosses the horizontal zero-force axis from repulsive (+) to attractive (−) at $r_0 = 0.500\text{ fm}$. Option B (0.500 fm) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Equilibrium zero-force separation $0.500\text{ fm}$ (0.500 fm, option B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Gives the outer cut-off range (~3 fm) instead of the repulsive-to-attractive zero-force crossing.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Gives the separation of peak attraction rather than the zero-crossing equilibrium point.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Reads the right-hand axis endpoint rather than the curve intercept.

items.stem: Magnesium diboride becomes superconducting at a critical temperature of $T_{\text{c}} = 39.0\text{ K}$. A sample starts at room temperature ($293\text{ K}$). Calculate the temperature drop needed to reach $T_{\text{c}}$.
items.workedSolution: $\Delta T = 293 - 39.0 = 254 K$. Option B (254 K) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Temperature drop $= 254 K$ (254 K, option B).

items.stem: A capacitor storing initial charge Q₀ = 400 μC discharges through a resistor such that ΔQ/Δt = −(0.20 s⁻¹)Q. A spreadsheet models the discharge using fixed steps Δt = 1.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) τ = 5.00 s. (b) 320 μC. (c) 205 μC. (d) Reducing the time step makes the iterative model closer to the true exponential curve because the rate is updated more often as the curve becomes less steep.

markScheme.criterion: Finds τ = RC = 5.00 s.
Obtains Q(1.0 s) = 320 μC.
Calculates Q(2.0 s) = 256 μC with updated ΔQ = −64 μC.
Calculates third-step loss ΔQ = −51.2 μC.
Obtains Q(3.0 s) = 205 μC.
States accuracy improves and modelled values move up closer to exact exponential.
Explains current/rate is updated more frequently as the discharge curve flattens.

items.stem: For a cooling copper sphere obeying $\Delta\theta = A e^{-\lambda t}$ in Paper 3A, a semi-log plot of ln(Δθ / °C) against t / s starts at a false origin of $t = 20$ s. Its line passes through $(30, 3.60)$ and $(110, 2.00)$. Determine the decay constant $\lambda$.
items.workedSolution: Gradient $-\lambda = (2 - 3.6) / (110 - 30) = -0.0200 s⁻¹$. Substituting $(30, 3.6)$ gives $\ln A = 4.20$, so $A = e^{\ln A} = 66.7$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly evaluates the decay constant $\lambda = 0.0200 s⁻¹$ without falling for the false-origin intercept trap.

items.stem: Falling paper cones obey $F = k v^n$. On a log-log plot of lg(F / mN) against lg(v / m s⁻¹) with a false origin at $x_{\min} = 0.40$, the best-fit line passes through $(0.50, 0.60)$ and $(1.30, 2.04)$. Calculate the constant $k$.
items.workedSolution: Gradient $n = (2.04 - 0.6) / (1.3 - 0.5) = 1.80$. Because the horizontal axis has a false origin, substitute $(0.5, 0.6)$ into $\lg y = n \lg x + \lg k$: $\lg k = -0.300$, giving $k = 10^{\lg k} = 0.501$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly evaluates the constant $k = 0.501$ without falling for the false-origin intercept trap.

items.stem: A graph of $T^2$ against slotted mass $m$ in Required Practical 7 gives a straight line of gradient 1.94 s² kg⁻¹. Find the spring constant $k$.
items.workedSolution: Comparing $T^2 = (4\pi^2 / k)m$ with $y = mx$, $k = 4\pi^2 / 1.94 = 20.3 N m⁻¹$.

items.stem: A straight-line plot of $T^2$ against pendulum length $L$ in Required Practical 7 has gradient 3.98 s² m⁻¹. Determine the experimental value of $g$.
items.workedSolution: Comparing $T^2 = (4\pi^2 / g)L$ with $y = mx$, $g = 4\pi^2 / 3.98 = 9.92 m s⁻²$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines the value $ 9.92 m s⁻²$.

items.stem: In an RC discharge practical, a student logs voltage across a 50 kΩ resistor. Plotting ln(V / V) versus time t yields a line through (0 s, 2.303) and (40 s, 0.303).
items.workedSolution: (a) Taking natural logarithms gives a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the reciprocal of the time constant and a vertical intercept equal to the natural logarithm of the initial potential difference. (b) Using the two plotted points, slope m = -0.05000 s⁻¹, so τ = −1/m = 20.00 s ≈ 20.0 s. (c) C = τ/R = 400 μF. (d) Uses all measured data points along a straight line of best fit rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.

markScheme.criterion: Shows taking natural logs produces a linear relation between ln(V) and t.
Identifies gradient = −1/τ and vertical intercept = ln(V₀).
Evaluates negative gradient m = -0.0500 s⁻¹ and uses τ = −1/m.
Correct time constant τ = 20.0 s.
Correct capacitance C = τ / R = 400 μF.
States that it uses all measured data points along a straight line of best fit rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.

parts.prompt: Explain why plotting the natural logarithm of potential difference against time yields a straight line, identifying the physical meaning of its gradient and vertical intercept.
parts.expectedAnswer: From the exponential discharge equation, taking natural logarithms gives a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the reciprocal of the time constant and a vertical intercept equal to the natural logarithm of the initial potential difference.
workingSteps: Take natural logarithms of both sides of the exponential decay equation.
Compare with a linear equation to identify the negative gradient and the vertical intercept.

parts.prompt: Determine the time constant τ of the RC circuit from the gradient of the graph.
workingSteps: Time constant τ = −1 / m = 20.00 s ≈ 20.0 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the capacitance of the capacitor in μF given R = 50 kΩ.
State why determining τ from the gradient of a ln(V) against t graph is more reliable than drawing an initial tangent to a V against t curve.
parts.expectedAnswer: The logarithmic gradient method is more reliable because it uses all measured data points along a straight line of best fit rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.
workingSteps: Drawing a tangent to a curve by eye is subjective and sensitive to noise at a single point, whereas a linear best-fit averages random errors over all readings.

items.stem: Shown below is a 20.0 s velocity–time plot for a crane trolley, which begins 30.0 m past the end-stop. Use the graph area to calculate its average speed over 20.0 s.
items.workedSolution: The shaded v–t area yields Δx = ½(20 + 10)(14) = 210 m (independent of the 30 m starting offset). Therefore mean speed = 210 / 20 = 10.5 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Divides trapezium distance (210 m) by 20 s to obtain 10.5 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: Plotted below is tensile stress against strain for a polymer band. The graph is linear from 0.0 to 0.3 and ends at 0.6. What is the Young's modulus of this sample in MPa?
items.workedSolution: At the proportionality limit (ε = 0.3), the graph shows 210 MPa. Therefore E = σ / ε = 210 / 0.3 = 700 MPa.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates initial linear gradient E = 210 / 0.3 = 700 MPa (D).

items.stem: For r⁻² up to 80.0 m⁻², calculate the straight-line slope in N m² for two charged metal-coated spheres on a balance.
items.workedSolution: At r⁻² = 0.0 m⁻², tare offset F₀ = 0.2 N; at r⁻² = 80 m⁻², F = 1.8 N. Gradient = (1.8 − 0.2) / 80 = 0.0200 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts tare offset F₀ = 0.2 N to get (1.8 − 0.2) / 80 = 0.0200 N m² (A).

items.stem: The graph shows the non-linear V–I characteristic for a filament lamp. Calculate the electrical resistance of the component at a current of 2.0 A.
items.workedSolution: Electrical resistance at an operating point is defined by R = V / I (not the local slope ΔV / ΔI). At I = 2 A, V = 15 V, so R = 15 / 2 = 7.50 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses static ratio R = V / I = 15 / 2 = 7.50 Ω (D).

options.distractorRationale: Evaluates the low-current resistance near the origin rather than at the specified operating current.

options.label: C

items.stem: In a photodiode experiment, the graph shows the steepest line of worst fit drawn from 0.4 mW to 2.0 mW. Calculate the gradient of this worst-fit line.
items.workedSolution: At x₁ = 0.4 mW, y₁ = 1 μA; at x₂ = 2 mW, y₂ = 6.6 μA. Worst-fit gradient m_worst = (6.6 − 1) / (2 − 0.4) = 3.50 μA mW⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δy / Δx = (6.6 − 1) / (2 − 0.4) = 3.50 μA mW⁻¹ (C).

options.distractorRationale: Inverts Δx / Δy instead of evaluating Δy / Δx.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts y₁ in the numerator but divides by x₂ instead of the horizontal span (x₂ − x₁).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the secant y₂ / x₂ as though the worst-fit line passed through the origin (0, 0) rather than (x₁, y₁).

items.stem: On a suppressed-origin plot for a steel spring, vertical error bars are ±0.01 m. The best-fit line has gradient 0.01140 m N⁻¹, while the shallowest acceptable worst-fit line has gradient 9.900 × 10⁻³ m N⁻¹. Find the absolute uncertainty in the gradient.
items.workedSolution: The gradient uncertainty equals Δm = |m_worst − m_best| = |9.900 × 10⁻³ − 0.01140| = 1.500 × 10⁻³ m N⁻¹ ≈ 1.50 × 10⁻³ m N⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δm = |m_worst − m_best| = 1.50 × 10⁻³ m N⁻¹.

items.stem: On a frictionless ramp (sin θ = 0.3, g = 9.8 m s⁻²), light gates record speed v of a dynamics cart, giving a v² against s line from s = 0.0 m to s = 2.0 m. Passing the first gate with speed u₀ > 0, it obeys v² = u₀² + 2as. What is the gradient Δ(v²) / Δs of this line?
items.workedSolution: From v² = u₀² + (2g sin θ)s, the vertical intercept is u₀² = 2.5 m² s⁻² and at s = 2 m, v² = 14.26 m² s⁻². Gradient = (14.26 − 2.5) / 2 = 2(9.8)(0.3) = 5.88 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept u₀² = 2.5 m² s⁻² (or evaluates 2 × 9.8 × 0.3) to get 5.88 m s⁻² (B).

items.stem: A student stretches a metal spring with slotted masses in Paper 3A and plots five error-bar points. Best-fit coordinates $(0.200, 4.30)$ and $(1.00, 19.1)$ are marked. The steepest and shallowest worst-fit lines have gradients 21.8 N m⁻¹ and 15.5 N m⁻¹, with vertical intercepts -1.41 N and 2.41 N.
items.workedSolution: (a) Using the large gradient triangle: $m = (19.1 - 4.30) / (1.00 - 0.200) = 18.5 N m⁻¹$. (b) $\Delta m = \frac{1}{2}(21.8 - 15.5) = 3.18 N m⁻¹$, giving percentage uncertainty $= 17.2\%$. (c) $\Delta c = \frac{1}{2}(2.41 - -1.41) = 1.91 N$. (d) All error bars have identical constant size because absolute uncertainty is fixed; a non-zero intercept indicates a systematic error.

markScheme.criterion: Uses large gradient triangle spanning >50% of line.
Best-fit gradient $m = 18.5 N m⁻¹$.
Calculates half-spread $\Delta m = 3.18 N m⁻¹$.
Percentage uncertainty $= 17.2\%$.
Applies $\Delta c = \frac{1}{2}(c_{\max} - c_{\min})$.
Absolute intercept uncertainty $\Delta c = 1.91 N$.
All error bars have identical constant size because absolute uncertainty is fixed
Identifies non-zero vertical intercept as a systematic error (reject random error).

parts.prompt: Determine the gradient $m$ of the line of best fit, showing your working clearly.
workingSteps: Triangle spans more than 50% of the plotted line.

parts.prompt: Use the steepest and shallowest worst-fit gradients to calculate the percentage uncertainty in $m$.
workingSteps: Percentage uncertainty $= (3.18 / 18.5) \times 100\% = 17.2\%$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the absolute uncertainty $\Delta c$ in the vertical intercept.
Explain how the lengths of the vertical error bars change across the plotted range and state what a non-zero vertical intercept indicates.
parts.expectedAnswer: All error bars have identical constant size because absolute uncertainty is fixed; a non-zero intercept indicates a systematic zero offset.
workingSteps: Identify constant absolute vs constant percentage uncertainty scaling.
Link non-zero intercept when theory predicts direct proportionality to a systematic error.

items.stem: Rising-edge D-type flip-flops form the modulo-10 counter in the timing diagram below. An 800 Hz clock signal drives the circuit.
items.workedSolution: (a) $f_{\mathrm{out}} = 80.0 Hz$. (b) Count after 64 pulses is 4. (c) Q3 and Q1 connected to an AND gate driving master reset.

markScheme.criterion: Divides clock frequency by modulus 10.
Obtains 80.0 Hz.
Finds remainder of 64 divided by 10.
Obtains decimal state 4.
Converts decimal 10 to binary 1010.
Identifies Q3 and Q1 connected to an AND gate driving master reset.

parts.prompt: Calculate the repetition frequency of the counter's full output cycle in Hz.
workingSteps: $f_{\mathrm{out}} = \frac{f_{\mathrm{clk}}}{10} = \frac{800}{10} = 80.0 Hz$.

parts.prompt: Starting from zero, determine the decimal count stored after 64 rising clock pulses.
workingSteps: Take remainder modulo 10: 64 mod 10 = 4.

parts.prompt: Specify which counter output bits must feed an active-high AND gate to reset this counter automatically on count 10.
parts.expectedAnswer: Q3 and Q1 connected to an AND gate driving master reset.
workingSteps: Write decimal 10 in 4-bit binary: 1010.
Connect the HIGH bits (Q3 and Q1 connected to an AND gate driving master reset).

items.stem: The displacement–time graph shows the motion of a trolley moving along a straight track. Calculate its constant velocity between t = 0.0 s and t = 3.0 s.
items.workedSolution: At t = 0.0 s, s₀ = 9 m; at t = 3 s, s₁ = 37 m. Velocity v = Δs / Δt = (37 − 9) / 3 = 9.33 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts initial position s₀ = 9 m to obtain v = (37 − 9) / 3 = 9.33 m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: A uniform metal wire has cross-sectional area 8.00 × 10⁻⁸ m² and length 2.00 m. Its linear plot of current I (y-axis) against potential difference V (x-axis) links the origin to (6.00 V, 0.500 A). Deduce the resistivity of the metal.
items.workedSolution: Using the two plotted points, slope m = ΔI / ΔV = 0.5000 A / 6.000 V = 0.08333 A V⁻¹. Since gradient = 1/R, R = 1/m = 12.00 Ω. Therefore ρ = R A / L = 4.800 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 4.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses R = 1 / gradient and ρ = R A / L to obtain 4.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

items.stem: The graph shows how the force on a spring varies with compression up to 1.0 m. The compressed spring is released from rest on a smooth horizontal bench to launch a 0.5 kg block.
items.workedSolution: (a) k = 90 / 1 = 90.0 N m⁻¹. (b) Elastic energy E_p = ½(90)(1) = 45.0 J. (c) Launch speed v = √(2(45.0)/0.5) = 13.4 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies k as the gradient ΔF / Δx.
Obtains k = 90.0 N m⁻¹.
Uses triangular area ½Fx.
Obtains E_p = 45.0 J.
Equates ½(0.5)v² to stored elastic energy from (b).
Obtains v = 13.4 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A hospital ECG unit uses Ag/AgCl skin electrodes with shielded cables connected to a differential amplifier of voltage gain $1500$. The measured skin R-wave peak is $1.05\text{ mV}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Conducting gel lowers contact resistance and high input resistance prevents loading, ensuring the full millivolt cardiac signal reaches the input. (b) Shielded cables and differential rejection suppress 50 Hz mains hum, while keeping the patient relaxed prevents skeletal EMG noise. (c) $V_{\text{out}} = 1500 \times 1.05 \times 10^{-3} = 1.58 V$.

markScheme.criterion: Explains that conducting gel lowers contact resistance and high input resistance prevents loading.
Notes negligible current prevents potential drop across skin resistance.
Identifies 50 Hz mains pickup mitigated by shielding and differential amplifier.
Identifies skeletal muscle potentials mitigated by patient remaining still and relaxed.
Substitutes $1.05 \times 10^{-3}\text{ V} \times 1500$.
Correct peak output 1.58 V.

parts.prompt: Explain why conducting gel is applied beneath the electrodes and why the amplifier must have a very high input resistance.
parts.expectedAnswer: Because conducting gel lowers contact resistance and high input resistance prevents loading of the small cardiac voltage signal.
workingSteps: Conducting gel fills air gaps and lowers electrode–skin contact resistance.
High input resistance ensures negligible current is drawn so almost all potential appears across the amplifier input.

parts.prompt: Identify two unwanted electrical signals that can corrupt an ECG trace and state how each is reduced.
parts.expectedAnswer: 50 Hz mains interference (reduced by shielded leads and differential amplification) and skeletal muscle action potentials (reduced by keeping the patient still and relaxed).
workingSteps: State mains hum reduced via screened cables and differential cancellation.
State skeletal muscle EMG artefacts reduced by keeping the patient relaxed and stationary.

parts.prompt: Calculate the peak voltage delivered to the monitor display for the $1.05\text{ mV}$ R wave.
workingSteps: Multiply $1.05 \times 10^{-3}\text{ V}$ by $1500$.
Obtain $V_{\text{out}} = 1.58 V$.

items.stem: A student tracks a trolley along a straight track and plots its velocity against time. Determine the signed acceleration between t = 6.0 s and t = 9.0 s.
items.workedSolution: Between t = 6 s and t = 9 s, velocity changes from +16 m s⁻¹ to −8 m s⁻¹. Acceleration a = Δv / Δt = (−8 − 16) / (9 − 6) = -8.00 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δv / Δt = (−8 − 16) / (3) = -8.00 m s⁻² (D).

items.stem: Initially at momentum 6.0 kg m s⁻¹, a puck of mass 2.0 kg receives a forward force over 0.8 s as plotted below. Determine how much its speed increases.
items.workedSolution: Impulse J = area under F–t trapezium = ½(0.8 + 0.4)(50) = 30.0 N s. Speed increase Δv = J / m = 30.0 / 2 = 15.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes J = 30.0 N s and Δv = J / 2 = 15.0 m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: An engineer tests a $2.50\text{ m}$ metal wire of cross-sectional area $0.900\text{ mm}^2$. Within its linear region, a $180\text{ N}$ tension stretches it by $2.50\text{ mm}$. The stress–strain graph compares three materials labelled A, B, and C.
items.workedSolution: (a) $E = 200 GPa$. (b) A brittle material fractures after very small plastic strain, a ductile material yields with permanent plastic strain, and rubber forms an elastic hysteresis loop; clearly separates stiffness, strength, and toughness.

markScheme.criterion: Calculate tensile stress $\sigma = 2.00 \times 10^8\text{ Pa}$ (correct $10^{-6}$ area conversion).
Calculate tensile strain $\varepsilon = 1.00 \times 10^{-3}$.
Young modulus $= 200 GPa$.
L1 (Area 1): Clearly distinguishes stiffness (linear gradient E) from strength (peak stress / UTS).
L1 (Area 1): Identifies toughness as total area under the stress–strain curve up to fracture (energy absorbed per unit volume).
L2 (Area 2): Explains brittle A breaks suddenly after very small plastic strain giving no warning of failure.
L2 (Area 2): Explains ductile B shows visible plastic yielding/necking before breaking and absorbs large energy (tough), unloading parallel to initial slope with permanent strain.
L3 (Area 3): Explains rubber C shows large reversible non-linear elastic strain without permanent deformation.
L3 (Area 3): Links rubber's enclosed hysteresis loop area directly to thermal energy dissipated per unit volume per cycle, making it effective for damping vibrations.

parts.prompt: Calculate the Young modulus of the alloy wire in GPa.
workingSteps: Stress $\sigma = 180 / (0.900 \times 10^{-6}) = 2.00 \times 10^8\text{ Pa}$.
Strain $\varepsilon = 2.50 \times 10^{-3} / 2.50 = 1.00 \times 10^{-3}$.
Young modulus $E = \sigma/\varepsilon = 200 GPa$.

parts.prompt: Using curves A, B, and C, evaluate why a ductile metal (B) is safer than a brittle ceramic (A) for a lift cable, why rubber (C) is suited to vibration dampers instead, and how stiffness, strength, and toughness differ on the graph.
parts.expectedAnswer: On a stress–strain graph, initial linear gradient measures stiffness ($E$), peak vertical height measures ultimate tensile strength (UTS), and total area under the curve to fracture measures toughness. Comparing curves A, B, and C: a brittle material fractures after very small plastic strain, a ductile material yields with permanent plastic strain, and rubber forms an elastic hysteresis loop. A brittle material (A) breaks suddenly without warning once overloaded; a ductile metal (B) absorbs huge fracture energy (high toughness) and visibly stretches/necks plastically before breaking, giving warning of overload (unloading parallel to initial gradient with permanent strain). Rubber (C) stretches elastically to large strain and dissipates vibrational mechanical energy as heat per cycle equal to its enclosed hysteresis loop area.
workingSteps: Area 1 (L1): Distinguish stiffness (gradient E), strength (UTS), and toughness (total area to fracture).
Area 2 (L2): Contrast brittle sudden fracture (very small plastic strain, low toughness) vs ductile warning via plastic deformation/necking and high toughness.
Area 3 (L3): Explain rubber polymer hysteresis loop dissipating vibrational energy as thermal energy per unit volume.

items.stem: A lift starts moving upward at 9.0 m s⁻¹. Its upward acceleration over 6.0 s is graphed below. What is its upward velocity at t = 6.0 s?
items.workedSolution: Positive a–t area (0 to 3 s) = 24.0 m s⁻¹; negative area magnitude (3 s to 6 s) = 15.0 m s⁻¹. Net Δv = 24.0 − 15.0 = 9.00 m s⁻¹. Final velocity = 9 + (9.00) = 18.0 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: In a kinematics practical (g = 9.81 m s⁻²), a trolley travels down a smooth inclined ramp (sin θ = 0.4) and v² is plotted against s over 2.0 m. Deduce the gradient of the v² against s line.
items.workedSolution: From v² = u₀² + (2g sin θ)s, the vertical intercept is u₀² = 4 m² s⁻² and at s = 2 m, v² = 19.696 m² s⁻². Gradient = (19.696 − 4) / 2 = 2(9.81)(0.4) = 7.85 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept u₀² = 4 m² s⁻² (or evaluates 2 × 9.81 × 0.4) to get 7.85 m s⁻² (C).

items.stem: Shown below is a force–distance graph from x = 0.0 m to x = 12.0 m for a block (mass 4.0 kg, initial speed 4.0 m s⁻¹). Deduce the net work done by the resultant force.
items.workedSolution: Calculating the positive area (0 to 10 m) = 120 J; resistive work (10 m to 12 m) = −4.00 J. Net work = 120 − 4.00 = 116 J.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts resistive triangle (4.00 J) from positive trapezium (120 J) to get 116 J (D).

options.distractorRationale: Computes total final kinetic energy (½mu₀² + W) rather than the net work done W.

items.stem: A constant resultant force acts between t = 1.0 s and t = 5.0 s on a block of mass 0.8 kg sliding on a frictionless table, whose momentum–time graph is shown below.
items.workedSolution: (a) Rate of change of momentum gives F = Δp / Δt = (7.2 − 1.6) / (5 − 1) = 1.40 N. (b) Change in kinetic energy gives W = ΔE_k = (7.2² − 1.6²) / (2 × 0.8) = 30.8 J.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies resultant force as gradient Δp / Δt of the p–t graph.
Obtains F = 1.40 N.
Relates net work to ΔE_k = (p₂² − p₁²) / (2m).
Substitutes p₁ = 1.6 kg m s⁻¹, p₂ = 7.2 kg m s⁻¹, and m = 0.8 kg.
Obtains W = 30.8 J.

items.stem: Resistance R of a semiconductor bar rises linearly with L / A reaching 250.0 m⁻¹ on the plot below. The measurements include a constant contact resistance R₀. Allowing for the intercept, calculate resistivity ρ.
items.workedSolution: From the linear relation R = ρ(L / A) + R₀, subtracting the intercept gives ρ via ΔR / Δ(L / A) = (32 − 8) / 250 = 0.0960 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept R₀ = 8 Ω to obtain ρ = (32 − 8) / 250 = 0.0960 Ω m (A).

items.stem: Data for a cell produce the plotted terminal potential difference V versus current I from zero to 2.0 A. The line obeys V = ε − Ir. Use the graph to calculate the signed gradient.
items.workedSolution: At I = 0.0 A, V = ε = 7 V; at I = 2 A, V = 3.4 V. Gradient = (3.4 − 7) / 2 = -1.80 V A⁻¹ (equal to −r).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates (3.4 − 7) / 2 = -1.80 V A⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: The resistance R of a metal wire is plotted against temperature θ from (20 °C, 12.0 ± 0.6 Ω) to (100 °C, 20.0 ± 0.6 Ω). Dashed maximum and minimum lines join opposite ends of the first and last uncertainty bars. Calculate the uncertainty Δc in the vertical intercept at θ = 0 °C.

markScheme.criterion: Extrapolates both extreme lines to θ = 0 °C and computes Δc = 0.900 Ω.

items.stem: The graph shows both the strong nuclear force and the electrostatic force acting between two protons.
items.workedSolution: (a) Virtual photon mediates electromagnetic repulsion while pions mediate the strong nuclear force. (b) At $1.4\text{ fm}$, strong nuclear force is attractive overcoming electrostatic proton repulsion.

markScheme.criterion: Virtual photon for electromagnetic interaction.
Pion (condone gluon) for strong nuclear interaction.
Recognise 1.4 fm lies within the 0.5–3 fm attractive region.
State strong nuclear attraction is greater than electrostatic repulsion at this separation.

parts.prompt: Name the exchange particle for each of the two plotted interactions.
parts.expectedAnswer: A virtual photon mediates electromagnetic repulsion while pions mediate the strong nuclear force between nucleons (condone gluons between quarks).
workingSteps: Name virtual photon for the electromagnetic force.
Name pion (or gluon) for the strong nuclear force.

parts.prompt: Explain why two protons held at a separation of $1.4\text{ fm}$ remain bound rather than accelerating apart.
parts.expectedAnswer: At $1.4\text{ fm}$ the strong nuclear force is attractive overcoming electrostatic proton repulsion because its magnitude is much larger than the Coulomb repulsion.
workingSteps: Note 1.4 fm lies inside the 0.5–3 fm attractive window.
Compare strong attraction magnitude with smaller electrostatic repulsion.

items.stem: An MRI coil uses YBCO superconducting tape ($T_{\text{c}} = 92.0\text{ K}$) cooled in liquid nitrogen at $77.0\text{ K}$ carrying $80.0\text{ A}$. Just above $T_{\text{c}}$, the coil resistance is $0.650\,\Omega$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Zero electrical resistance at or below the critical temperature; operates in superconducting state with zero resistance and zero heating loss. (b) $P = I^2R = 4.16 × 10³ W$. (c) Expensive low-temperature cooling is required to stay below the critical temperature.

markScheme.criterion: Zero electrical resistance / resistivity at or below critical temperature $T_{\text{c}}$.
Correctly identify superconducting state with zero resistance and zero heating loss.
Substitute current and normal resistance into $P = I^2R$.
Expensive / technically difficult low-temperature cooling required below $T_{\text{c}}$.

parts.prompt: Define the critical temperature $T_{\text{c}}$ of a superconductor and state whether this conductor is superconducting at its operating temperature.
parts.expectedAnswer: Critical temperature is the transition temperature at or below which a superconductor has zero electrical resistance; at $77\text{ K}$ it is in the superconducting state with zero resistance and zero heating loss.
workingSteps: Define Tc as transition to exact zero resistance (at or below Tc).
Compare operating temperature 77 K against Tc = 92 K.

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal power that would be dissipated if the coil accidentally warmed just above $T_{\text{c}}$ while still carrying the same current.
State one major practical limitation preventing widespread room-temperature use of superconducting power cables.
parts.expectedAnswer: A major limitation is that expensive low-temperature cooling is required to stay below the critical temperature.
workingSteps: State cost and difficulty of maintaining low-temperature cooling below Tc.

items.stem: A tangent is drawn to a radioactive decay curve at t = 4.0 s, where N = 3084 nuclei remain. The tangent has a gradient of −200.5 s⁻¹. Calculate the decay constant λ of this nuclide.

markScheme.criterion: Computes λ = |gradient| / N = 0.0650 s⁻¹.

items.stem: In Paper 3A practical work, why should the vertical axis of a semi-log damping graph be labelled $\ln(x / \mathrm{mm})$ rather than $\ln(x)$ in mm?
items.workedSolution: Paper 3A logarithmic linearization principle: The argument of a logarithm must be a dimensionless ratio. Taking natural logarithms gives ln y = ln A − λt. With a false origin, a point on the line must be substituted rather than reading the vertical axis crossing.

markScheme.criterion: The argument of a logarithm must be a dimensionless ratio. Taking natural logarithms gives ln y = ln A − λt. With a false origin, a point on the line must be substituted rather than reading the vertical axis crossing.

options.distractorRationale: Dividing by mm simply makes the numerical value dimensionless in millimetres; ln A then reflects A in mm.

options.label: B
options.text: Because natural logarithms can only be taken for quantities smaller than one.
options.distractorRationale: Natural logarithms are defined for any positive dimensionless ratio.

options.label: C
options.text: The argument of a logarithm must be a dimensionless ratio; taking natural logarithms gives ln y equals ln A minus lambda t and the false origin requires substituting a point on the line rather than reading the vertical axis crossing.

options.label: D
options.text: Because dividing by mm cancels the decay constant λ out of the gradient.
options.distractorRationale: Changing the unit of x shifts ln A vertically by an additive constant without changing the gradient −λ.

items.stem: A student claims repeating timings of 20 oscillations in RP7 eliminates random error completely. Which critique and experimental best practice is accurate?
items.workedSolution: RP7 mark-scheme precision: Repeats reduce random error but never eliminate it; students should place the fiducial marker at the equilibrium position where speed is maximum, discard anomalous timings before averaging, and time many oscillations to reduce reaction-time uncertainty.

markScheme.criterion: Repeats reduce random error but never eliminate it; students should place the fiducial marker at the equilibrium position where speed is maximum, discard anomalous timings before averaging, and time many oscillations to reduce reaction-time uncertainty.

options.text: Repeats eliminate both random timing errors and systematic stopwatch calibration errors.
options.distractorRationale: Repeats only reduce random error; they never eliminate random or systematic errors.

options.label: B
options.text: Timing 20 oscillations eliminates random error completely without needing any repeat trials.
options.distractorRationale: Multiple repeats are still required to spot anomalies (like miscounting 19 instead of 20 cycles) and reduce random spread.

options.label: C
options.text: Repeats reduce random error but never eliminate it; students should place the fiducial marker at equilibrium where speed is maximum discard anomalous timings before averaging and time many oscillations to reduce reaction time uncertainty.

options.label: D
options.text: Always count 'one' at the moment the stopwatch starts so 20 full cycles are timed.
options.distractorRationale: Counting 'one' at t = 0 times only 19 oscillations; always count 'zero' at release/start.

options.text: Release the pendulum from 45° so the bob passes equilibrium at higher speed while measuring L to the top of the bob.
options.distractorRationale: Small-angle approximation sin θ ≈ θ breaks down above ~15°, and measuring to the top of the bob introduces a systematic offset equal to bob radius.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep all four timing trials including a 4 s anomaly so the average stays statistically unbiased.
options.distractorRationale: Clear anomalies must always be discarded before calculating the mean.

options.label: D
options.text: Use a long stretchy rubber band instead of inextensible string so amplitude stays constant.
options.distractorRationale: Elastic stretching couples vertical oscillations into the pendulum and invalidates constant L.

items.stem: Plotted below for discharge through a 50 kΩ resistor is ln(V / V) against t. The line starts at intercept 2.485 and passes through (60 s, 0.485). What is the initial potential difference V₀ at t = 0?
items.workedSolution: Since ln(V) = −t/τ + ln(V₀), the vertical intercept is ln(V₀) = 2.485. Taking the exponential gives V₀ = e^(2.485) = 12.00 V ≈ 12.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Extracts linearized graph parameters accurately to obtain 12.0 V.

items.stem: From t = 7.0 s to t = 10.0 s, a small locomotive brakes uniformly to rest. At t = 0.0 s it started 25.0 m ahead of the reference mark, completing the 10.0 s graph shown.
items.workedSolution: (a) Area under the v–t trapezium is Δx = ½(10 + 5)(16) = 120 m. (b) Final distance from the reference mark = 25 + 120 = 145 m. (c) Mean speed = 120 / 10 = 12.0 m s⁻¹. (d) Braking acceleration = (0 − 16) / (10 − 7) = -5.33 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Identifies distance travelled as the area under the v–t trapezium.
Obtains Δx = 120 m.
Adds 25 m offset to obtain 145 m.
Divides distance travelled from (a) by 10 s.
Obtains mean speed = 12.0 m s⁻¹.
Obtains braking acceleration = -5.33 m s⁻².

parts.prompt: Calculate the distance travelled during the 10.0 s journey.
workingSteps: Distance equals the trapezium area under the v–t curve.

parts.prompt: Hence state its final distance from the reference mark at t = 10.0 s.
Determine the mean speed over the 10.0 s run.
workingSteps: v_mean = Δx / t_total = 120 / 10 = 12.0 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the acceleration between t = 7.0 s and t = 10.0 s.

items.stem: When stretched to a tensile strain of 0.5, a polymer strip produces the stress–strain graph below. The limit of proportionality is at 0.25.
items.workedSolution: (a) Using E = stress / strain gives E = 180 / 0.25 = 720 MPa. (b) Energy per unit volume = ½(0.25)(180) + ½(180 + 260)(0.25) = 77.5 MJ m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates initial gradient σ / ε up to ε = 0.25.
Obtains E = 720 MPa.
Identifies work per unit volume as total area under the σ–ε graph.
Splits area into initial triangle plus upper trapezium.
Obtains 77.5 MJ m⁻³.

items.stem: Over values of r⁻² reaching 16.0 m⁻², the force reading F is plotted for two charged metal-coated spheres on a balance.
items.workedSolution: (a) At r⁻² = 0, systematic tare offset F₀ = 0.120 N. (b) Gradient = (1.16 − 0.12) / 16 = 0.0650 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Reads intercept F₀ = 0.120 N.
Evaluates ΔF = 1.16 − 0.12 using intercept from (a).
Divides ΔF by 16 m⁻² and states correct unit N m².
Obtains 0.0650 N m².

items.stem: A student uses a variable DC supply, an ammeter, and a voltmeter to test a metal filament lamp. The graph shows the potential difference V against current I up to 1.2 A.
items.workedSolution: (a) At I = 1.2 A, V = 12.6 V. (b) Static resistance R = V / I = 12.6 / 1.2 = 10.5 Ω (the upper segment gradient 18.0 Ω is ΔV / ΔI, not R).

markScheme.criterion: Reads V = 12.6 V at I = 1.2 A.
Selects R = V / I rather than local segment gradient ΔV / ΔI.
Substitutes V = 12.6 V and I = 1.2 A.
Obtains R = 10.5 Ω.

items.stem: In a thermocouple experiment, a student plots data with vertical error bars from 1.0 K to 5.0 K. The graph shows the shallowest acceptable line of worst fit through the error bars.
items.workedSolution: (a) At 5 K, y₂ = 17.0 mV. (b) Worst-fit gradient = (17 − 5) / (5 − 1) = 3.00 mV K⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Reads y₂ = 17.0 mV.
Reads y₁ = 5 mV at x₁ = 1 K and forms Δy / Δx.
Subtracts x₁ = 1 K in the denominator (5 − 1).
Obtains 3.00 mV K⁻¹.

items.stem: Data recorded for a sealed flask of nitrogen gas are shown on a suppressed-origin plot with vertical error bars of ±1.8 kPa. The best-fit line contains (25.0 °C, 115.9 kPa) and (85.0 °C, 140.8 kPa). Passing through all error bars, the shallowest acceptable line has gradient 0.3475 kPa K⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) From the large gradient triangle, m_best = (140.8 − 115.9) / (85.0 − 25.0) = 0.4150 kPa K⁻¹ ≈ 0.415 kPa K⁻¹. (b) Δm = |0.3475 − 0.4150| = 0.0675 kPa K⁻¹. (c) A suppressed origin expands the plotted data to fill more than half of the grid improving reading precision.

items.stem: In a practical measuring the potential difference across a heating coil, the best-fit line has gradient 3.40 Ω. The steepest and shallowest worst-fit lines through all error bars have gradients 3.99 Ω and 2.86 Ω. Calculate the absolute uncertainty in the gradient.
items.workedSolution: The absolute uncertainty in the gradient is half the difference between the steepest and shallowest worst-fit lines: $\Delta m = \frac{1}{2}(3.99 - 2.86) = 0.565 Ω$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly applies half-spread rule to obtain 0.565 Ω (3 sf).

items.stem: A modulo-6 counter is clocked at 750 Hz and counts from 0 to 5 before resetting on binary 110. Calculate the period of its divided output cycle in ms.
items.workedSolution: Output frequency $f_{\mathrm{out}} = \frac{750}{6} = 125\text{ Hz}$, giving output period $T = \frac{1}{125} = 8.00 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s} = 8.00 ms$.

markScheme.criterion: Divided output period equals 8.00 ms.

items.stem: The displacement–time graph shows the motion of a trolley moving along a straight track over 16.0 s. It moves back toward the start between t = 10.0 s and t = 16.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Maximum displacement at the plateau = 48.0 m. (b) Return-stage velocity = (24 − 48) / (16 − 10) = -4.00 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Reads plateau displacement = 48.0 m.
Uses gradient formula Δs / Δt = (24 − 48) / (16 − 10).
Retains negative sign for motion back toward the origin.

items.stem: With cross-sectional area 5.90 × 10⁻⁸ m² and length 1.50 m, a uniform metal wire produces a linear I–V line from the origin to I = 0.640 A at V = 8.00 V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area. (b) Gradient = 0.08000 A V⁻¹, so R = 1 / gradient = 12.5 Ω. (c) ρ = RA/L = 4.917 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 4.92 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: States resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area.
Correctly specifies all quantities (or notes constant temperature / material property).
Computes large-triangle gradient m = ΔI/ΔV = 0.0800 A V⁻¹ and takes its reciprocal R = 1/m.
Correct wire resistance R = 12.5 Ω.
Substitutes R, A, and L correctly into ρ = RA/L.
Correct resistivity 4.92 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m with unit Ω m.

parts.expectedAnswer: Electrical resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area, where resistance, cross-sectional area, and length are measured for a uniform sample at constant temperature.

workingSteps: Because I is on the vertical axis, R = 1 / m = 12.50 Ω ≈ 12.5 Ω.

workingSteps: Evaluate ρ = 4.917 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 4.92 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

items.stem: The graph shows how the force on a metal spring varies with extension up to 0.0 m. The spring obeys Hooke's law. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored at x = 1.0 m.
items.workedSolution: Elastic potential energy equals the triangular area under the F–x line: E_p = ½ F x = ½(70)(1) = 35.0 J.

markScheme.criterion: Computes triangular area ½(70)(1) = 35.0 J (D).

items.stem: A student uses a Geiger–Müller tube to measure the background-corrected count rate C of a short-lived radioisotope sample over 20.0 s. The graph shows ln(C / s⁻¹) plotted against time t.
items.workedSolution: (a) Vertical intercept at t = 0 is ln(C₀ / s⁻¹) = 7.80. (b) Gradient = (3.4 − 7.8) / 20 = -0.220 s⁻¹ (which equals −λ).

markScheme.criterion: Reads vertical intercept = 7.80.
Uses large triangle (3.4 − 7.8) / 20.
Includes negative sign and unit s⁻¹.
Obtains gradient = -0.220 s⁻¹.

items.stem: Surface electrodes detect an ECG R-wave peak of $1.35\text{ mV}$. This signal passes into a differential amplifier of voltage gain $1200$. Calculate the peak output voltage.
items.workedSolution: Convert $1.35\text{ mV} = 1.35 \times 10^{-3}\text{ V}$. Output $V_{\text{out}} = 1200 \times 1.35 \times 10^{-3} = 1.62 V$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 1.62 V.

items.stem: A student logs a glider along a straight air track for 20.0 s on the velocity–time graph below. Velocity in the positive x-direction is positive. It slows and changes direction between t = 10.0 s and t = 15.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Direction reverses at t = 13.75 s. Positive area = 281 m and unsigned negative area = 56.3 m, giving total distance = 338 m. (b) Net displacement = 281 − 56.3 = 225 m; average velocity = 225 / 20 = 11.3 m s⁻¹. (c) Acceleration = (−10 − 30) / (15 − 10) = -8.00 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Finds zero-crossing t = 13.75 s and evaluates both unsigned areas (281 m and 56.3 m).
Obtains total distance = 338 m.
Subtracts areas for net displacement (225 m) and divides by 20 s.
Obtains average velocity = 11.3 m s⁻¹.
Obtains acceleration = -8.00 m s⁻² including negative sign.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total distance travelled between t = 0.0 s and t = 20.0 s.
workingSteps: Velocity crosses zero at t = 13.75 s; forward area = 281 m.
Unsigned reverse area = 56.3 m, so total distance = 281 + 56.3 = 338 m.

parts.prompt: Determine the net displacement and hence calculate the average velocity over the 20.0 s interval.
workingSteps: Net displacement Δs = 281 − 56.3 = 225 m.
Average velocity = Δs / Δt = 225 / 20 = 11.3 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Graph data below display the forward resultant force over 2.5 s acting on a small cart of mass 3.0 kg whose initial momentum at t = 0.0 s is 9.0 kg m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) From the force–time graph area, J = ½(2.5 + 1.5)(46) = 92.0 N s. (b) Final momentum p_f = 9 + 92.0 = 101 kg m s⁻¹. (c) Speed increase Δv = 92.0 / 3 = 30.7 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes impulse from the trapezium area under the F–t curve.
Obtains J = 92.0 N s.
Adds 9 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 101 kg m s⁻¹.
Divides impulse from (a) by 3 kg.
Obtains Δv = 30.7 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Reading the I–V plot of a filament lamp at the marked point gives V = 9.00 V and I = 1.20 A. Calculate the static resistance.
items.workedSolution: Static resistance equals potential difference divided by current: R = V / I = 9.000 V / 1.200 A = 7.500 Ω ≈ 7.50 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates R = V / I accurately to obtain 7.50 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly converts mC to C and obtains 250 μF.

items.stem: The stress–strain graph shows loading and unloading of a rubber band returning to zero strain. What physical quantity is represented by the shaded area between the two curves?
items.workedSolution: Area under loading curve = work done per unit volume; area under unloading curve = elastic energy recovered per unit volume; enclosed hysteresis loop area equals thermal energy dissipated per unit volume. Therefore option B is correct: area enclosed by the hysteresis loop equals thermal energy dissipated per unit volume.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: area enclosed by the hysteresis loop equals thermal energy dissipated per unit volume.

options.label: A
options.text: For a complete stretch–release cycle, the area enclosed equals the Young modulus of the rubber
options.distractorRationale: Young modulus is gradient (σ/ε) on a linear section, not an enclosed area.

options.label: B
options.text: For a complete stretch–release cycle, the area enclosed by the hysteresis loop equals thermal energy dissipated per unit volume

options.label: C
options.text: For a complete stretch–release cycle, the area enclosed equals total elastic potential energy recovered during unloading
options.distractorRationale: Energy recovered per unit volume is the area under the unloading curve alone; the loop area is the energy LOST as heat.

options.label: D
options.text: For a complete stretch–release cycle, the area enclosed equals the permanent plastic extension of the rubber band
options.distractorRationale: The unloading curve returns to the origin (zero permanent strain), so rubber deforms elastically despite hysteresis.

items.stem: In a motion test over 10.0 s, a small cart begins at t = 0.0 s at 4.0 m s⁻¹ forward. The graph displays its forward acceleration.
items.workedSolution: (a) Acceleration switches from positive to negative at t = 5.00 s. (b) Positive area = 28.0 m s⁻¹, giving v_max = 4 + 28.0 = 32.0 m s⁻¹. (c) Negative area magnitude = 16.0 m s⁻¹, so v_final = 32.0 − 16.0 = 16.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: States t = 5.00 s.
Evaluates positive area up to 5 s (28.0 m s⁻¹) and adds u₀ = 4 m s⁻¹.
Obtains v_max = 32.0 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts negative area (16.0 m s⁻¹) from v_max.
Obtains final velocity = 16.0 m s⁻¹.

items.workedSolution: (a) At s = 0.0 m, u₀² = 3.00 m² s⁻². (b) Gradient = (12.81 − 3) / 2 = 4.91 m s⁻².

items.stem: In a lab trial across 20.0 m, a small boat of mass 5.0 kg starts at x = 0.0 m with speed 6.0 m s⁻¹ under the force shown.
items.workedSolution: (a) Evaluating the net F–x area yields W = 276 − 12.0 = 264 J. (b) v = √(6² + 2(264)/5) = 11.9 m s⁻¹. (c) Mean force = 264 / 20 = 13.2 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates positive (276 J) and negative (−12.0 J) areas.
Obtains net work W = 264 J.
Uses ½mv² = ½(5)(6²) + W.
Obtains v = 11.9 m s⁻¹.
Divides net work by 20 m to get 13.2 N.

workingSteps: Positive area (0 to 16 m) = ½(16 + 7)(24) = 276 J; negative area (16 m to 20 m) = −½(4)(6) = −12.0 J.

parts.prompt: Calculate its speed at x = 20.0 m.
State the mean resultant force over the 20.0 m displacement.

items.stem: Motion-sensor readings for a glider of mass 0.8 kg on a horizontal air track produce the momentum–time curve below. Use the graph gradient between t = 2.0 s and t = 5.0 s to calculate the resultant force.
items.workedSolution: Resultant force is the rate of change of momentum. Reading the slope gives F = Δp / Δt = (6.4 − 1.6) / (5 − 2) = 1.60 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates F = Δp / Δt = (6.4 − 1.6) / (3) = 1.60 N (C).

options.distractorRationale: Computes the secant ratio p₂ / t₂ from the origin, ignoring both initial momentum p₁ and start time t₁.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies Δp by Δt instead of evaluating the rate of change of momentum Δp / Δt.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides Δp / Δt by mass m, obtaining acceleration rather than resultant force.

items.stem: A conducting polymer strip is tested over L / A from 0.0 m⁻¹ to 400.0 m⁻¹, producing the linear R against L / A graph shown. A fixed lead resistance R₀ shifts the line, while the slope gives resistivity ρ.
items.workedSolution: (a) Extrapolating to the vertical axis gives R₀ = 8.00 Ω. (b) Slope of the plot gives ρ = (36 − 8) / 400 = 0.0700 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: States R₀ = 8.00 Ω.
Identifies ρ with the gradient ΔR / Δ(L / A).
Subtracts R₀ = 8 Ω from 36 Ω before dividing by 400 m⁻¹.
Obtains ρ = 0.0700 Ω m.

items.stem: A dry cell supplies current I over the current range 0.0 A to 2.0 A to a variable resistor. Its terminal potential difference V is plotted below.
items.workedSolution: (a) Open-circuit intercept gives ε = 10.6 V. (b) Gradient = (5 − 10.6) / 2 = -2.80 V A⁻¹. (c) Mean terminal p.d. = ½(10.6 + 5) = 7.80 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reads ε = 10.6 V at I = 0.
Evaluates (5 − 10.6) / 2 including negative sign.
Obtains -2.80 V A⁻¹.
Uses ½(10.6 + 5) or area divided by 2 A.
Obtains 7.80 V.

items.stem: A student uses IB Tool 2 video-analysis software at 60 Hz to track a falling steel sphere and plots drop height h against t² from (0.040 s², 0.22 ± 0.05 m) to (0.360 s², 1.78 ± 0.05 m). For one check trial, h = 1.800 ± 0.036 m and t = 0.600 ± 0.015 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) 4.88 m s⁻². (b) Δm = 0.313 m s⁻². (c) 7.00%. (d) 7.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. (e) Using a calibrated digital sensor or high-frame-rate video tracker reduces human reaction-time random uncertainty and allows rapid sampling, while calibration removes any constant systematic zero offset.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δh/Δ(t²) across full linear span.
Obtains gradient = 4.88 m s⁻² (implying g ≈ 9.75 m s⁻², consistent with 9.8 m s⁻²).
Calculates Δm = (m_max − m_min)/2 = 0.313 m s⁻².
Applies fractional uncertainty rule Δh/h + 2(Δt/t).
Obtains percentage uncertainty = 7.00%.
Converts 4.50 eV to 7.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
States high-frame-rate video tracking eliminates human reaction-time random scatter.
Notes scale/zero calibration in the plane of motion is needed to prevent systematic bias.

items.stem: Why do stable heavy nuclei require a greater proportion of neutrons to protons than light nuclei?
items.workedSolution: Because the strong nuclear force is short-range ($0.5\text{–}3\text{ fm}$) while electrostatic repulsion acts across the entire nucleus, extra neutrons add strong attraction without adding proton repulsion. Therefore option A is correct: strong nuclear force is repulsive below zero point five fm and attractive up to three fm balancing electrostatic proton repulsion.

markScheme.criterion: Select option A: strong nuclear force is repulsive below zero point five fm and attractive up to three fm balancing electrostatic proton repulsion.

options.label: A
options.text: Extra neutrons are needed because the strong nuclear force is repulsive below zero point five fm and attractive up to three fm balancing electrostatic proton repulsion whereas infinite-range electrostatic repulsion acts across all protons

options.label: B
options.text: Extra neutrons are needed because neutrons carry negative charge that neutralises proton repulsion
options.distractorRationale: Neutrons are electrically neutral (Q = 0).

options.label: C
options.text: Extra neutrons are needed because the strong nuclear force has infinite range and grows faster than electrostatic repulsion
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the ranges: strong force is short-range (~3 fm), while electrostatic repulsion is infinite-range.

options.label: D
options.text: Extra neutrons are needed because neutrons experience gravitational attraction stronger than Coulomb repulsion
options.distractorRationale: Gravitational attraction between nucleons is ~10⁻³⁶ times weaker than electrostatic repulsion.

items.stem: Why have superconducting cables not yet replaced ordinary copper overhead lines across national electricity grids?
items.workedSolution: Maintaining very cold liquid coolants (liquid helium or liquid nitrogen) along long corridors is costly and difficult. Therefore option C is correct: expensive low-temperature cooling is required to stay below the critical temperature.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: expensive low-temperature cooling is required to stay below the critical temperature.

options.distractorRationale: Superconductors dissipate zero I²R heat once below Tc.

options.distractorRationale: Superconductors sustain steady DC currents with exact zero resistance.

options.label: D
options.text: The main practical engineering barrier is that superconductors violate Ohm's law by creating infinite voltage
options.distractorRationale: Zero resistance means V = IR = 0 across the superconducting wire for finite current.

items.stem: A student reduces the time step Δt in a spreadsheet decay model from 2.5 s to 0.25 s while keeping N₀ and λ fixed. How and why does this change the modelled curve?
items.workedSolution: Halving or tenth-ing Δt updates the rate ΔN/Δt = −λN much more often so each linear step tracks the curvature closely. Therefore the correct statement is: In numerical modelling, reducing the time step makes the iterative model closer to the true exponential curve because the rate is updated more often as the curve becomes less steep.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: reducing the time step makes the iterative model closer to the true exponential curve because the rate is updated more often as the curve becomes less steep.

options.text: Reducing Δt increases the total error because ten times as many subtraction rows compound the underestimate.
options.distractorRationale: Global Euler truncation error scales linearly with Δt, so smaller steps converge toward the exact exponential.

options.label: C

options.distractorRationale: Updating N more frequently changes the intermediate decay rates and yields a noticeably more accurate result.

options.label: D
options.text: Reducing Δt causes the modelled points to rise above the analytical curve because the gradient becomes steeper.
options.distractorRationale: Euler points approach the exact exponential curve from below as Δt → 0.

items.stem: A student tests $\Delta\theta = A e^{-\lambda t}$ using a semi-log graph whose horizontal axis starts at $t = 20$ s. How should the student find $\lambda$ and $A$?
items.workedSolution: Paper 3A logarithmic linearization principle: Taking natural logarithms gives ln y equals ln A minus lambda t and the false origin requires substituting a point on the line rather than reading the vertical axis crossing.

markScheme.criterion: Taking natural logarithms gives ln y equals ln A minus lambda t and the false origin requires substituting a point on the line rather than reading the vertical axis crossing.

items.stem: To test $T = k L^n$ in a Paper 3A practical, a student plots $\lg(T / \mathrm{ms})$ against $\lg(L / \mathrm{cm})$ with a false origin at $\lg(L / \mathrm{cm}) = 0.60$. Which statement correctly describes how to find $n$ and $k$?
items.workedSolution: Paper 3A logarithmic linearization principle: Taking base ten logarithms gives lg y equals n lg x plus lg k and a false origin requires substituting a point on the line to find the intercept.

markScheme.criterion: Taking base ten logarithms gives lg y equals n lg x plus lg k and a false origin requires substituting a point on the line to find the intercept.

items.stem: In RP7, a student plots $T^2$ against slotted mass $m$ for a vertical spring. The straight line has a small positive vertical intercept. What causes this intercept, and how should the oscillations be timed?
items.workedSolution: RP7 mark-scheme precision: The effective mass of the oscillating spring and hanger shifts the line upward; for timing, place the fiducial marker at the equilibrium position where speed is maximum, discard anomalous timings before averaging, and time many oscillations to reduce reaction-time uncertainty.

markScheme.criterion: The effective mass of the oscillating spring and hanger shifts the line upward; for timing, place the fiducial marker at the equilibrium position where speed is maximum, discard anomalous timings before averaging, and time many oscillations to reduce reaction-time uncertainty.
