options.label: A
options.text: The positive vertical intercept proves Hooke's law fails for small masses and invalidates the gradient.
options.distractorRationale: Effective spring mass m_eff adds a constant horizontal shift T² = (4π²/k)(m + m_eff) without altering the gradient 4π²/k.

options.label: B
options.text: The effective mass of the oscillating spring and hanger shifts the line upward; for timing, place the fiducial marker at equilibrium where speed is maximum discard anomalous timings before averaging and time many oscillations to reduce reaction time uncertainty.

options.label: C
options.text: The positive intercept is caused by human reaction time and can be eliminated by taking fewer repeat readings.
options.distractorRationale: Reaction time is primarily random; the vertical intercept is the physical mass of the spring/hanger.

options.label: D
options.text: Force the best-fit line through the origin so k is computed accurately.
options.distractorRationale: Forcing through the origin biases the gradient and ignores the spring's own mass.

items.stem: Why should the fiducial marker in Required Practical 7 be placed at the equilibrium position rather than at maximum amplitude?
items.workedSolution: RP7 mark-scheme precision: Place the fiducial marker at the equilibrium position where speed is maximum, discard anomalous timings before averaging, and time many oscillations to reduce reaction-time uncertainty.

markScheme.criterion: Place the fiducial marker at the equilibrium position where speed is maximum, discard anomalous timings before averaging, and time many oscillations to reduce reaction-time uncertainty.

options.label: A
options.text: Place the fiducial marker at maximum displacement because the bob momentarily stops, giving zero timing uncertainty.
options.distractorRationale: At turning points the object moves slowest and lingers, making it hard to judge the exact reversal instant.

options.label: B
options.text: Place the fiducial marker at equilibrium purely because acceleration is zero there, which stops air damping.
options.distractorRationale: AQA mark schemes explicitly note 'zero acceleration' is insufficient without stating maximum speed minimizes time uncertainty.

options.label: C
options.text: Time one single oscillation with a 0.01 s stopwatch because timing 20 oscillations multiplies reaction-time error by 20.
options.distractorRationale: Reaction-time error Δt occurs only at start/stop, so dividing by N cuts absolute and percentage uncertainty in T by N.

options.label: D
options.text: Place the fiducial marker at equilibrium where speed is maximum discard anomalous timings before averaging and time many oscillations to reduce reaction time uncertainty.

items.stem: A 25 kΩ resistor is connected across a charged capacitor. The decaying voltage gives a linear ln(V / V) against t graph through (0 s, 2.140) and (25 s, 0.140).
items.workedSolution: (a) Taking natural logarithms gives a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the reciprocal of the time constant and a vertical intercept equal to the natural logarithm of the initial potential difference. (b) The line has gradient m = -0.08000 s⁻¹, so τ = −1/m = 12.50 s ≈ 12.5 s. (c) C = τ/R = 500 μF. (d) Uses all measured data points along a straight line of best fit rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.

markScheme.criterion: Shows taking natural logs produces a linear relation between ln(V) and t.
Identifies gradient = −1/τ and vertical intercept = ln(V₀).
Evaluates negative gradient m = -0.0800 s⁻¹ and uses τ = −1/m.
Correct time constant τ = 12.5 s.
Correct capacitance C = τ / R = 500 μF.
States that it uses all measured data points along a straight line of best fit rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.

parts.prompt: Explain why plotting the natural logarithm of potential difference against time yields a straight line, identifying the physical meaning of its gradient and vertical intercept.
parts.expectedAnswer: From the exponential discharge equation, taking natural logarithms gives a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the reciprocal of the time constant and a vertical intercept equal to the natural logarithm of the initial potential difference.
workingSteps: Take natural logarithms of both sides of the exponential decay equation.
Compare with a linear equation to identify the negative gradient and the vertical intercept.

parts.prompt: Determine the time constant τ of the RC circuit from the gradient of the graph.
workingSteps: Time constant τ = −1 / m = 12.50 s ≈ 12.5 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the capacitance of the capacitor in μF given R = 25 kΩ.
State why determining τ from the gradient of a ln(V) against t graph is more reliable than drawing an initial tangent to a V against t curve.
parts.expectedAnswer: The logarithmic gradient method is more reliable because it uses all measured data points along a straight line of best fit rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.
workingSteps: Drawing a tangent to a curve by eye is subjective and sensitive to noise at a single point, whereas a linear best-fit averages random errors over all readings.

items.stem: In a 12.0 s test run, a lift cage begins 30.0 m from the reference mark and follows the velocity–time graph below. Use the trapezium area to calculate its average speed.
items.workedSolution: The shaded v–t area yields Δx = ½(12 + 5)(14) = 119 m (independent of the 30 m starting offset). Therefore mean speed = 119 / 12 = 9.92 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Divides trapezium distance (119 m) by 12 s to obtain 9.92 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: Stretching a thin plastic strip from zero to strain 0.4 gives the curve below, which is linear up to strain 0.2. Determine the energy stored per unit volume in MJ m⁻³.
items.workedSolution: Integrating via geometric areas under the σ–ε graph (1 MPa × 1 = 1 MJ m⁻³) gives u = ½(0.2)(120) + ½(120 + 180)(0.2) = 42.0 MJ m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Sums triangle and trapezium areas under σ–ε curve to obtain 42.0 MJ m⁻³ (C).

items.stem: Data collected from two light charged spheres above an electronic balance produce a straight line of force F against r⁻² reaching 80.0 m⁻². Use the plotted points to calculate ΔF / Δ(r⁻²).
items.workedSolution: At r⁻² = 0.0 m⁻², tare offset F₀ = 0.4 N; at r⁻² = 80 m⁻², F = 2.4 N. Gradient = (2.4 − 0.4) / 80 = 0.0250 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts tare offset F₀ = 0.4 N to get (2.4 − 0.4) / 80 = 0.0250 N m² (C).

items.stem: The graph shows the potential difference–current characteristic for a filament lamp up to I = 1.0 A. Calculate the electrical resistance of the component when the current is 1.0 A.
items.workedSolution: Electrical resistance at an operating point is defined by R = V / I (not the local slope ΔV / ΔI). At I = 1 A, V = 13.5 V, so R = 13.5 / 1 = 13.5 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses static ratio R = V / I = 13.5 / 1 = 13.5 Ω (A).

items.stem: In a force-sensor experiment, the graph shows the steepest line of worst fit drawn from 0.5 N to 2.5 N. Calculate the gradient of this worst-fit line.
items.workedSolution: At x₁ = 0.5 N, y₁ = 1.2 mV; at x₂ = 2.5 N, y₂ = 8.4 mV. Worst-fit gradient m_worst = (8.4 − 1.2) / (2.5 − 0.5) = 3.60 mV N⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes the secant y₂ / x₂ as though the worst-fit line passed through the origin (0, 0) rather than (x₁, y₁).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts y₁ in the numerator but divides by x₂ instead of the horizontal span (x₂ − x₁).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inverts Δx / Δy instead of evaluating Δy / Δx.

items.stem: For a metal wire, two far-apart points on the best-fit line of a suppressed-origin graph are (20.0 N, 2.760 mm) and (60.0 N, 4.840 mm). What is the best-fit gradient?
items.workedSolution: Evaluating rise over run from the two points: gradient = (4.840 − 2.760) / (60.0 − 20.0) = 0.05200 mm N⁻¹ ≈ 0.0520 mm N⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates best-fit gradient = 0.0520 mm N⁻¹ from Δy / Δx.

items.stem: For a small puck rolling down a tilted air track at sin θ = 0.45 (take g = 9.8 m s⁻²), v² is plotted against s starting at s = 0.0 m up to s = 1.2 m. Use the plotted line to calculate Δ(v²) / Δs.
items.workedSolution: From v² = u₀² + (2g sin θ)s, the vertical intercept is u₀² = 3.8 m² s⁻² and at s = 1.2 m, v² = 14.384 m² s⁻². Gradient = (14.384 − 3.8) / 1.2 = 2(9.8)(0.45) = 8.82 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept u₀² = 3.8 m² s⁻² (or evaluates 2 × 9.8 × 0.45) to get 8.82 m s⁻² (D).

items.stem: Tracking a trolley down a tilted air track for Paper 3A gives five plotted points with error bars. Two points on the best-fit line are $(0.500, 4.30)$ and $(2.50, 17.1)$. Its steepest and shallowest worst-fit lines have gradients 7.58 m s⁻² and 5.33 m s⁻², with vertical intercepts -0.668 m² s⁻² and 2.70 m² s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Using the large gradient triangle: $m = (17.1 - 4.30) / (2.50 - 0.500) = 6.40 m s⁻²$. (b) $\Delta m = \frac{1}{2}(7.58 - 5.33) = 1.12 m s⁻²$, giving percentage uncertainty $= 17.5\%$. (c) $\Delta c = \frac{1}{2}(2.70 - -0.668) = 1.68 m² s⁻²$. (d) All error bars have identical constant size because absolute uncertainty is fixed; a non-zero intercept indicates a systematic error.

markScheme.criterion: Uses large gradient triangle spanning >50% of line.
Best-fit gradient $m = 6.40 m s⁻²$.
Calculates half-spread $\Delta m = 1.12 m s⁻²$.
Percentage uncertainty $= 17.5\%$.
Applies $\Delta c = \frac{1}{2}(c_{\max} - c_{\min})$.
Absolute intercept uncertainty $\Delta c = 1.68 m² s⁻²$.
All error bars have identical constant size because absolute uncertainty is fixed
Identifies non-zero vertical intercept as a systematic error (reject random error).

items.stem: A digital clock needs a divide-by-10 (BCD) counter built from edge-triggered D-type flip-flops to drive a 7-segment display. A control circuit needs a decade counter to switch ten valves on one at a time.
items.workedSolution: Each rising clock edge toggles the first D-type flip-flop to divide frequency by two and an AND gate decodes the target reset state to clear all flip-flops ($Q_3 \cdot Q_1$ for binary 1010 in BCD). BCD suits 7-segment display decoders via binary weights, whereas a Johnson decade counter directly activates one of ten sequential outputs for the solenoids without external decoding logic.

markScheme.criterion: Explains that wiring $\bar{Q}$ to $D$ makes each rising-edge D-type flip-flop toggle, dividing frequency by two.
Explains cascading four flip-flops to create a 4-bit binary ripple counter.
Identifies binary 1010 (decimal 10) as the first unwanted state for a BCD modulo-10 counter.
Explains connecting $Q_3$ and $Q_1$ to an AND gate driving the master reset to clear all flip-flops back to 0000.
Explains that a BCD counter produces 4-bit binary-weighted outputs suited to driving a BCD-to-7-segment decoder.
Contrasts with a Johnson decade counter activating one of ten decoded outputs one at a time without extra decoding gates for the solenoid sequence.

parts.prompt: Explain how D-type flip-flops are connected to build a modulo-10 BCD counter (including frequency division and reset decoding), and compare the BCD counter with a Johnson decade counter for these two applications.
parts.expectedAnswer: To build a 4-bit ripple counter, four rising-edge D-type flip-flops each have their inverted output connected back to their D input, and each stage clocks the next from its inverted output so the count advances cleanly in binary. Specifically, each rising clock edge toggles the first D-type flip-flop to divide frequency by two and an AND gate decodes the target reset state to clear all flip-flops: for modulo-10 BCD, binary 1010 is decoded by connecting $Q_3$ and $Q_1$ to an AND gate wired to the asynchronous master reset, resetting 1010 almost instantaneously to 0000 so only states 0 to 9 persist. For the digital clock, the BCD counter's compact 4-bit binary-weighted outputs directly feed a BCD-to-7-segment decoder; in contrast, for the ten sequential solenoids, a Johnson decade counter is superior because it activates one of ten decoded outputs HIGH in turn per clock pulse with no external decoding gates, though it uses more internal stages and does not output binary weights directly.
workingSteps: L1: Explain $\bar{Q} \to D$ feedback on each D-type flip-flop causing toggling on each rising edge ($f/2$).
L1: State that cascading 4 flip-flops yields a 4-bit ripple counter with 16 natural states (0000 to 1111).
L2: Explain modulo-10 reset decoding: binary 10 is $1010$, so $Q_3$ and $Q_1$ feed an AND gate connected to Master Reset (MR).
L2: Note the brief glitch on state 1010 clearing all flip-flops back to 0000 so states 0–9 cycle at $f_{\mathrm{clk}}/10$.
L3: Compare BCD (4 binary-weighted outputs ideal for 7-segment BCD decoders) vs Johnson (10 sequential one-hot decoded outputs ideal for sequential actuators/LEDs without extra gates).
L3: Mention practical propagation ripple delay or illegal-state recovery considerations.

items.stem: The displacement–time graph shows the motion of a trolley moving along a straight track over 10.0 s. Calculate its average velocity over the entire 10.0 s interval.
items.workedSolution: Initial displacement at t = 0.0 s is 5 m and final displacement at t = 10 s is 13 m. Average velocity = (13 − 5) / 10 = 0.800 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates net displacement (13 − 5) / 10 = 0.800 m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: In a school lab test, current I (y-axis) is graphed against V (x-axis) for a uniform metal wire of length 1.00 m and area 5.80 × 10⁻⁸ m². Passing through the origin and (10.0 V, 0.400 A), what resistivity does the metal have?
items.workedSolution: The line has gradient m = ΔI / ΔV = 0.4000 A / 10.00 V = 0.04000 A V⁻¹. Since gradient = 1/R, R = 1/m = 25.00 Ω. Therefore ρ = R A / L = 1.450 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m ≈ 1.45 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses R = 1 / gradient and ρ = R A / L to obtain 1.45 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m.

items.stem: An ECG trace recorded after exercise shows an R–R interval of $0.60\text{ s}$. The R-wave height is $1.44\text{ mV}$ and the P-wave height is $0.16\text{ mV}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\text{HR} = 60 / 0.60 = 100 beats min⁻¹$. (b) Ratio $= 1.44 / 0.16 = 9.00$. (c) The T wave represents ventricular repolarisation, taking longer than the QRS spike because recovery across ventricular muscle occurs more gradually.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $\text{HR} = 60 / 0.60$.
Correct heart rate 100 beats min⁻¹.
Correct amplitude ratio 9.00.
Identifies ventricular repolarisation.
Explains repolarisation spreads more slowly than rapid ventricular depolarisation.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heart rate during this recording.
workingSteps: Apply $\text{HR} = 60 / T_{\text{RR}}$.
Calculate $60 / 0.60 = 100 beats min⁻¹$.

parts.prompt: Determine the ratio of the R-wave peak potential to the P-wave peak potential.
workingSteps: Divide $1.44\text{ mV}$ by $0.16\text{ mV}$ to obtain 9.00.

parts.prompt: Identify the electrical process producing the T wave and explain why it lasts longer than the QRS complex.
parts.expectedAnswer: The T wave arises from ventricular repolarisation, which progresses more slowly across the ventricular myocardium than rapid conduction through Purkinje fibres.
workingSteps: Link T wave to ventricular repolarisation.
Contrast slower repolarisation with rapid bundle-of-His/Purkinje depolarisation.

items.stem: For a trolley along a straight track, velocity against time is plotted below. What is its net displacement at t = 12.0 s?
items.workedSolution: Splitting positive and negative areas at t = 8 s. Positive area = 96.0 m and area below the axis has magnitude 28.0 m. Net displacement = 96.0 − 28.0 = 68.0 m.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts reverse area (28.0 m) from forward area (96.0 m) to obtain 68.0 m (B).

items.stem: Force against time is plotted for 1.0 s as a trolley of mass 1.2 kg is pushed forward from momentum 3.6 kg m s⁻¹. Find the mean resultant force during the pulse.
items.workedSolution: Total impulse J = ½(1 + 0.4)(40) = 28.0 N s. Mean force F_mean = J / Δt = 28.0 / 1 = 28.0 N.

markScheme.criterion: Divides impulse (28.0 N s) by 1 s to obtain 28.0 N (B).

items.stem: Current against potential difference is graphed below for a filament lamp. At the marked operating point on the characteristic, V = 7.50 V and I = 0.600 A.
items.workedSolution: (a) R = V / I = 12.50 Ω ≈ 12.5 Ω. (b) Connect a potential divider with a series protective resistor, an ammeter in series, and a voltmeter in parallel across the component, and reverse the supply connections for negative readings. (c) Resistance increases with potential difference because heating increases lattice ion vibration amplitude and electron collisions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the static resistance of the component at the highlighted operating point.
workingSteps: Recall that static resistance at a point is R = V / I (not the inverse of the local tangent).
Substitute V = 7.500 V and I = 0.6000 A to obtain R = 12.50 Ω ≈ 12.5 Ω.

parts.prompt: Describe the circuit arrangement and experimental procedure used to obtain a complete I–V characteristic safely across positive and negative potential differences.
parts.expectedAnswer: To obtain the full characteristic safely, connect a potential divider with a series protective resistor, an ammeter in series, and a voltmeter in parallel across the component, and reverse the supply connections for negative readings.
workingSteps: Use a potential divider to vary potential difference smoothly from zero while limiting excessive current with a protective resistor.
Measure current with a series ammeter, potential difference with a parallel voltmeter, and reverse the supply leads for negative polarity.

parts.prompt: Explain the physical shape of the I–V characteristic in terms of charge carriers and resistance.
parts.expectedAnswer: The curve shows that the component resistance increases with potential difference because heating increases lattice ion vibration amplitude and electron collisions.

items.stem: A capacitor charges steadily from zero until Q = 3.00 mC at V = 12.0 V. The plotted line relates charge Q to potential difference V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Capacitance is the charge stored per unit potential difference across the plates. (b) C = Q / V = 250 μF. (c) Triangular area E = ½ Q V = 0.01800 J ≈ 0.0180 J.

markScheme.criterion: States charge stored per unit potential difference across the plates.
Correct capacitance 250 μF.
Recognises triangular area E = ½ Q V and converts mC to C.
Correct stored energy 0.0180 J.

items.stem: The tensile stress–strain graph compares three solid materials labelled A, B, and C. It shows a dashed unloading path on B and a loading–unloading loop on C.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 (5–6 marks): A brittle material fractures after very small plastic strain, a ductile material yields with permanent plastic strain, and rubber forms an elastic hysteresis loop; distinguishes limit of proportionality vs elastic limit, stiffness vs strength vs toughness, parallel unloading on B, and hysteresis thermal dissipation on C.

markScheme.criterion: L1 (Area 1): Defines stress σ = F/A, strain ε = ΔL/L, and linear gradient = Young modulus E (stiffness) up to limit of proportionality P.
L1 (Area 1): Distinguishes limit of proportionality (end of straight line) from elastic limit (maximum stress for complete return to original length).
L2 (Area 2): Identifies A as brittle: steep linear gradient (high stiffness) fracturing after very small plastic strain with no necking (reject 'no strain').
L2 (Area 2): Identifies B as ductile: shows yield, large plastic deformation, UTS, necking, and unloads parallel to initial linear gradient leaving permanent plastic strain.
L3 (Area 3): Identifies C as polymeric/rubber: non-linear large elastic extension as chains uncoil, returning to zero strain when unloaded.
L3 (Area 3): Explains unloading curve lies below loading curve forming a hysteresis loop whose enclosed area equals thermal energy dissipated per unit volume.

parts.prompt: Identify the material class represented by each curve A, B, and C, and compare their mechanical behaviour up to fracture or unloading. Refer explicitly to Young modulus, limit of proportionality, elastic limit, plastic deformation, unloading, and energy dissipation.
parts.expectedAnswer: Stress is $\sigma = F/A$, strain is $\varepsilon = \Delta L/L$, and in the initial straight-line Hookean region up to the limit of proportionality $P$ the gradient equals Young modulus $E = \sigma/\varepsilon$ (stiffness). Comparing the three curves: a brittle material fractures after very small plastic strain, a ductile material yields with permanent plastic strain, and rubber forms an elastic hysteresis loop. Material A (brittle, e.g. Glass) has the steepest linear gradient (stiffest) and fractures suddenly near $P$ with very little plastic deformation and no necking. Material B (ductile metal, e.g. Copper/steel) passes its limit of proportionality and elastic limit, yields and extensive plastic deformation up to its ultimate tensile stress (UTS) followed by necking, and when unloaded from the plastic region follows a straight line parallel to its initial linear gradient leaving permanent plastic strain. Material C (polymeric rubber) shows large non-linear elastic strain as tangled polymer chains uncoil, returns to zero strain on unloading, and encloses a hysteresis loop whose area represents thermal energy dissipated per unit volume.
workingSteps: Area 1 (L1): Define σ=F/A, ε=ΔL/L, gradient E = σ/ε up to limit of proportionality P, and elastic limit.
Area 2 (L2): Contrast A (brittle: stiff, fractures after very small plastic strain, no necking) vs B (ductile: yield, plastic flow, UTS, necking, parallel unloading leaving permanent strain).
Area 3 (L3): Explain C (polymeric rubber: non-linear large elastic strain, returns to zero strain, hysteresis loop area = thermal energy dissipated per unit volume).

items.stem: With initial upward velocity 18.0 m s⁻¹ at t = 0.0 s, a lift cage accelerates over 12.0 s as shown on the graph. Use the net area under the graph to calculate the final upward velocity.
items.workedSolution: Positive a–t area (0 to 6 s) = 36.0 m s⁻¹; negative area magnitude (6 s to 12 s) = 18.0 m s⁻¹. Net Δv = 36.0 − 18.0 = 18.0 m s⁻¹. Final velocity = 18 + (18.0) = 36.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Combines net signed area (18.0 m s⁻¹) with u₀ = 18 m s⁻¹ to obtain 36.0 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: What is the gradient of the v²–s line below? A trolley descends a smooth inclined ramp up to 2.5 m (sin θ = 0.2, g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: From v² = u₀² + (2g sin θ)s, the vertical intercept is u₀² = 2.8 m² s⁻² and at s = 2.5 m, v² = 12.61 m² s⁻². Gradient = (12.61 − 2.8) / 2.5 = 2(9.81)(0.2) = 3.92 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept u₀² = 2.8 m² s⁻² (or evaluates 2 × 9.81 × 0.2) to get 3.92 m s⁻² (B).

items.stem: Over a 16.0 m distance, the plotted resultant force acts on a small boat (mass 5.0 kg) moving forward at 5.0 m s⁻¹ at x = 0.0 m. Deduce the total work done over the 16.0 m displacement.
items.workedSolution: Calculating the positive area (0 to 14 m) = 200 J; resistive work (14 m to 16 m) = −5.00 J. Net work = 200 − 5.00 = 195 J.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts resistive triangle (5.00 J) from positive trapezium (200 J) to get 195 J (B).

items.stem: The linear momentum of a puck of mass 1.0 kg on a smooth air table is plotted below against time. From t = 2.0 s to t = 6.0 s, the resultant force is uniform.
items.workedSolution: (a) Reading rise over run on the plot: F = Δp / Δt = (9 − 3) / (6 − 2) = 1.50 N. (b) Calculating kinetic energy gain: W = ΔE_k = (9² − 3²) / (2 × 1) = 36.0 J.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies resultant force as gradient Δp / Δt of the p–t graph.
Obtains F = 1.50 N.
Relates net work to ΔE_k = (p₂² − p₁²) / (2m).
Substitutes p₁ = 3 kg m s⁻¹, p₂ = 9 kg m s⁻¹, and m = 1 kg.
Obtains W = 36.0 J.

items.stem: Over L / A from zero to 250.0 m⁻¹, find resistivity ρ in Ω m for a conducting plastic strip from the R against L / A plot. The measurements include a constant contact resistance R₀.
items.workedSolution: In R = ρ(L / A) + R₀, the vertical intercept is the contact offset and resistivity ρ is ΔR / Δ(L / A) = (35 − 5) / 250 = 0.120 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept R₀ = 5 Ω to obtain ρ = (35 − 5) / 250 = 0.120 Ω m (C).

items.stem: A cell is tested over current I from 0.0 A to 0.8 A, giving the downward linear V–I graph below. Find the mean terminal potential difference over this range.
items.workedSolution: For a uniform fall from 4.2 V (I = 0.0 A) to 2.2 V (I = 0.8 A), mean p.d. is V_mean = ½(4.2 + 2.2) = 3.20 V.

markScheme.criterion: Averages endpoint voltages ½(4.2 + 2.2) = 3.20 V (D).

items.stem: An experiment tests a power-law relation y = kxⁿ where k and n are unknown positive constants. How does plotting ln y against ln x allow both constants to be found?
items.workedSolution: Taking natural logarithms of y = kxⁿ yields ln y = n ln x + ln k, matching Y = mX + c with m = n and c = ln k (so k = e^c). Therefore the correct statement is: Linearizing the power law by logarithms, taking natural logarithms of a power law gives ln y = n ln x + ln k, a straight line with gradient n and vertical intercept ln k.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: taking natural logarithms of a power law gives ln y = n ln x + ln k, a straight line with gradient n and vertical intercept ln k.

options.label: A
options.text: Linearizing the power law by logarithms, taking natural logarithms of a power law yields ln y equals n ln x plus ln k, giving a straight line whose gradient equals the exponent n and whose vertical intercept equals ln k.

options.label: B
options.text: Linearizing the power law by logarithms, the gradient equals the prefactor k directly and the vertical intercept equals the exponent n.
options.distractorRationale: Swaps the roles of gradient (n) and vertical intercept (ln k).

options.label: C
options.text: Linearizing the power law by logarithms, plotting ln y against x gives a straight line of gradient n for every power-law relationship.
options.distractorRationale: A semi-log plot (ln y vs x) linearizes an exponential function y = y₀e^(−λx), not a power law y = kxⁿ.

options.label: D
options.text: Linearizing the power law by logarithms, the vertical intercept equals k directly without needing to take the exponential function e^c.
options.distractorRationale: Because the intercept is c = ln k, the constant k must be recovered via k = e^c.

items.stem: Heavy nuclei with nucleon numbers above $200$ are often unstable and emit alpha particles. Refer to the strong nuclear force graph shown.
items.workedSolution: (a) $r_0 \approx 0.5\text{ fm}$ and maximum range $\approx 3.00\text{ fm}$. (b) Strong nuclear force is repulsive below zero point five fm and attractive up to three fm balancing electrostatic proton repulsion; virtual photons mediate infinite-range proton repulsion while pions mediate short-range strong attraction, making very large nuclei unstable to alpha decay.

markScheme.criterion: State equilibrium separation $\approx 0.5\text{ fm}$ (accept 0.4–0.6 fm).
State maximum strong-force range $\approx 3.00\text{ fm}$ (accept 3–4 fm).
L1 (Area 1): Identifies infinite-range electrostatic repulsion between protons and short-range strong nuclear attraction between nucleons.
L1 (Area 1): States that strong nuclear force acts equally between protons and neutrons (hadrons).
L2 (Area 2): Quotes short-range profile: repulsive below 0.5 fm (prevents collapse) and attractive between 0.5 fm and 3 fm.
L2 (Area 2): Names virtual photon (electromagnetic) and pion / gluon (strong) exchange particles.
L3 (Area 3): Explains that in heavy nuclei whose diameter exceeds ~3 fm, distant protons repel without feeling strong attraction from one another.
L3 (Area 3): Concludes clearly why heavy nuclei require excess neutrons and shed alpha particles to reduce electrostatic repulsion and reach stability.

parts.prompt: State the approximate equilibrium separation $r_0$ and maximum effective range of the strong nuclear force from the graph.
parts.expectedAnswer: Equilibrium separation $r_0 \approx 0.5\text{ fm}$ and maximum range $3.00\text{ fm}$
workingSteps: Read zero-force crossing at $0.5\text{ fm}$.
Read asymptotic outer range at $3.00\text{ fm}$.

parts.prompt: Using your knowledge of nuclear forces and exchange particles, explain why light nuclei can be stable with equal numbers of protons and neutrons whereas very heavy nuclei become unstable and emit alpha particles.
parts.expectedAnswer: In every nucleus, protons repel each other via the infinite-range electromagnetic force (mediated by virtual photons) while nucleons interact via the short-range strong nuclear force (mediated by pions). The strong nuclear force is repulsive below zero point five fm and attractive up to three fm balancing electrostatic proton repulsion. In light nuclei, nuclear diameter is smaller than 3 fm so every nucleon attracts every other nucleon strongly; in very heavy nuclei, diameter exceeds 3 fm so distant protons still repel electrostatically without strong attraction, reducing binding stability until alpha emission lowers both proton number and size.
workingSteps: Area 1 (L1): Contrast infinite-range electrostatic repulsion between protons with short-range strong nuclear force between nearest-neighbour nucleons.
Area 2 (L2): Give quantitative ranges (<0.5 fm repulsive, 0.5–3 fm attractive, ~0 beyond 3 fm) and name exchange particles (virtual photon, pion).
Area 3 (L3): Explain why heavy nuclei exceeding ~3 fm diameter require excess neutrons and eventually shed alpha particles to restore force balance.

items.stem: A DC conductor made from magnesium diboride ($T_{\text{c}} = 39.0\text{ K}$) carries $100\text{ A}$ at $25.0\text{ K}$. Above $T_{\text{c}}$, its resistance is $0.250\,\Omega$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Zero electrical resistance at or below the critical temperature; operates in superconducting state with zero resistance and zero heating loss. (b) $P = I^2R = 2.50 × 10³ W$. (c) Expensive low-temperature cooling is required to stay below the critical temperature.

markScheme.criterion: Zero electrical resistance / resistivity at or below critical temperature $T_{\text{c}}$.
Correctly identify superconducting state with zero resistance and zero heating loss.
Substitute current and normal resistance into $P = I^2R$.
Expensive / technically difficult low-temperature cooling required below $T_{\text{c}}$.

parts.prompt: Define the critical temperature $T_{\text{c}}$ of a superconductor and state whether this conductor is superconducting at its operating temperature.
parts.expectedAnswer: Critical temperature is the transition temperature at or below which a superconductor has zero electrical resistance; at $25\text{ K}$ it is in the superconducting state with zero resistance and zero heating loss.
workingSteps: Define Tc as transition to exact zero resistance (at or below Tc).
Compare operating temperature 25 K against Tc = 39 K.

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal power that would be dissipated if the coil accidentally warmed just above $T_{\text{c}}$ while still carrying the same current.
State one major practical limitation preventing widespread room-temperature use of superconducting power cables.
parts.expectedAnswer: A major limitation is that expensive low-temperature cooling is required to stay below the critical temperature.
workingSteps: State cost and difficulty of maintaining low-temperature cooling below Tc.

items.stem: To determine capacitance in an RC circuit (R = 25 kΩ), a student plots ln(V / V) against t through (0 s, 2.079) and (20 s, 0.079). Calculate the capacitance.
items.workedSolution: Calculating the slope gives gradient m = (0.079 − 2.079) / (20 − 0) = -0.1000 s⁻¹. Time constant τ = −1/m = 10.00 s. Capacitance C = τ / R = 10.00 s / (25 × 10³ Ω) = 400 μF.

markScheme.criterion: Extracts linearized graph parameters accurately to obtain 400 μF.

items.stem: Over 10.0 s, a conveyor cart follows the velocity–time plot below after starting at rest 25.0 m past the starting mark (t = 0.0 s). Braking lasts from t = 7.0 s to t = 10.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Distance equals the trapezium area Δx = ½(10 + 5)(16) = 120 m. (b) Final distance from the reference mark = 25 + 120 = 145 m. (c) Mean speed = 120 / 10 = 12.0 m s⁻¹. (d) Braking acceleration = (0 − 16) / (10 − 7) = -5.33 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Identifies distance travelled as the area under the v–t trapezium.
Obtains Δx = 120 m.
Adds 25 m offset to obtain 145 m.
Divides distance travelled from (a) by 10 s.
Obtains mean speed = 12.0 m s⁻¹.
Obtains braking acceleration = -5.33 m s⁻².

items.stem: A rubber strip is pulled in tension until its strain reaches 0.8. On the graph below, the limit of proportionality occurs at 0.4.
items.workedSolution: (a) From the proportional region slope, E = 170 / 0.4 = 425 MPa. (b) Energy per unit volume = ½(0.4)(170) + ½(170 + 240)(0.4) = 116 MJ m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates initial gradient σ / ε up to ε = 0.4.
Obtains E = 425 MPa.
Identifies work per unit volume as total area under the σ–ε graph.
Splits area into initial triangle plus upper trapezium.
Obtains 116 MJ m⁻³.

workingSteps: Read σ = 170 MPa at ε = 0.4.

parts.prompt: Calculate the work done per unit volume in stretching the sample from zero strain to 0.8.
workingSteps: Area from 0 to 0.4 = ½(0.4)(170) = 34.0 MJ m⁻³.
Area from 0.4 to 0.8 = ½(170 + 240)(0.4) = 82.0 MJ m⁻³; total = 116 MJ m⁻³.

items.stem: Graphing force F against r⁻² up to 60.0 m⁻² gives the linear plot below for two charged metal-coated spheres on a balance. The balance carries a steady zero offset F₀.
items.workedSolution: (a) At r⁻² = 0, systematic tare offset F₀ = 0.300 N. (b) Gradient = (1.9 − 0.3) / 60 = 0.0267 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Reads intercept F₀ = 0.300 N.
Evaluates ΔF = 1.9 − 0.3 using intercept from (a).
Divides ΔF by 60 m⁻² and states correct unit N m².
Obtains 0.0267 N m².

items.stem: A student measures the potential difference V across a non-ohmic resistor as the current I increases from 0.0 A to 1.0 A. The graph shows the resulting non-linear V–I characteristic.
items.workedSolution: (a) At I = 1 A, V = 9.00 V. (b) Static resistance R = V / I = 9 / 1 = 9.00 Ω (the upper segment gradient 12.0 Ω is ΔV / ΔI, not R).

markScheme.criterion: Reads V = 9.00 V at I = 1 A.
Selects R = V / I rather than local segment gradient ΔV / ΔI.
Substitutes V = 9 V and I = 1 A.
Obtains R = 9.00 Ω.

items.stem: In a photodiode experiment, a student plots data with vertical error bars from 4.0 mW to 20.0 mW. The graph shows the shallowest acceptable line of worst fit through the error bars.
items.workedSolution: (a) At 20 mW, y₂ = 52.0 μA. (b) Worst-fit gradient = (52 − 12) / (20 − 4) = 2.50 μA mW⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Reads y₂ = 52.0 μA.
Reads y₁ = 12 μA at x₁ = 4 mW and forms Δy / Δx.
Subtracts x₁ = 4 mW in the denominator (20 − 4).
Obtains 2.50 μA mW⁻¹.

items.stem: A practical investigation of a metal wire produces the suppressed-origin graph below with vertical error bars of ±0.14 mm. Best-fit points (20.0 N, 2.760 mm) and (60.0 N, 4.840 mm) are marked. The shallowest acceptable line has gradient 0.04360 mm N⁻¹. Separately, the wire diameter is d = 0.48 ± 0.012 mm.
items.workedSolution: (a) Best-fit gradient m_best = (4.840 − 2.760) / (60.0 − 20.0) = 0.05200 mm N⁻¹ ≈ 0.0520 mm N⁻¹. (b) Δm = |0.04360 − 0.05200| = 8.40 × 10⁻³ mm N⁻¹. (c) A suppressed origin expands the plotted data to fill more than half of the grid improving reading precision. (d) %Δm = 16.15%, %ΔA = 2 × %Δd = 5.000%, total = 21.15% ≈ 21.2%.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly substitutes large-triangle coordinates (4.840 − 2.760) / (60.0 − 20.0).
Obtains best-fit gradient = 0.0520 mm N⁻¹ with correct compound SI unit.
Calculates Δm = |m_worst − m_best| = 8.40 × 10⁻³ mm N⁻¹.
States that a false origin expands the plotted data to fill more than half of the grid improving reading precision.
Evaluates %Δm = 16.2% and %ΔA = 2 × %Δd = 5.00%.
Sums percentage uncertainties to obtain 21.2%.

items.stem: From five error-bar points for a trolley on a tilted air track (Paper 3A), the best-fit line has gradient 6.40 m s⁻². Steepest and shallowest worst-fit lines through all error bars have gradients 7.58 m s⁻² and 5.33 m s⁻². Determine the percentage uncertainty in the gradient.
items.workedSolution: First calculate the half-spread $\Delta m = \frac{1}{2}(m_{\max} - m_{\min}) = \frac{1}{2}(7.58 - 5.33) = 1.12 m s⁻²$. Then percentage uncertainty $= (\Delta m / m_{\mathrm{best}}) \times 100\% = 17.5\%$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly applies half-spread rule to obtain 17.5% (3 sf).

items.stem: Starting from decimal 0, a 4-stage binary ripple counter receives 39 rising clock pulses. What decimal value is then stored in the counter?
items.workedSolution: A 4-bit binary counter has $2^4 = 16$ states ($0$ to $15$). After 39 pulses, $39 = 2 \times 16 + 7$, so the stored decimal count is 7 (binary 0111).

markScheme.criterion: Stored decimal value equals 7.

items.stem: The displacement–time graph shows the motion of a remote-controlled car moving in a straight line over 15.0 s. It moves back toward the start between t = 9.0 s and t = 15.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Maximum displacement at the plateau = 53.0 m. (b) Return-stage velocity = (19 − 53) / (15 − 9) = -5.67 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Reads plateau displacement = 53.0 m.
Uses gradient formula Δs / Δt = (19 − 53) / (15 − 9).
Retains negative sign for motion back toward the origin.
Obtains -5.67 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Current I against potential difference V is plotted below for a uniform metal wire. Its length is 2.00 m, its cross-sectional area is 8.40 × 10⁻⁸ m², and the line runs from the origin to I = 0.500 A at V = 5.00 V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area. (b) Gradient = 0.1000 A V⁻¹, so R = 1 / gradient = 10.0 Ω. (c) ρ = RA/L = 4.200 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 4.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: States resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area.
Correctly specifies all quantities (or notes constant temperature / material property).
Computes large-triangle gradient m = ΔI/ΔV = 0.100 A V⁻¹ and takes its reciprocal R = 1/m.
Correct wire resistance R = 10.0 Ω.
Substitutes R, A, and L correctly into ρ = RA/L.
Correct resistivity 4.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m with unit Ω m.

parts.prompt: Define the electrical resistivity of a material.
parts.expectedAnswer: Electrical resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area, where resistance, cross-sectional area, and length are measured for a uniform sample at constant temperature.
workingSteps: State the definition in terms of a conductor of unit length and unit cross-sectional area.
Identify that resistivity is an intrinsic property of the material at constant temperature.

parts.prompt: Determine the resistance of the wire from the gradient of the I–V line of best fit using a large triangle.
workingSteps: Because I is on the vertical axis, R = 1 / m = 10.00 Ω ≈ 10.0 Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resistivity of the alloy, stating the appropriate SI unit.
workingSteps: Evaluate ρ = 4.200 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 4.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

items.stem: The graph shows how the force on a spring varies with extension up to 0.4 m. The spring obeys Hooke's law. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored at x = 0.4 m.
items.workedSolution: Elastic potential energy equals the triangular area under the F–x line: E_p = ½ F x = ½(64)(0.4) = 12.8 J.

markScheme.criterion: Computes triangular area ½(64)(0.4) = 12.8 J (C).

items.stem: A student uses a Geiger–Müller tube to measure the corrected count rate C of a short-lived radioisotope sample over 80.0 s. The straight-line semi-log graph shows ln(C / s⁻¹) plotted against time t.
items.workedSolution: (a) Vertical intercept at t = 0 is ln(C₀ / s⁻¹) = 8.20. (b) Gradient = (3.4 − 8.2) / 80 = -0.0600 s⁻¹ (which equals −λ).

markScheme.criterion: Reads vertical intercept = 8.20.
Uses large triangle (3.4 − 8.2) / 80.
Includes negative sign and unit s⁻¹.
Obtains gradient = -0.0600 s⁻¹.

items.stem: The resting ECG trace of a patient shows a regular R–R interval of $T_{\text{RR}} = 0.80\text{ s}$. Calculate the patient's resting heart rate in beats per minute.
items.workedSolution: Heart rate is given by $\text{HR} = \frac{60}{T_{\text{RR}}} = \frac{60}{0.80} = 75.0 beats min⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 75.0 beats min⁻¹.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes beat frequency in Hz rather than multiplying by 60 to obtain beats per minute.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies 60 by the period instead of dividing 60 by the R–R interval.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Doubles the cardiac rate by counting two waves per cardiac cycle.

items.stem: Velocity versus time over 16.0 s is graphed below for a camera trolley on a straight track. Positive values represent northward velocity. Between t = 8.0 s and t = 12.0 s, it brakes and reverses.
items.workedSolution: (a) The curve crosses the time axis at t = 11 s. Positive area = 90.0 m and unsigned negative area = 18.0 m, giving total distance = 108 m. (b) Net displacement = 90.0 − 18.0 = 72.0 m; average velocity = 72.0 / 16 = 4.50 m s⁻¹. (c) Acceleration = (−4 − 12) / (12 − 8) = -4.00 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Finds zero-crossing t = 11 s and evaluates both unsigned areas (90.0 m and 18.0 m).
Obtains total distance = 108 m.
Subtracts areas for net displacement (72.0 m) and divides by 16 s.
Obtains average velocity = 4.50 m s⁻¹.
Obtains acceleration = -4.00 m s⁻² including negative sign.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total distance travelled between t = 0.0 s and t = 16.0 s.
workingSteps: Velocity crosses zero at t = 11 s; forward area = 90.0 m.
Unsigned reverse area = 18.0 m, so total distance = 90.0 + 18.0 = 108 m.

parts.prompt: Determine the net displacement and hence calculate the average velocity over the 16.0 s interval.
workingSteps: Net displacement Δs = 90.0 − 18.0 = 72.0 m.
Average velocity = Δs / Δt = 72.0 / 16 = 4.50 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: The force–time graph below tracks a 1.0 s forward force pulse on a puck of mass 2.5 kg. Initially, the object has momentum 10.0 kg m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Calculating the F–t area gives impulse J = ½(1 + 0.6)(60) = 48.0 N s. (b) Final momentum p_f = 10 + 48.0 = 58.0 kg m s⁻¹. (c) Speed increase Δv = 48.0 / 2.5 = 19.2 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes impulse from the trapezium area under the F–t curve.
Obtains J = 48.0 N s.
Adds 10 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 58.0 kg m s⁻¹.
Divides impulse from (a) by 2.5 kg.
Obtains Δv = 19.2 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Plotted below is current I (vertical axis) against potential difference V (horizontal axis) for a filament lamp. Which statement correctly explains the curve's shape?
items.workedSolution: On an I–V graph (I on the vertical axis, V on the horizontal axis), gradient equals reciprocal of resistance. For this filament lamp, resistance increases with potential difference because heating increases lattice ion vibration amplitude and electron collisions.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that resistance increases with potential difference because heating increases lattice ion vibration amplitude and electron collisions.

options.label: A
options.text: Resistance decreases with potential difference because heating frees additional metallic conduction electrons.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses a metal filament with an NTC semiconductor thermistor.

options.label: B
options.text: It exhibits resistance increases with potential difference because heating increases lattice ion vibration amplitude and electron collisions.

options.label: C
options.text: Resistance stays constant across the entire voltage range because the curve passes through the origin.
options.distractorRationale: Passing through the origin does not imply linearity or constant resistance.

options.label: D
options.text: Resistance drops to zero once the potential difference becomes negative.
options.distractorRationale: A filament lamp is symmetric in reverse polarity and still resists current.

items.stem: From the origin to the endpoint Q = 6.00 mC, V = 15.0 V, a capacitor gives a linear charging plot. Calculate its capacitance.
items.workedSolution: First convert charge to SI units: Q = 6 mC = 6.000 × 10⁻³ C. Capacitance C = Q / V = 4.000 × 10⁻⁴ F = 400 μF.

items.stem: Which statement correctly states Hooke's law for a stretched wire?
items.workedSolution: Hooke's law holds only up to the limit of proportionality (distinct from the elastic limit where permanent plastic deformation starts). Therefore option D is correct: extension is directly proportional to force up to the limit of proportionality.

markScheme.criterion: Select option D: extension is directly proportional to force up to the limit of proportionality.

items.stem: Shown below is an acceleration–time graph lasting 12.0 s for a glider. At t = 0.0 s, it moves eastward at 12.0 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Maximum speed is reached as acceleration drops through zero at t = 6.00 s. (b) Positive area = 25.0 m s⁻¹, giving v_max = 12 + 25.0 = 37.0 m s⁻¹. (c) Negative area magnitude = 9.00 m s⁻¹, so v_final = 37.0 − 9.00 = 28.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: States t = 6.00 s.
Evaluates positive area up to 6 s (25.0 m s⁻¹) and adds u₀ = 12 m s⁻¹.
Obtains v_max = 37.0 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts negative area (9.00 m s⁻¹) from v_max.
Obtains final velocity = 28.0 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Shown below is the force–distance curve over 8.0 m for a trolley of mass 1.6 kg moving at 4.5 m s⁻¹ at x = 0.0 m.
items.workedSolution: (a) Combining forward and resistive areas gives W = 54.0 − 4.00 = 50.0 J. (b) v = √(4.5² + 2(50.0)/1.6) = 9.10 m s⁻¹. (c) Mean force = 50.0 / 8 = 6.25 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates positive (54.0 J) and negative (−4.00 J) areas.
Obtains net work W = 50.0 J.
Uses ½mv² = ½(1.6)(4.5²) + W.
Obtains v = 9.10 m s⁻¹.
Divides net work by 8 m to get 6.25 N.

items.stem: With mass 5.0 kg, a trolley on a straight horizontal track follows the momentum–time plot given below. Determine the net work done on the object between t = 2.0 s and t = 7.0 s.
items.workedSolution: Kinetic energy change gives the net work via E_k = p² / (2m): W = ΔE_k = (30² − 10²) / (2 × 5) = 80.0 J.

items.stem: Data collected for a conducting polymer strip produce the linear resistance R against L / A plot reaching 400.0 m⁻¹. A steady lead-resistance offset R₀ shifts the vertical intercept.
items.workedSolution: (a) At the vertical axis, offset R₀ = 8.00 Ω. (b) The gradient equals resistivity: ρ = (36 − 8) / 400 = 0.0700 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: States R₀ = 8.00 Ω.
Identifies ρ with the gradient ΔR / Δ(L / A).
Subtracts R₀ = 8 Ω from 36 Ω before dividing by 400 m⁻¹.
Obtains ρ = 0.0700 Ω m.

workingSteps: At L / A = 0.0 m⁻¹, the vertical intercept gives R₀ = 8.00 Ω.

workingSteps: From R = ρ(L / A) + R₀, ρ equals the gradient ΔR / Δ(L / A).

items.stem: A cell supplies current I across 0.0 A to 4.0 A to a variable resistor. Its terminal potential difference V is plotted below.
items.workedSolution: (a) Open-circuit intercept gives ε = 13.0 V. (b) Gradient = (7 − 13) / 4 = -1.50 V A⁻¹. (c) Mean terminal p.d. = ½(13 + 7) = 10.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reads ε = 13.0 V at I = 0.
Evaluates (7 − 13) / 4 including negative sign.
Obtains -1.50 V A⁻¹.
Uses ½(13 + 7) or area divided by 4 A.
Obtains 10.0 V.

items.stem: A student tests whether pendulum period T and length L obey T = k Lⁿ. The student plots ln(T / s) against ln(L / m) from (−1.60, −0.10 ± 0.06) to (0.00, 0.70 ± 0.06).
items.workedSolution: (a) Taking natural logarithms of a power law gives ln y = n ln x + ln k, a straight line with gradient n and vertical intercept ln k. (b) n = 0.500. (c) Δn = 0.0750. (d) k = 2.01 s m⁻¹/². (e) Random uncertainties scatter readings unpredictably around the trend line and are reduced by repeating and averaging trials. Systematic errors shift all readings in one direction and are not reduced by averaging.

markScheme.criterion: Writes ln T = n ln L + ln k.
Identifies gradient = n and vertical intercept = ln k.
Computes Δ(ln T)/Δ(ln L) over the plotted line.
Obtains exponent n = 0.500.
Computes m_max = 0.575 and m_min = 0.425 from endpoint uncertainty bars.
Obtains Δn = 0.0750.
Evaluates k = e^(0.70) = 2.01 s m⁻¹/².
Links stopwatch reaction scatter to random uncertainty reduced by timing 20 oscillations and averaging.
Links measuring to the top rather than centre of mass of the bob to constant systematic error.

parts.prompt: Explain how plotting ln T against ln L linearizes T = k Lⁿ and state the physical meaning of the gradient and vertical intercept.
parts.expectedAnswer: Taking natural logarithms of a power law gives ln y = n ln x + ln k, a straight line with gradient n and vertical intercept ln k.
workingSteps: Taking natural logarithms of a power law gives ln y = n ln x + ln k, a straight line with gradient n and vertical intercept ln k

parts.prompt: Determine the experimental exponent n from the best-fit line.
Calculate the absolute uncertainty Δn in the exponent using the dashed maximum and minimum gradient lines.
Determine the constant k from the vertical intercept ln k = 0.70 (note theoretical 2π/√g with g = 9.8 m s⁻² equals 2.01 s m⁻¹/²).
Distinguish between random uncertainties and systematic errors when measuring pendulum period with a handheld stopwatch and metre rule.
parts.expectedAnswer: Random uncertainties scatter readings unpredictably around the trend line and are reduced by repeating and averaging trials. Systematic errors shift all readings in one direction and are not reduced by averaging.
workingSteps: Random uncertainties scatter readings unpredictably around the trend line and are reduced by repeating and averaging trials, whereas systematic errors shift all readings in one direction and are not reduced by averaging

items.stem: Which statement correctly pairs the exchange particles for the electrostatic repulsion between protons and the strong nuclear force between nucleons?
items.workedSolution: Virtual photons mediate electromagnetic interactions, whereas pions (or gluons between quarks) mediate the strong nuclear force between nucleons. Therefore option C is correct: virtual photon mediates electromagnetic repulsion while pions mediate the strong nuclear force.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: virtual photon mediates electromagnetic repulsion while pions mediate the strong nuclear force. Reject 'force mediator'; use exchange particle / boson.

options.label: A
options.text: In AQA particle physics, W bosons mediate electromagnetic repulsion while virtual photons mediate the strong nuclear force
options.distractorRationale: Swaps the weak exchange bosons with the electromagnetic and strong exchange particles.

options.label: B
options.text: In AQA particle physics, gravitons mediate electrostatic repulsion while electrons mediate the strong nuclear force
options.distractorRationale: Electrons are leptons and do not act as strong force exchange particles.

options.label: C
options.text: In AQA particle physics, virtual photon mediates electromagnetic repulsion while pions mediate the strong nuclear force

options.label: D
options.text: In AQA particle physics, kaons mediate electrostatic repulsion while neutrinos mediate the strong nuclear force
options.distractorRationale: Neutrinos are leptons unaffected by the strong force and kaons are strange mesons.

items.stem: A copper cable of resistance $0.450\,\Omega$ carries a steady current of $60.0\text{ A}$. It is replaced by a superconducting cable cooled below its $92.0\text{ K}$ critical temperature carrying the same current. Calculate the electrical heating power saved.
items.workedSolution: Copper heating loss $= I^2R = 60.0^2 \times 0.450 = 1.62 × 10³ W$, whereas the superconductor dissipates $0\text{ W}$, saving 1.62 × 10³ W. Option A (1.62 × 10³ W) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Power saved $= 1.62 × 10³ W$ (1.62 × 10³ W, option A).

items.stem: Discharging through a 20 kΩ resistor, a capacitor gives a straight-line graph of ln(V / V) against time t. Two points on the line are (0 s, 1.872) and (14 s, -0.128).
items.workedSolution: (a) Taking natural logarithms gives a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the reciprocal of the time constant and a vertical intercept equal to the natural logarithm of the initial potential difference. (b) The line has gradient m = -0.1429 s⁻¹, so τ = −1/m = 7.000 s ≈ 7.00 s. (c) C = τ/R = 350 μF. (d) Uses all measured data points along a straight line of best fit rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.

markScheme.criterion: Shows taking natural logs produces a linear relation between ln(V) and t.
Identifies gradient = −1/τ and vertical intercept = ln(V₀).
Evaluates negative gradient m = -0.143 s⁻¹ and uses τ = −1/m.
Correct time constant τ = 7.00 s.
Correct capacitance C = τ / R = 350 μF.
States that it uses all measured data points along a straight line of best fit rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.

parts.prompt: Explain why plotting the natural logarithm of potential difference against time yields a straight line, identifying the physical meaning of its gradient and vertical intercept.
parts.expectedAnswer: From the exponential discharge equation, taking natural logarithms gives a straight line with a negative gradient equal to minus the reciprocal of the time constant and a vertical intercept equal to the natural logarithm of the initial potential difference.
workingSteps: Take natural logarithms of both sides of the exponential decay equation.
Compare with a linear equation to identify the negative gradient and the vertical intercept.

parts.prompt: Determine the time constant τ of the RC circuit from the gradient of the graph.
workingSteps: Time constant τ = −1 / m = 7.000 s ≈ 7.00 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the capacitance of the capacitor in μF given R = 20 kΩ.
State why determining τ from the gradient of a ln(V) against t graph is more reliable than drawing an initial tangent to a V against t curve.
parts.expectedAnswer: The logarithmic gradient method is more reliable because it uses all measured data points along a straight line of best fit rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.
workingSteps: Drawing a tangent to a curve by eye is subjective and sensitive to noise at a single point, whereas a linear best-fit averages random errors over all readings.

items.stem: From t = 12.0 s to rest at t = 16.0 s, a lift cage brakes uniformly along the velocity–time graph shown (initial offset 38.0 m from the reference mark). Use the braking slope to calculate its acceleration.
items.workedSolution: Acceleration equals the velocity–time slope from t = 12 s to t = 16 s, so a = (0 − 16) / (16 − 12) = -4.00 m s⁻².

items.stem: Shown below is the stress–strain plot for a thin plastic strip pulled up to strain 0.6. Beyond strain 0.3, the slope decreases. Use the graph area to find the work done per unit volume up to strain 0.6.
items.workedSolution: Integrating via geometric areas under the σ–ε graph (1 MPa × 1 = 1 MJ m⁻³) gives u = ½(0.3)(150) + ½(150 + 210)(0.3) = 76.5 MJ m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Sums triangle and trapezium areas under σ–ε curve to obtain 76.5 MJ m⁻³ (D).

items.stem: The straight-line plot tracks force F versus inverse-square separation r⁻² reaching 20.0 m⁻² for two charged metal-coated spheres on a balance. Find the gradient ΔF / Δ(r⁻²) of the line.
items.workedSolution: At r⁻² = 0.0 m⁻², tare offset F₀ = 0.1 N; at r⁻² = 20 m⁻², F = 0.7 N. Gradient = (0.7 − 0.1) / 20 = 0.0300 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts tare offset F₀ = 0.1 N to get (0.7 − 0.1) / 20 = 0.0300 N m² (D).

items.stem: The graph shows the non-linear V–I characteristic for a metal filament lamp. Calculate the electrical resistance of the component at a current of 4.0 A.
items.workedSolution: Electrical resistance at an operating point is defined by R = V / I (not the local slope ΔV / ΔI). At I = 4 A, V = 14 V, so R = 14 / 4 = 3.50 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses static ratio R = V / I = 14 / 4 = 3.50 Ω (A).

items.stem: In a magnetic-field coil experiment, the graph shows the steepest line of worst fit drawn from 1.0 A to 6.0 A. Calculate the gradient of this worst-fit line.
items.workedSolution: At x₁ = 1 A, y₁ = 3 mT; at x₂ = 6 A, y₂ = 22 mT. Worst-fit gradient m_worst = (22 − 3) / (6 − 1) = 3.80 mT A⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δy / Δx = (22 − 3) / (6 − 1) = 3.80 mT A⁻¹ (D).

options.distractorRationale: Subtracts y₁ in the numerator but divides by x₂ instead of the horizontal span (x₂ − x₁).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes the secant y₂ / x₂ as though the worst-fit line passed through the origin (0, 0) rather than (x₁, y₁).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inverts Δx / Δy instead of evaluating Δy / Δx.

items.stem: A suppressed-origin graph for a steel spring has best-fit gradient Δy / Δx = 0.01320 m N⁻¹, measured across 6.0 N to 22.0 N. Find the stiffness (1 / gradient) of the spring.
items.workedSolution: Because the axes plot length against load, stiffness k = 1 / gradient = 1 / 0.01320 = 75.76 N m⁻¹ ≈ 75.8 N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes reciprocal constant 1 / gradient = 75.8 N m⁻¹.

items.stem: Accelerating down a frictionless ramp with sin θ = 0.6, a dynamics cart yields the v²–s plot starting at s = 0.0 m up to s = 1.0 m (use g = 9.8 m s⁻²). Determine the slope Δ(v²) / Δs from the graph.
items.workedSolution: From v² = u₀² + (2g sin θ)s, the vertical intercept is u₀² = 3.2 m² s⁻² and at s = 1 m, v² = 14.96 m² s⁻². Gradient = (14.96 − 3.2) / 1 = 2(9.8)(0.6) = 11.8 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept u₀² = 3.2 m² s⁻² (or evaluates 2 × 9.8 × 0.6) to get 11.8 m s⁻² (A).

items.stem: A student plots spring load $F$ against extension $e$ using instruments with fixed absolute uncertainties $\pm \Delta F$ and $\pm \Delta e$. Which statement correctly describes the plotted error bars across all five points?
items.workedSolution: Under AQA Paper 3A graphical rules: All error bars have identical constant size because absolute uncertainty is fixed across the range.

markScheme.criterion: All error bars have identical constant size because absolute uncertainty is fixed across the range.

options.text: Error bars double in length each time the load doubles.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses fixed absolute uncertainty with fixed percentage uncertainty.

options.label: B
options.text: Only the highest and lowest points require error bars because intermediate points never constrain worst-fit lines.
options.distractorRationale: All plotted points carry error bars and every worst-fit line must pass through every error bar.

options.label: C
options.text: All error bars have identical constant size because absolute uncertainty is fixed across the range.

options.label: D
options.text: Error bars represent systematic zero error and therefore shift only in one direction from each point.
options.distractorRationale: Error bars represent random/reading uncertainty symmetrically as ±Δx and ±Δy.

items.stem: An electronics student tests a modulo-12 counter made from rising-edge D-type flip-flops with a 1500 Hz clock input. Its output signals are shown in the timing diagram.
items.workedSolution: (a) $f_{\mathrm{out}} = 125 Hz$. (b) Count after 55 pulses is 7. (c) Q3 and Q2 connected to an AND gate driving master reset.

markScheme.criterion: Divides clock frequency by modulus 12.
Obtains 125 Hz.
Finds remainder of 55 divided by 12.
Obtains decimal state 7.
Converts decimal 12 to binary 1100.
Identifies Q3 and Q2 connected to an AND gate driving master reset.

parts.prompt: Calculate the repetition frequency of the counter's full output cycle in Hz.
workingSteps: $f_{\mathrm{out}} = \frac{f_{\mathrm{clk}}}{12} = \frac{1500}{12} = 125 Hz$.

parts.prompt: Starting from zero, determine the decimal count stored after 55 rising clock pulses.
workingSteps: Take remainder modulo 12: 55 mod 12 = 7.

parts.prompt: Specify which counter output bits must feed an active-high AND gate to reset this counter automatically on count 12.
parts.expectedAnswer: Q3 and Q2 connected to an AND gate driving master reset.
workingSteps: Write decimal 12 in 4-bit binary: 1100.
Connect the HIGH bits (Q3 and Q2 connected to an AND gate driving master reset).

items.stem: The displacement–time graph shows the motion of a glider moving along an air track. Calculate its signed velocity during the return stage between t = 10.0 s and t = 20.0 s.
items.workedSolution: From t = 10 s to t = 20 s, displacement changes from 73 m to 39 m. Velocity v = (39 − 73) / (20 − 10) = -3.40 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: On the I–V graph below (y-axis: I, x-axis: V), data for a uniform metal wire pass through the origin and (5.00 V, 0.625 A). Its length is 1.50 m and its cross-sectional area is 7.20 × 10⁻⁸ m². Evaluate the resistivity of the metal.
items.workedSolution: Using the two plotted points, slope m = ΔI / ΔV = 0.6250 A / 5.000 V = 0.1250 A V⁻¹. Since gradient = 1/R, R = 1/m = 8.000 Ω. Therefore ρ = R A / L = 3.840 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 3.84 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses R = 1 / gradient and ρ = R A / L to obtain 3.84 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

items.stem: The graph shows how the force on a light spring varies with compression up to 0.5 m. The compressed spring is released from rest on a smooth horizontal bench to launch a 0.25 kg puck.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies k as the gradient ΔF / Δx.
Obtains k = 80.0 N m⁻¹.
Uses triangular area ½Fx.
Obtains E_p = 10.0 J.
Equates ½(0.25)v² to stored elastic energy from (b).
Obtains v = 8.94 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: When recording a surface ECG trace, conducting gel and a high-input-resistance differential amplifier are used. Why are both essential?
items.workedSolution: Abrading dead skin and applying conducting gel lowers contact resistance and high input resistance prevents loading, while shielded leads and patient stillness suppress mains hum and skeletal muscle EMG potentials.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that conducting gel lowers contact resistance and high input resistance prevents loading.

options.label: A
options.text: Conducting gel insulates the skin completely while low input resistance boosts current drawn from the heart.
options.distractorRationale: Gel reduces rather than increases skin impedance, and drawing current would collapse the tiny voltage signal.

options.label: B
options.text: Conducting gel generates the cardiac action potential while low input resistance blocks radio waves.
options.distractorRationale: The heart's pacemaker generates the action potential; shielded cables and differential rejection suppress interference.

options.label: C
options.text: Gel prevents thermal conduction while the amplifier converts AC mains directly into heart pulses.
options.distractorRationale: Mains pickup is unwanted noise rejected by differential amplification and shielding.

options.label: D
options.text: Because conducting gel lowers contact resistance and high input resistance prevents loading of the tiny millivolt cardiac potential difference.

items.stem: Between t = 0.0 s and t = 10.0 s, a student records the velocity of a trolley along a straight track on the plot below. Take eastward motion as positive. Determine the total distance covered during this motion.
items.workedSolution: Splitting the graph at the zero crossing at t = 7 s. Forward area (0 to 7 s) = ½(2)(16) + (3)(16) + ½(2)(16) = 80.0 m. Reverse area magnitude (7 s to 10 s) = ½(1)(8) + (2)(8) = 20.0 m. Total distance = 80.0 + 20.0 = 100 m.

markScheme.criterion: Sums unsigned positive (80.0 m) and negative (20.0 m) velocity–time areas to obtain 100 m (A).

items.stem: Starting with 6.0 kg m s⁻¹ of momentum, a small 2.0 kg block feels the 0.8 s forward resultant force plotted below. Find its momentum immediately after the pulse.
items.workedSolution: Impulse Δp = ½(0.8 + 0.4)(50) = 30.0 N s. Final momentum p_f = p₀ + Δp = 6 + 30.0 = 36.0 kg m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Adds impulse (30.0 N s) to p₀ = 6 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 36.0 kg m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: For a light-emitting diode (LED), current is graphed vertically against potential difference horizontally. One operating point is highlighted at V = 3.00 V and I = 30 mA.
items.workedSolution: (a) R = V / I = 100.0 Ω ≈ 100 Ω. (b) Connect a potential divider with a series protective resistor, an ammeter in series, and a voltmeter in parallel across the component, and reverse the supply connections for negative readings. (c) Conducts sharply above the forward threshold voltage and has very high resistance in reverse bias.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes operating-point values into R = V / I (converting mA to A if needed).
Correct static resistance 100 Ω.
Specifies potential divider (or variable supply) with series ammeter and parallel voltmeter.
Includes a series protective resistor and reversing supply connections for negative voltages.
Correctly describes how resistance changes across the graph.
Correct microscopic explanation: conducts sharply above the forward threshold voltage and has very high resistance in reverse bias.

parts.prompt: Calculate the static resistance of the component at the highlighted operating point.
workingSteps: Recall that static resistance at a point is R = V / I (not the inverse of the local tangent).
Substitute V = 3.000 V and I = 0.03000 A to obtain R = 100.0 Ω ≈ 100 Ω.

parts.prompt: Describe the circuit arrangement and experimental procedure used to obtain a complete I–V characteristic safely across positive and negative potential differences.
parts.expectedAnswer: To obtain the full characteristic safely, connect a potential divider with a series protective resistor, an ammeter in series, and a voltmeter in parallel across the component, and reverse the supply connections for negative readings.
workingSteps: Use a potential divider to vary potential difference smoothly from zero while limiting excessive current with a protective resistor.
Measure current with a series ammeter, potential difference with a parallel voltmeter, and reverse the supply leads for negative polarity.

parts.prompt: Explain the physical shape of the I–V characteristic in terms of charge carriers and resistance.
parts.expectedAnswer: The curve shows that the component conducts sharply above the forward threshold voltage and has very high resistance in reverse bias.
workingSteps: Link the changing ratio of potential difference to current directly to the microscopic conduction mechanism.

items.stem: During a charging test, a capacitor reaches Q = 4.50 mC when V = 18.0 V. The graph tracks Q from zero against potential difference V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Capacitance is the charge stored per unit potential difference across the plates. (b) C = Q / V = 250 μF. (c) Triangular area E = ½ Q V = 0.04050 J ≈ 0.0405 J.

markScheme.criterion: States charge stored per unit potential difference across the plates.
Correct capacitance 250 μF.
Recognises triangular area E = ½ Q V and converts mC to C.
Correct stored energy 0.0405 J.

parts.prompt: Define capacitance.
parts.expectedAnswer: Capacitance is the charge stored per unit potential difference across the plates.
workingSteps: State the definition as the ratio of charge stored to potential difference.

parts.prompt: Deduce the capacitance of the capacitor from the graph in μF.
Determine the electrical energy stored in the capacitor using the shaded triangular area under the graph.
workingSteps: Because V increases linearly from 0 to V_max as charge builds up, energy stored equals the triangular area E = ½ Q V.

items.stem: A steel wire has length $2.40\text{ m}$ and cross-sectional area $0.750\text{ mm}^2$. It extends elastically by $2.40\text{ mm}$ under a tensile load of $150\text{ N}$. Calculate the Young modulus of the steel in gigapascals.
items.workedSolution: $\sigma = 150 / (0.750 \times 10^{-6}) = 2.00 \times 10^8\text{ Pa}$; $\varepsilon = 2.40 \times 10^{-3} / 2.40 = 1.00 \times 10^{-3}$; $E = \sigma/\varepsilon = 200 GPa$. Option A (200 GPa) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Young modulus $E = 200 GPa$ (200 GPa, option A).

items.stem: Starting at t = 0.0 s at 11.0 m s⁻¹ forward, a train follows the acceleration–time curve below for 10.0 s. Use the graph area to calculate its maximum forward speed.
items.workedSolution: Because speed grows whenever a > 0 (from t = 0.0 s until a = 0 at t = 4 s). Positive area Δv_max = (2)(10) + ½(2)(10) = 30.0 m s⁻¹. Maximum speed = u₀ + Δv_max = 11 + 30.0 = 41.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Integrates positive acceleration up to t = 4 s (30.0 m s⁻¹) and adds 11 m s⁻¹ to get 41.0 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Speed squared v² is graphed against s from s = 0.0 m to s = 1.0 m as a steel ball descends a smooth inclined track (sin θ = 0.6). It enters the timed section with non-zero speed u₀. Use the graph to calculate its gradient.
items.workedSolution: From v² = u₀² + (2g sin θ)s, the vertical intercept is u₀² = 3.2 m² s⁻² and at s = 1 m, v² = 14.972 m² s⁻². Gradient = (14.972 − 3.2) / 1 = 2(9.81)(0.6) = 11.8 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept u₀² = 3.2 m² s⁻² (or evaluates 2 × 9.81 × 0.6) to get 11.8 m s⁻² (C).

items.stem: With initial speed 6.0 m s⁻¹, a toy car of mass 3.0 kg travels from x = 0.0 m to x = 15.0 m under the force plotted below. Deduce the net work done by the resultant force.
items.workedSolution: Splitting positive and negative areas: forward work (0 to 12 m) = 162 J; resistive work (12 m to 15 m) = −9.00 J. Net work = 162 − 9.00 = 153 J.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts resistive triangle (9.00 J) from positive trapezium (162 J) to get 153 J (A).

items.stem: Over the interval t = 2.0 s to t = 6.0 s, a uniform net force acts on a small cart of mass 3.0 kg on a smooth level track. Its momentum against time is plotted below.
items.workedSolution: (a) From the gradient of the p–t line, F = Δp / Δt = (18 − 6) / (6 − 2) = 3.00 N. (b) By the work–energy theorem, W = ΔE_k = (18² − 6²) / (2 × 3) = 48.0 J.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies resultant force as gradient Δp / Δt of the p–t graph.
Obtains F = 3.00 N.
Relates net work to ΔE_k = (p₂² − p₁²) / (2m).
Substitutes p₁ = 6 kg m s⁻¹, p₂ = 18 kg m s⁻¹, and m = 3 kg.
Obtains W = 48.0 J.

items.stem: Plotted below is total resistance R against L / A between 0.0 m⁻¹ and 160.0 m⁻¹ for a conducting polymer strip. Find the resistivity ρ of the material.
items.workedSolution: Because the straight line obeys R = ρ(L / A) + R₀, gradient equals ρ, yielding ΔR / Δ(L / A) = (26 − 6) / 160 = 0.125 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept R₀ = 6 Ω to obtain ρ = (26 − 6) / 160 = 0.125 Ω m (A).

items.stem: Across a cell, terminal potential difference V drops linearly with current I up to 4.0 A. Deduce the signed gradient ΔV / ΔI.
items.workedSolution: Reading the line endpoints gives V = ε = 15 V at I = 0.0 A and V = 5 V at I = 4 A. Hence Gradient = (5 − 15) / 4 = -2.50 V A⁻¹ (equal to −r).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates (5 − 15) / 4 = -2.50 V A⁻¹ (D).

options.distractorRationale: Evaluates internal resistance r = |ΔV / ΔI| but omits the negative sign of the downward V–I gradient.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Inverts ΔI / ΔV instead of computing ΔV / ΔI.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Assumes the line meets V = 0 at I = I_max instead of reading the non-zero terminal voltage V(I_max).

items.stem: A student tests Hooke's law (F = kx) using a spring balance. The best-fit line and both extreme lines are straight, but all miss the origin and cross the vertical axis above zero. What does this feature indicate?
items.workedSolution: When the origin falls outside the uncertainty band of the vertical intercept, a constant systematic zero error (e.g. Non-zeroed force sensor) is present while the gradient remains unaffected. Therefore the correct statement is: In IB experimental evaluation, a non-zero vertical intercept on a linear graph expected to pass through the origin indicates a constant systematic zero error that shifts every reading equally without changing the gradient.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: a non-zero vertical intercept on a linear graph expected to pass through the origin indicates a constant systematic zero error that shifts every reading equally without changing the gradient.

options.label: A
options.text: In IB experimental evaluation, a non-zero vertical intercept proves Hooke's law is false and that the gradient can no longer equal the spring constant k.
options.distractorRationale: A constant zero offset shifts y by +c without altering Δy/Δx, so the gradient still equals k accurately.

options.label: B
options.text: In IB experimental evaluation, a non-zero vertical intercept on a linear graph expected to pass through the origin indicates a constant systematic zero error that shifts every reading equally without changing the gradient.

options.label: C
options.text: In IB experimental evaluation, a non-zero vertical intercept is caused by random scatter and can be eliminated by taking ten repeat trials at each load.
options.distractorRationale: Repeating measurements reduces random uncertainty, never a constant systematic zero error.

options.label: D
options.text: In IB experimental evaluation, a student should force the line of best fit through (0, 0) even if it misses all error bars so the law is satisfied.
options.distractorRationale: A best-fit line must pass through the uncertainty bars of the valid data rather than being forced arbitrarily through the origin.

items.stem: Which particles experience the strong nuclear force shown in the graph?
items.workedSolution: The strong nuclear force acts only on hadrons (such as protons and neutrons) and has zero effect on leptons. Therefore option D is correct: acts equally between all nucleons and has no effect on leptons.

markScheme.criterion: Select option D: acts equally between all nucleons and has no effect on leptons.

options.label: A
options.text: The strong nuclear force acts only on positively charged protons and ignores neutral neutrons
options.distractorRationale: Confuses strong nuclear interaction with electrostatic interaction; neutrons feel the exact same strong force.

options.label: B
options.text: The strong nuclear force acts equally on protons, neutrons, and orbital electrons
options.distractorRationale: Electrons are leptons and do not experience the strong nuclear force.

options.label: C
options.text: The strong nuclear force acts only on unstable radioactive isotopes
options.distractorRationale: All stable and unstable nuclei are held together by the strong nuclear force.

options.label: D
options.text: The strong nuclear force acts equally between all nucleons and has no effect on leptons

items.stem: Which statement correctly defines a superconductor as shown by the solid blue $R\text{–}T$ graph?
items.workedSolution: AQA requires stating exact zero electrical resistance (or zero resistivity) at or below the critical temperature $T_{\text{c}}$. Therefore option D is correct: zero electrical resistance at or below the critical temperature.

markScheme.criterion: Select option D: zero electrical resistance at or below the critical temperature.

options.label: A
options.text: A superconductor is a material that has a small residual resistance that gradually approaches zero only at absolute zero
options.distractorRationale: Describes a normal pure metal, not a superconductor's sharp drop to exact zero at finite Tc.

options.label: B
options.text: A superconductor is a material that has infinite resistance below the critical temperature so no current flows
options.distractorRationale: Inverts conductivity and resistivity; superconductors have zero resistance below Tc.

options.label: C
options.text: A superconductor is a material that has zero resistance at room temperature once magnetised
options.distractorRationale: All known practical superconductors require cooling to or below their critical temperature Tc.

options.label: D
options.text: A superconductor is a material that has zero electrical resistance at or below the critical temperature

items.stem: Radioactive decay (ΔN/Δt = −λN) and capacitor discharge (ΔQ/Δt = −Q/(RC)) share the same exponential decay shape. Why do both processes produce this curve?
items.workedSolution: Constant fractional change per unit time (Δx/Δt = −kx) is the exact mathematical signature of exponential decay. Therefore the correct statement is: In both physical systems, exponential decay arises whenever the rate of decrease of a quantity is directly proportional to the amount remaining at that instant.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: exponential decay arises whenever the rate of decrease of a quantity is directly proportional to the amount remaining at that instant.

options.label: A
options.text: Both processes remove a fixed constant amount of charge or nuclei during every equal time interval until reaching zero.
options.distractorRationale: Removing a constant absolute amount per second gives a straight line reaching zero in finite time.

options.label: B
options.text: Both systems experience a rate of decrease proportional to the square of the remaining quantity.
options.distractorRationale: Exponential decay specifically requires direct proportionality to the first power of the remaining quantity.

options.label: C
options.text: In both physical systems, exponential decay arises whenever the rate of decrease of a quantity is directly proportional to the amount remaining at that instant.

options.label: D
options.text: Both processes obey an inverse-square law with elapsed time so the half-life doubles after every cycle.
options.distractorRationale: A defining property of exponential decay is a constant half-life independent of starting value.

items.stem: From (0 s, 2.398) to (30 s, 0.398), the straight line shows ln(V / V) versus t as a capacitor discharges through R = 25 kΩ. Evaluate the capacitance.
items.workedSolution: The line has gradient m = (0.398 − 2.398) / (30 − 0) = -0.06667 s⁻¹. Time constant τ = −1/m = 15.00 s. Capacitance C = τ / R = 15.00 s / (25 × 10³ Ω) = 600 μF.

markScheme.criterion: Extracts linearized graph parameters accurately to obtain 600 μF.

items.stem: A crane trolley begins at rest 25.0 m beyond the end-stop at t = 0.0 s and moves forward for 10.0 s as graphed. It slows uniformly between t = 7.0 s and t = 10.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Distance equals the trapezium area Δx = ½(10 + 5)(16) = 120 m. (b) Final distance from the reference mark = 25 + 120 = 145 m. (c) Mean speed = 120 / 10 = 12.0 m s⁻¹. (d) Braking acceleration = (0 − 16) / (10 − 7) = -5.33 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Identifies distance travelled as the area under the v–t trapezium.
Obtains Δx = 120 m.
Adds 25 m offset to obtain 145 m.
Divides distance travelled from (a) by 10 s.
Obtains mean speed = 12.0 m s⁻¹.
Obtains braking acceleration = -5.33 m s⁻².
