items.stem: During a tensile test to strain 0.5, a thin plastic strip gives the stress–strain curve shown. Proportionality holds up to strain 0.25.
items.workedSolution: (a) Gradient of the linear section gives Young's modulus E = 180 / 0.25 = 720 MPa. (b) Energy per unit volume = ½(0.25)(180) + ½(180 + 260)(0.25) = 77.5 MJ m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates initial gradient σ / ε up to ε = 0.25.
Obtains E = 720 MPa.
Identifies work per unit volume as total area under the σ–ε graph.
Splits area into initial triangle plus upper trapezium.
Obtains 77.5 MJ m⁻³.

items.stem: Data from two small charged metal spheres on a digital balance produce the linear graph of force F against r⁻² reaching 80.0 m⁻² below.
items.workedSolution: (a) At r⁻² = 0, systematic tare offset F₀ = 0.200 N. (b) Gradient = (2.2 − 0.2) / 80 = 0.0250 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Reads intercept F₀ = 0.200 N.
Evaluates ΔF = 2.2 − 0.2 using intercept from (a).
Divides ΔF by 80 m⁻² and states correct unit N m².
Obtains 0.0250 N m².

workingSteps: As r → ∞, r⁻² → 0, where the vertical intercept gives F₀ = 0.200 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the gradient k|Q₁Q₂| of the linearized plot over 0.0 m⁻² to 80.0 m⁻².
workingSteps: Read F = 2.2 N at r⁻² = 80 m⁻².

items.stem: A student measures the potential difference V across a filament lamp as the current I increases from 0.0 A to 0.8 A. The graph shows the resulting non-linear V–I characteristic.
items.workedSolution: (a) At I = 0.8 A, V = 6.40 V. (b) Static resistance R = V / I = 6.4 / 0.8 = 8.00 Ω (the upper segment gradient 10.0 Ω is ΔV / ΔI, not R).

markScheme.criterion: Reads V = 6.40 V at I = 0.8 A.
Selects R = V / I rather than local segment gradient ΔV / ΔI.
Substitutes V = 6.4 V and I = 0.8 A.
Obtains R = 8.00 Ω.

items.stem: In a twisted-wire experiment, a student plots data with vertical error bars from 3.0 N m to 15.0 N m. The graph shows the shallowest acceptable line of worst fit through the error bars.
items.workedSolution: (a) At 15 N m, y₂ = 42.0 rad. (b) Worst-fit gradient = (42 − 9) / (15 − 3) = 2.75 rad N⁻¹ m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Reads y₂ = 42.0 rad.
Reads y₁ = 9 rad at x₁ = 3 N m and forms Δy / Δx.
Subtracts x₁ = 3 N m in the denominator (15 − 3).
Obtains 2.75 rad N⁻¹ m⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the gradient of this shallowest line of worst fit between 3.0 N m and 15.0 N m.

items.stem: During a practical on a brass wire, a student plots data on a suppressed-origin grid using ±0.12 mm vertical error bars. Coordinates (15.0 N, 2.120 mm) and (55.0 N, 3.880 mm) lie on the best-fit line. The shallowest acceptable line through every error bar has gradient 0.03680 mm N⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Computing rise over run gives m_best = (3.880 − 2.120) / (55.0 − 15.0) = 0.04400 mm N⁻¹ ≈ 0.0440 mm N⁻¹. (b) Δm = |0.03680 − 0.04400| = 7.20 × 10⁻³ mm N⁻¹. (c) A suppressed origin expands the plotted data to fill more than half of the grid improving reading precision.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly substitutes large-triangle coordinates (3.880 − 2.120) / (55.0 − 15.0).
Obtains best-fit gradient = 0.0440 mm N⁻¹ with correct compound SI unit.
Calculates Δm = |m_worst − m_best| = 7.20 × 10⁻³ mm N⁻¹.
States that a false origin expands the plotted data to fill more than half of the grid improving reading precision.

options.label: A
options.text: Draw worst-fit lines through the outermost points only even if they miss an intermediate error bar, using two adjacent points for the gradient.
options.distractorRationale: Violates both the all-error-bars rule and the >50% triangle span requirement.

options.label: B
options.text: Force the best-fit line through the origin regardless of systematic intercept and compute gradient from a single point.
options.distractorRationale: A non-zero intercept reveals systematic error; using one point assumes zero intercept.

options.label: C
options.text: Use only the highest and lowest raw table entries for the gradient without drawing any line of best fit.
options.distractorRationale: Raw table endpoints ignore scatter across intermediate data points.

options.label: D
options.text: Worst fit lines must pass through every error bar and the gradient triangle must span more than half of the plotted line.

items.stem: A 4-bit binary counter ($Q_3 Q_2 Q_1 Q_0$) is modified to count from 0 to 9 and reset on the 10th pulse (binary 1010). Which active-high reset connection produces this modulo-10 BCD counter?
items.workedSolution: Decimal 10 is binary $1010$ ($Q_3 = 1, Q_2 = 0, Q_1 = 1, Q_0 = 0$), so Q3 and Q1 connected to an AND gate driving master reset clears all flip-flops briefly on count 10.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that Q3 and Q1 connected to an AND gate driving master reset.

options.label: A
options.text: Q3 and Q0 connected to an AND gate driving master reset.
options.distractorRationale: Detects binary 1001 (decimal 9), truncating the count to modulo-9 (0 to 8).

options.label: B
options.text: Q3 and Q2 connected to an AND gate driving master reset.
options.distractorRationale: Detects binary 1100 (decimal 12), creating a modulo-12 counter.

options.label: C
options.text: Q3 and Q1 connected to an AND gate driving master reset.

options.label: D
options.text: Q2 and Q1 connected to an AND gate driving master reset.
options.distractorRationale: Detects binary 0110 (decimal 6), creating a modulo-6 counter.

items.stem: The displacement–time graph shows the motion of a toy train moving along a straight track from t = 0.0 s to t = 20.0 s. It stops briefly and then returns between t = 12.0 s and t = 20.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Maximum displacement at the plateau = 64.0 m. (b) Return-stage velocity = (28 − 64) / (20 − 12) = -4.50 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Reads plateau displacement = 64.0 m.
Uses gradient formula Δs / Δt = (28 − 64) / (20 − 12).
Retains negative sign for motion back toward the origin.
Obtains -4.50 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Passing from the origin to I = 0.600 A at V = 6.00 V, the plotted I–V line describes a uniform metal wire. Its length is 1.80 m and cross-sectional area is 8.60 × 10⁻⁸ m².
items.workedSolution: (a) Resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area. (b) Gradient = 0.1000 A V⁻¹, so R = 1 / gradient = 10.0 Ω. (c) ρ = RA/L = 4.778 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 4.78 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: States resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area.
Correctly specifies all quantities (or notes constant temperature / material property).
Computes large-triangle gradient m = ΔI/ΔV = 0.100 A V⁻¹ and takes its reciprocal R = 1/m.
Correct wire resistance R = 10.0 Ω.
Substitutes R, A, and L correctly into ρ = RA/L.
Correct resistivity 4.78 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m with unit Ω m.

parts.prompt: Define the electrical resistivity of a material.
parts.expectedAnswer: Electrical resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area, where resistance, cross-sectional area, and length are measured for a uniform sample at constant temperature.
workingSteps: State the definition in terms of a conductor of unit length and unit cross-sectional area.
Identify that resistivity is an intrinsic property of the material at constant temperature.

parts.prompt: Determine the resistance of the wire from the gradient of the I–V line of best fit using a large triangle.
workingSteps: Because I is on the vertical axis, R = 1 / m = 10.00 Ω ≈ 10.0 Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resistivity of the alloy, stating the appropriate SI unit.
workingSteps: Evaluate ρ = 4.778 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 4.78 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

items.stem: The graph shows how the applied force on a light spring varies with extension from 0.0 m to 0.4 m. The spring obeys Hooke's law over this range. Calculate the spring constant k.
items.workedSolution: Spring constant k = gradient ΔF / Δx = 80 / 0.4 = 200 N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gradient k = 80 / 0.4 = 200 N m⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: Why is the sharp R spike of the QRS complex much larger in amplitude than the P wave on a normal ECG trace?
items.workedSolution: Because the ventricles contain much thicker muscular walls than the atria, ventricular depolarisation produces the largest surface potential change (typically $\approx 1\text{ mV}$).

markScheme.criterion: Identifies ventricular depolarisation.

options.label: A
options.text: It arises from slow atrial repolarisation occurring after blood enters the aorta.
options.distractorRationale: Atrial repolarisation is tiny and masked inside the QRS complex.

options.label: B
options.text: It reflects ventricular depolarisation through a far greater mass of heart muscle than the thin-walled atria.

options.label: C
options.text: It is caused by mains interference induced in the patient leads during each heartbeat.
options.distractorRationale: Mains interference occurs at 50 Hz continuously rather than synchronously with systole.

options.label: D
options.text: It marks ventricular relaxation when muscle cells hyperpolarise below resting potential.
options.distractorRationale: Ventricular repolarisation produces the broader, lower-amplitude T wave.

items.stem: Recorded between t = 0.0 s and t = 16.0 s, the velocity–time plot below tracks a camera trolley on a straight track. Positive values represent northward velocity. It slows to zero and reverses from t = 8.0 s to t = 12.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Direction reverses at t = 11 s. Positive area = 90.0 m and unsigned negative area = 18.0 m, giving total distance = 108 m. (b) Net displacement = 90.0 − 18.0 = 72.0 m; average velocity = 72.0 / 16 = 4.50 m s⁻¹. (c) Acceleration = (−4 − 12) / (12 − 8) = -4.00 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Finds zero-crossing t = 11 s and evaluates both unsigned areas (90.0 m and 18.0 m).
Obtains total distance = 108 m.
Subtracts areas for net displacement (72.0 m) and divides by 16 s.
Obtains average velocity = 4.50 m s⁻¹.
Obtains acceleration = -4.00 m s⁻² including negative sign.

parts.prompt: Determine the net displacement and hence calculate the average velocity over the 16.0 s interval.

Average velocity = Δs / Δt = 72.0 / 16 = 4.50 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A model boat (mass 2.5 kg) travels in a straight line with initial momentum 10.0 kg m s⁻¹. The force–time graph shows a forward force applied for 1.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Calculating the F–t area gives impulse J = ½(1 + 0.6)(60) = 48.0 N s. (b) Final momentum p_f = 10 + 48.0 = 58.0 kg m s⁻¹. (c) Speed increase Δv = 48.0 / 2.5 = 19.2 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes impulse from the trapezium area under the F–t curve.
Obtains J = 48.0 N s.
Adds 10 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 58.0 kg m s⁻¹.
Divides impulse from (a) by 2.5 kg.
Obtains Δv = 19.2 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Curve P and Curve Q show the I–V characteristics of an NTC thermistor under two different conditions (I on the vertical axis, V on the horizontal axis). Which statement explains its behaviour?
items.workedSolution: On an I–V graph (I on the vertical axis, V on the horizontal axis), gradient equals reciprocal of resistance. For this negative temperature coefficient thermistor, resistance decreases as temperature increases because more charge carriers are released so the curve becomes steeper.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that resistance decreases as temperature increases because more charge carriers are released so the curve becomes steeper.

options.label: A
options.text: Resistance increases as temperature increases because lattice vibrations block every carrier.
options.distractorRationale: Describes a metallic filament rather than an NTC semiconductor thermistor.

options.label: B
options.text: Resistance stays strictly constant at all temperatures because both curves are straight lines.
options.distractorRationale: A steeper I–V gradient means a smaller resistance, not constant resistance.

options.label: C
options.text: Curve Q represents the hotter state because a shallower I–V gradient indicates lower resistance.
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the meaning of I–V gradient (gradient equals reciprocal of resistance).

options.label: D
options.text: It exhibits resistance decreases as temperature increases because more charge carriers are released so the curve becomes steeper.

items.stem: Starting at (0, 0), a capacitor's Q–V graph rises linearly to Q = 9.00 mC and V = 12.0 V. What electrical energy is stored in it?
items.workedSolution: From the triangular area beneath the line, E = ½ Q V = 0.5 × (9 × 10⁻³ C) × 12 V = 0.05400 J ≈ 0.0540 J.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly converts mC to C and obtains 0.0540 J.

options.distractorRationale: Ductile metals show yield, extensive plastic deformation, and necking (Curve B).

options.label: C

options.distractorRationale: Rubber-like polymers follow the non-linear hysteresis S-curve (Curve C).

options.label: D
options.text: Curve A represents a brittle material fractures after very small plastic strain with no necking

items.stem: Across 10.0 s, the graph plots the upward acceleration of a test lift whose initial velocity is 10.0 m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Speed peaks where a crosses zero at t = 6.00 s. (b) Positive area = 18.0 m s⁻¹, giving v_max = 10 + 18.0 = 28.0 m s⁻¹. (c) Negative area magnitude = 9.00 m s⁻¹, so v_final = 28.0 − 9.00 = 19.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: States t = 6.00 s.
Evaluates positive area up to 6 s (18.0 m s⁻¹) and adds u₀ = 10 m s⁻¹.
Obtains v_max = 28.0 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts negative area (9.00 m s⁻¹) from v_max.
Obtains final velocity = 19.0 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Force sensors log the resultant force from x = 0.0 m to x = 10.0 m on a block (mass 4.0 kg) travelling at 5.5 m s⁻¹ at x = 0.0 m.
items.workedSolution: (a) Total area under the force–distance curve gives W = 144 − 8.00 = 136 J. (b) v = √(5.5² + 2(136)/4) = 9.91 m s⁻¹. (c) Mean force = 136 / 10 = 13.6 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates positive (144 J) and negative (−8.00 J) areas.
Obtains net work W = 136 J.
Uses ½mv² = ½(4)(5.5²) + W.
Obtains v = 9.91 m s⁻¹.
Divides net work by 10 m to get 13.6 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the net work done on the 4.0 kg object between x = 0.0 m and x = 10.0 m.
workingSteps: Positive area (0 to 8 m) = ½(8 + 4)(24) = 144 J; negative area (8 m to 10 m) = −½(2)(8) = −8.00 J.

parts.prompt: Calculate its speed at x = 10.0 m.
State the mean resultant force over the 10.0 m displacement.

items.stem: What net force acts from t = 4.0 s to t = 10.0 s? The p–t graph tracks a 6.0 kg glider on a horizontal air track.
items.workedSolution: Resultant force is the rate of change of momentum. Reading the slope gives F = Δp / Δt = (36 − 12) / (10 − 4) = 4.00 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates F = Δp / Δt = (36 − 12) / (6) = 4.00 N (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes the secant ratio p₂ / t₂ from the origin, ignoring both initial momentum p₁ and start time t₁.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies Δp by Δt instead of evaluating the rate of change of momentum Δp / Δt.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Divides Δp / Δt by mass m, obtaining acceleration rather than resultant force.

items.stem: A ceramic heating rod is tested over L / A between 0.0 m⁻¹ and 50.0 m⁻¹, producing the linear R against L / A graph shown.
items.workedSolution: (a) The y-intercept equals lead resistance R₀ = 2.00 Ω. (b) Computing rise over run yields ρ = (14 − 2) / 50 = 0.240 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: States R₀ = 2.00 Ω.
Identifies ρ with the gradient ΔR / Δ(L / A).
Subtracts R₀ = 2 Ω from 14 Ω before dividing by 50 m⁻¹.
Obtains ρ = 0.240 Ω m.

items.stem: Plotted below is the terminal potential difference V of a solar cell against current I between 0.0 A and 4.0 A.
items.workedSolution: (a) Open-circuit intercept gives ε = 13.0 V. (b) Gradient = (7 − 13) / 4 = -1.50 V A⁻¹. (c) Mean terminal p.d. = ½(13 + 7) = 10.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reads ε = 13.0 V at I = 0.
Evaluates (7 − 13) / 4 including negative sign.
Obtains -1.50 V A⁻¹.
Uses ½(13 + 7) or area divided by 4 A.
Obtains 10.0 V.

parts.prompt: State the electromotive force ε of the source.
Determine the signed gradient of the V–I graph between 0.0 A and 4.0 A.
workingSteps: At I = 4 A, V = 7 V.

parts.prompt: Calculate the mean terminal potential difference across the 0.0 A to 4.0 A interval.

items.stem: Five of the six data points on the IB Paper 1B graph fit a straight line within their uncertainty bars. The fourth point (circled) lies far above the line. What is the valid scientific way to handle this point?
items.workedSolution: IB Inquiry 2 requires identifying outliers transparently (circling them on the plot) and justifying their exclusion from the best-fit and extreme gradient lines. Therefore the correct statement is: Under IB Inquiry data-processing standards, an anomalous data point whose uncertainty bar lies clearly outside the linear trend of the remaining points should be circled and excluded from the best-fit gradient with an experimental justification rather than silently deleted.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: an anomalous data point whose uncertainty bar lies clearly outside the linear trend of the remaining points should be circled and excluded from the best-fit gradient with an experimental justification rather than silently deleted.

items.stem: At the marked nucleon separation inside a stable helium nucleus, how does the strong nuclear force behave?
items.workedSolution: Between roughly $0.5\text{ fm}$ and $3.0\text{ fm}$, the strong nuclear force is attractive, overcoming electrostatic proton–proton repulsion. Therefore option A is correct: attractive overcoming electrostatic proton repulsion.

markScheme.criterion: Select option A: attractive overcoming electrostatic proton repulsion.

options.label: A
options.text: In this intermediate separation band the strong nuclear force is attractive overcoming electrostatic proton repulsion

options.label: B
options.text: In this intermediate separation band the strong nuclear force is repulsive and pushes protons apart
options.distractorRationale: Between 0.5 fm and 3 fm the strong nuclear force is attractive, not repulsive.

options.label: C
options.text: In this intermediate separation band the strong nuclear force is infinite in range like gravity
options.distractorRationale: The strong nuclear force falls to zero around 3 fm rather than extending to infinity.

options.label: D
options.text: In this intermediate separation band the strong nuclear force acts only between protons
options.distractorRationale: It acts equally between p–p, p–n, and n–n pairs.

items.stem: Which pair of applications directly uses the zero resistance of superconductors to carry very large currents without $I^2R$ heating?
items.workedSolution: Zero resistance allows huge persistent currents for high-field MRI electromagnets, particle-accelerator magnets, and lossless electrical power cables. Therefore option B is correct: high field MRI electromagnets and lossless electrical power cables.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: high field MRI electromagnets and lossless electrical power cables.

items.stem: On a capacitor discharge Q–t curve, a tangent drawn at t = 2.0 s meets the horizontal time axis at t = 8.25 s. What is the RC time constant of the discharge circuit?
items.workedSolution: For an exponential Q = Q₀e^(−t/RC), the subtangent along the time axis equals RC: τ = 8.25 − 2.0 = 6.25 s.

markScheme.criterion: Determines time constant RC = 6.25 s.

items.stem: On a ln(V / V) against time t graph for a capacitor discharging through 80 kΩ, the line crosses the vertical axis at 2.015 and passes through (32 s, 0.015). Calculate V₀ at t = 0.
items.workedSolution: Since ln(V) = −t/τ + ln(V₀), the vertical intercept is ln(V₀) = 2.015. Taking the exponential gives V₀ = e^(2.015) = 7.500 V ≈ 7.50 V.

markScheme.criterion: Extracts linearized graph parameters accurately to obtain 7.50 V.

items.stem: In a 16.0 s test run, a conveyor cart begins 35.0 m from the starting mark and follows the velocity–time graph below. Deduce the mean speed for the 16.0 s interval.
items.workedSolution: Evaluating the trapezium area gives Δx = ½(16 + 6)(19) = 209 m (independent of the 35 m starting offset); hence mean speed = 209 / 16 = 13.1 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Divides trapezium distance (209 m) by 16 s to obtain 13.1 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: Measurements on a nylon thread loaded to strain 1.0 give a straight segment from 0.0 to 0.5. Calculate the material's Young's modulus, expressed in MPa.
items.workedSolution: At the proportionality limit (ε = 0.5), the graph shows 250 MPa. Therefore E = σ / ε = 250 / 0.5 = 500 MPa.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates initial linear gradient E = 250 / 0.5 = 500 MPa (D).

items.stem: Graphing force F versus r⁻² from 0.0 m⁻² to 40.0 m⁻² produces the straight line shown for two charged metal-coated spheres on a balance. A constant zero offset F₀ shifts every balance reading. Determine the slope ΔF / Δ(r⁻²) from the graph.
items.workedSolution: At r⁻² = 0.0 m⁻², tare offset F₀ = 0.15 N; at r⁻² = 40 m⁻², F = 1.35 N. Gradient = (1.35 − 0.15) / 40 = 0.0300 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts tare offset F₀ = 0.15 N to get (1.35 − 0.15) / 40 = 0.0300 N m² (A).

items.stem: The graph shows the potential difference–current characteristic for a filament lamp up to I = 2.0 A. Calculate the electrical resistance of the component when the current is 2.0 A.
items.workedSolution: Electrical resistance at an operating point is defined by R = V / I (not the local slope ΔV / ΔI). At I = 2 A, V = 16 V, so R = 16 / 2 = 8.00 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses static ratio R = V / I = 16 / 2 = 8.00 Ω (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the local segment gradient ΔV / ΔI instead of the static ratio V / I defining electrical resistance.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the ratio to I / V (conductance in S) rather than V / I.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates the low-current resistance near the origin rather than at the specified operating current.

items.stem: In a photodiode experiment, a student draws the steepest line of worst fit between error bars at 2.0 mW and 10.0 mW. Calculate the gradient m_worst of this worst-fit line.
items.workedSolution: At x₁ = 2 mW, y₁ = 6 μA; at x₂ = 10 mW, y₂ = 38 μA. Worst-fit gradient m_worst = (38 − 6) / (10 − 2) = 4.00 μA mW⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δy / Δx = (38 − 6) / (10 − 2) = 4.00 μA mW⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: To measure the best-fit gradient on a steel-spring false-origin plot, a student draws a dashed triangle spanning over half the line. What is the purpose of using a large gradient triangle?
items.workedSolution: On a suppressed-origin NCUK graph, the procedure reduces percentage reading uncertainty when calculating the gradient.

markScheme.criterion: States accurately that the graphing technique reduces percentage reading uncertainty when calculating the gradient.

options.text: It alters the true physical stiffness of the specimen to a larger value
options.distractorRationale: Triangle size affects measurement uncertainty only, not the physical property.

options.label: B
options.text: Because it reduces percentage reading uncertainty when calculating the gradient

options.label: C
options.text: It removes random scatter from the plotted experimental crosses completely
options.distractorRationale: Random scatter is already fixed in the recorded data points.

options.label: D
options.text: It allows the student to pick two raw plotted data crosses instead of points on the best-fit line
options.distractorRationale: Gradient triangles should always use widely separated points lying directly on the line of best fit.

items.stem: Data from a trolley on a smooth inclined ramp (sin θ = 0.2, g = 9.8 m s⁻²) are graphed as v² against distance s over 2.5 m. Calculate the straight-line gradient, expressed in m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: From v² = u₀² + (2g sin θ)s, the vertical intercept is u₀² = 2.8 m² s⁻² and at s = 2.5 m, v² = 12.6 m² s⁻². Gradient = (12.6 − 2.8) / 2.5 = 2(9.8)(0.2) = 3.92 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept u₀² = 2.8 m² s⁻² (or evaluates 2 × 9.8 × 0.2) to get 3.92 m s⁻² (C).

items.stem: In a calorimetry graph question, a student loses a mark for their gradient calculation even though their arithmetic is correct. Which error explains the lost mark?
items.workedSolution: Under AQA Paper 3A graphical rules: Worst fit lines must pass through every error bar and the gradient triangle must span more than half of the plotted line, whereas the student used a tiny triangle.

markScheme.criterion: Worst fit lines must pass through every error bar and the gradient triangle must span more than half of the plotted line, whereas the student used a tiny triangle.

options.text: The student used grid-line intersections on the line of best fit rather than raw plotted data crosses.

options.label: C
options.text: The student plotted the independent variable along the horizontal axis instead of the vertical axis.
options.distractorRationale: Plotting the independent variable on the horizontal axis is standard convention.

options.label: D

options.distractorRationale: Half the spread between extreme worst-fit gradients is the exact AQA method.

items.stem: How is a single rising-edge triggered D-type flip-flop wired to act as a divide-by-2 frequency divider?
items.workedSolution: Because $D = \bar{Q}$ supplies the opposite logic level before each clock edge, connecting not-Q back to the D input toggles Q on every rising clock edge dividing frequency by two.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that connecting not-Q back to the D input toggles Q on every rising clock edge dividing frequency by two.

options.text: Connecting Q directly back to the D input toggles Q on every rising clock edge.
options.distractorRationale: Connecting Q to D latches the current state permanently without toggling.

options.label: B
options.text: Connecting not-Q back to the D input toggles Q on every rising clock edge dividing frequency by two.

options.label: C
options.text: Holding D permanently at logic 1 makes Q oscillate at half the clock frequency.
options.distractorRationale: Holding $D = 1$ locks $Q = 1$ after the first rising edge.

options.label: D
options.text: Connecting the clock signal directly to the master reset pin halves the output frequency.
options.distractorRationale: Clocking reset clears Q to 0 rather than toggling.

items.stem: The displacement–time graph shows the motion of a remote-controlled car moving in a straight line from t = 0.0 s to t = 20.0 s. Calculate its velocity during the initial stage from t = 0.0 s to t = 5.0 s.
items.workedSolution: At t = 0.0 s, s₀ = 20 m; at t = 5 s, s₁ = 65 m. Velocity v = Δs / Δt = (65 − 20) / 5 = 9.00 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Linear readings of current I (y-axis) versus potential difference V (x-axis) pass through the origin and (8.00 V, 0.500 A) for a uniform metal wire (1.80 m, area 8.10 × 10⁻⁸ m²). Determine the resistivity of the metal.
items.workedSolution: Calculating the slope gives gradient m = ΔI / ΔV = 0.5000 A / 8.000 V = 0.06250 A V⁻¹. Since gradient = 1/R, R = 1/m = 16.00 Ω. Therefore ρ = R A / L = 7.200 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 7.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses R = 1 / gradient and ρ = R A / L to obtain 7.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

items.stem: The graph shows the force–extension line for a spring up to 0.4 m. The spring obeys Hooke's law. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored when it is extended by 0.4 m.
items.workedSolution: Elastic potential energy equals the triangular area under the F–x line: E_p = ½ F x = ½(60)(0.4) = 12.0 J.

markScheme.criterion: Computes triangular area ½(60)(0.4) = 12.0 J (A).

items.stem: Following the QRS complex on a normal human ECG, what physiological event produces the smooth, broader T wave?
items.workedSolution: The T wave corresponds to ventricular repolarisation; it is wider and lower than the QRS spike because recovery occurs more gradually across the ventricular wall.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies ventricular repolarisation.

options.label: A
options.text: Atrial depolarisation initiated by the sinoatrial node at the start of the beat.
options.distractorRationale: Atrial depolarisation corresponds to the initial P wave.

options.label: B
options.text: Simultaneous contraction of both atria and ventricles in a single pulse.
options.distractorRationale: Atria and ventricles contract one after the other rather than at the same time.

options.label: C
options.text: The slower wave of ventricular repolarisation restoring ventricular cells to their resting potential.

options.label: D
options.text: Electrical conduction delay across the atrioventricular node before ventricular firing.
options.distractorRationale: AV-node delay corresponds to the flat P–R segment, not the T wave.

items.stem: Plotted below is velocity against time for a glider along a horizontal air track. Find its signed acceleration from t = 7.0 s to t = 10.0 s.
items.workedSolution: Between t = 7 s and t = 10 s, velocity changes from +20 m s⁻¹ to −10 m s⁻¹. Acceleration a = Δv / Δt = (−10 − 20) / (10 − 7) = -10.0 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δv / Δt = (−10 − 20) / (3) = -10.0 m s⁻² (A).

items.stem: Over 0.8 s, a variable forward force pushes a small cart of mass 2.0 kg whose initial momentum is 6.0 kg m s⁻¹. Determine the speed increase Δv of the object.
items.workedSolution: Impulse J = area under F–t trapezium = ½(0.8 + 0.4)(50) = 30.0 N s. Speed increase Δv = J / m = 30.0 / 2 = 15.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes J = 30.0 N s and Δv = J / 2 = 15.0 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: With potential difference V on the horizontal axis and current I on the vertical axis, the graph tracks a metal wire resistor. Why does the curve have this shape?
items.workedSolution: On an I–V graph (I on the vertical axis, V on the horizontal axis), gradient equals reciprocal of resistance. For this ohmic metallic resistor at constant temperature, constant resistance because current is directly proportional to potential difference at constant temperature.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that constant resistance because current is directly proportional to potential difference at constant temperature.

options.label: A
options.text: Resistance increases smoothly with voltage because the gradient of the straight line is constant.
options.distractorRationale: Constant gradient on an I–V graph means constant resistance, not increasing resistance.

options.label: B
options.text: It exhibits constant resistance because current is directly proportional to potential difference at constant temperature.

options.label: C
options.text: Resistance equals the gradient of the I–V line rather than its reciprocal.
options.distractorRationale: With I on the vertical axis and V on the horizontal axis, gradient equals 1/R.

options.label: D
options.text: Current flows only above a forward threshold potential difference.
options.distractorRationale: Describes a diode rather than an ohmic metallic resistor.

items.stem: Charging a capacitor produces a straight line from (0, 0) up to Q = 2.50 mC at V = 10.0 V. Use the area beneath the graph to calculate the stored energy.
items.workedSolution: Energy stored equals the area of the Q–V triangle: E = ½ Q V = 0.5 × (2.5 × 10⁻³ C) × 10 V = 0.01250 J ≈ 0.0125 J.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly converts mC to C and obtains 0.0125 J.

items.stem: A ductile copper wire (Curve B) is stretched beyond its elastic limit and then unloaded to zero stress, as shown by the dashed line. Why does the unloading line return to a non-zero strain?
items.workedSolution: The unloading curve is parallel to the initial linear section leaving permanent plastic strain. Therefore option A is correct: unloading curve is parallel to the initial linear section leaving permanent plastic strain.

markScheme.criterion: Select option A: unloading curve is parallel to the initial linear section leaving permanent plastic strain.

options.text: After plastic deformation, the unloading curve is parallel to the initial linear section leaving permanent plastic strain

options.label: B
options.text: After plastic deformation, the unloading curve retraces the exact loading path back to the origin
options.distractorRationale: Only elastic deformation below the elastic limit returns to zero strain.

options.label: C
options.text: After plastic deformation, the unloading curve drops vertically to zero stress at constant strain
options.distractorRationale: The elastic portion of strain recovers along a line parallel to the initial Young modulus gradient.

options.label: D
options.text: After plastic deformation, the unloading curve has a much shallower slope because Young modulus halves permanently
options.distractorRationale: Interatomic bond stiffness (Young modulus E) stays essentially unchanged, so the unloading line is parallel to the linear loading line.

items.stem: A train starts at t = 0.0 s moving forward at 14.0 m s⁻¹. Its forward acceleration over 12.0 s is graphed below. Determine the peak forward speed reached.
items.workedSolution: Because speed grows whenever a > 0 (from t = 0.0 s until a = 0 at t = 6 s). Positive area Δv_max = (2)(6) + ½(4)(6) = 24.0 m s⁻¹. Maximum speed = u₀ + Δv_max = 14 + 24.0 = 38.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Integrates positive acceleration up to t = 6 s (24.0 m s⁻¹) and adds 14 m s⁻¹ to get 38.0 m s⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: With sin θ = 0.3 and g = 9.81 m s⁻², a trolley accelerates along a smooth inclined ramp. Speed v is logged to plot v² against s up to 2.5 m. Use the graph to calculate its gradient.
items.workedSolution: From v² = u₀² + (2g sin θ)s, the vertical intercept is u₀² = 3.5 m² s⁻² and at s = 2.5 m, v² = 18.215 m² s⁻². Gradient = (18.215 − 3.5) / 2.5 = 2(9.81)(0.3) = 5.89 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept u₀² = 3.5 m² s⁻² (or evaluates 2 × 9.81 × 0.3) to get 5.89 m s⁻² (B).

items.stem: A 3.0 kg small sled moves forward at initial speed 6.0 m s⁻¹. Between x = 0.0 m and x = 15.0 m, the resultant force follows the graph below. Use the signed area under the graph to calculate the net work done.
items.workedSolution: Calculating the positive area (0 to 12 m) = 162 J; resistive work (12 m to 15 m) = −9.00 J. Net work = 162 − 9.00 = 153 J.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts resistive triangle (9.00 J) from positive trapezium (162 J) to get 153 J (C).

items.stem: A 3.2 kg glider on a horizontal air track moves along its path while its linear momentum is graphed against time. Deduce the constant resultant force acting from t = 3.0 s to t = 8.0 s.
items.workedSolution: From Newton's second law, the line gradient equals resultant force: F = Δp / Δt = (22.4 − 6.4) / (8 − 3) = 3.20 N.

items.stem: Resistance R of a conducting plastic strip rises linearly with L / A from 0.0 m⁻¹ to 160.0 m⁻¹ on the plot below. What is the resistivity ρ of this material?
items.workedSolution: Matching R = ρ(L / A) + R₀ with y = mx + c shows that resistivity ρ equals ΔR / Δ(L / A) = (20 − 4) / 160 = 0.100 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept R₀ = 4 Ω to obtain ρ = (20 − 4) / 160 = 0.100 Ω m (A).

items.stem: What is the signed gradient of the V–I graph for a cell (up to 2.0 A)? The line obeys V = ε − Ir.
items.workedSolution: At I = 0.0 A, V = ε = 6 V; at I = 2 A, V = 2.4 V. Gradient = (2.4 − 6) / 2 = -1.80 V A⁻¹ (equal to −r).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates (2.4 − 6) / 2 = -1.80 V A⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: Which statement correctly compares random uncertainties and systematic errors in a physics experiment?
items.workedSolution: Averaging repeated trials narrows random scatter (improving precision), whereas identifying calibration/zero offsets is required to remove systematic bias (improving accuracy). Therefore the correct statement is: When processing experimental measurements, random uncertainties scatter readings unpredictably around the trend line and are reduced by repeating and averaging trials. Systematic errors shift all readings in one direction and are not reduced by averaging.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: random uncertainties scatter readings unpredictably around the trend line and are reduced by repeating and averaging trials. Systematic errors shift all readings in one direction and are not reduced by averaging.

options.label: A
options.text: When processing experimental measurements, systematic errors scatter points equally above and below the trend line and vanish when the mean of five trials is calculated.
options.distractorRationale: Describes random uncertainties; systematic errors shift every measurement in one consistent direction.

options.label: B
options.text: When processing experimental measurements, random uncertainties shift all data points by a fixed constant offset and can only be removed by zeroing the meter.
options.distractorRationale: Swaps random uncertainties and systematic zero errors.

options.label: C
options.text: When processing experimental measurements, random uncertainties scatter readings unpredictably around the trend line and are reduced by repeating and averaging trials, whereas systematic errors bias all readings in one direction and are not reduced by averaging.

options.label: D
options.text: When processing experimental measurements, both random and systematic errors are completely eliminated whenever uncertainty bars are plotted on the graph.
options.distractorRationale: Uncertainty bars quantify estimated uncertainty visually; they do not eliminate underlying experimental errors.

items.stem: The graph shows the strong nuclear force between two nucleons against their separation. What is the nature and role of the strong nuclear force in the shaded region closest to the vertical axis?
items.workedSolution: Below $0.5\text{ fm}$ the strong nuclear force turns positive (repulsive), preventing nucleons from collapsing onto one another. Therefore option D is correct: strongly repulsive preventing nuclear collapse.

markScheme.criterion: Select option D: strongly repulsive preventing nuclear collapse.

options.label: A
options.text: At very small separations the force is strongly attractive causing nucleons to fuse together
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the sign below 0.5 fm; attraction at zero separation would collapse the nucleus.

options.label: B
options.text: At very small separations the force is zero so only electrostatic repulsion acts
options.distractorRationale: The strong nuclear force crosses zero at ~0.5 fm and becomes intensely repulsive below 0.5 fm.

options.label: C
options.text: At very small separations the force is weak nuclear attraction balancing gravity
options.distractorRationale: Gravity is negligible on nuclear scales and the weak force does not bind nucleons.

options.label: D
options.text: At very small separations the force is strongly repulsive preventing nuclear collapse

items.stem: A yttrium barium copper oxide (YBCO) superconductor has a critical temperature above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen. It is placed in liquid nitrogen and carries a steady current. What electrical state is it in?
items.workedSolution: Since $77\text{ K} \le 92\text{ K}$, YBCO is in its superconducting state with zero resistance and zero heating loss. Therefore option A is correct: superconducting state with zero resistance and zero heating loss.

markScheme.criterion: Select option A: superconducting state with zero resistance and zero heating loss.

options.label: A
options.text: Because its temperature is below the transition threshold, it operates in the superconducting state with zero resistance and zero heating loss

options.label: B
options.text: Because its temperature is below the transition threshold, it operates in the normal resistive state dissipating large heating power
options.distractorRationale: At T <= Tc, resistance drops suddenly to zero so I²R heating drops to zero.

options.label: C
options.text: Because its temperature is below the transition threshold, it operates as an insulator blocking all current
options.distractorRationale: A superconductor conducts persistent currents without potential difference or energy loss.

options.label: D
options.text: Because its temperature is below the transition threshold, it operates with half its room-temperature resistance
options.distractorRationale: Resistance drops cleanly to exact zero, not merely to a fraction of its normal value.

items.stem: A student uses a spreadsheet to model capacitor discharge via ΔQ/Δt = −Q/(RC), with columns for t, Q, and ΔQ. Which iterative rule correctly calculates each next row?
items.workedSolution: At row k, ΔQ_k = −(1/RC)·Q_k·Δt, and row k+1 sets Q_{k+1} = Q_k + ΔQ_k. Therefore the correct statement is: To step forward cleanly in time, each spreadsheet row calculates the decrease by multiplying the previous value by the rate constant and time step, then subtracts it to get the next value.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: each spreadsheet row calculates the decrease by multiplying the previous value by the rate constant and time step, then subtracts it to get the next value.

options.label: A
options.text: Each spreadsheet row subtracts the constant initial charge loss ΔQ₀ repeatedly from every subsequent row.
options.distractorRationale: Subtracting a constant ΔQ₀ produces linear decay rather than exponential discharge.

options.label: B
options.text: To step forward cleanly in time, each spreadsheet row calculates the decrease by multiplying the previous value by the rate constant and time step, then subtracts it to get the next value.

options.label: C
options.text: Each spreadsheet row divides Q by the elapsed total time t rather than the fixed step size Δt.
options.distractorRationale: The incremental change depends on the small time step Δt, not the cumulative time t.

options.label: D
options.text: Each spreadsheet row multiplies Q by RC instead of dividing by RC to find the charge lost in Δt.
options.distractorRationale: Because ΔQ = −(Q/RC)Δt, multiplying by RC has wrong units and inverts the discharge rate.

items.stem: A resistor R = 30 kΩ discharges a capacitor. Its ln(V / V) against t graph is straight and passes through (0 s, 2.197) and (24 s, 0.197). Determine the capacitance.
items.workedSolution: The line has gradient m = (0.197 − 2.197) / (24 − 0) = -0.08333 s⁻¹. Time constant τ = −1/m = 12.00 s. Capacitance C = τ / R = 12.00 s / (30 × 10³ Ω) = 400 μF.

markScheme.criterion: Extracts linearized graph parameters accurately to obtain 400 μF.

items.stem: In an 8.0 s run, a small rover begins at t = 0.0 s 12.0 m beyond the base marker and follows the graph below. Determine its final distance from the base marker.
items.workedSolution: Using the area of the velocity–time trapezium over the 8 s run equals the trapezium area: Δx = ½(8 + 4)(8) = 48.0 m. Final position from the base marker = x₀ + Δx = 12 + 48.0 = 60.0 m.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Treats the entire journey as constant-speed motion at peak velocity before adding x₀.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts the initial forward position x₀ from the integrated displacement instead of adding it.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the trapezium displacement correctly but forgets to add the initial position offset x₀.

items.stem: In a materials practical, a thin plastic strip is loaded up to strain 0.6. The gradient of the stress–strain curve shifts at 0.3. Deduce the strain energy per unit volume stored at a strain of 0.6.
items.workedSolution: Integrating via geometric areas under the σ–ε graph (1 MPa × 1 = 1 MJ m⁻³) gives u = ½(0.3)(180) + ½(180 + 250)(0.3) = 91.5 MJ m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Sums triangle and trapezium areas under σ–ε curve to obtain 91.5 MJ m⁻³ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Integrates only up to the limit of proportionality at ε₁ and omits the trapezium from ε₁ to ε_max.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Approximates the entire bilinear curve as a single triangle from (0, 0) to (ε_max, σ_max).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies peak stress by maximum strain without integrating the piecewise area.

items.stem: Find the gradient in N m² from the graph of F versus r⁻² from 0.0 m⁻² to 50.0 m⁻² using two charged metal-coated spheres on a balance.
items.workedSolution: At r⁻² = 0.0 m⁻², tare offset F₀ = 0.3 N; at r⁻² = 50 m⁻², F = 1.9 N. Gradient = (1.9 − 0.3) / 50 = 0.0320 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts tare offset F₀ = 0.3 N to get (1.9 − 0.3) / 50 = 0.0320 N m² (B).

items.stem: The graph shows the non-linear V–I characteristic for a non-ohmic resistor. Calculate the electrical resistance of the component at a current of 2.4 A.
items.workedSolution: Electrical resistance at an operating point is defined by R = V / I (not the local slope ΔV / ΔI). At I = 2.4 A, V = 14.4 V, so R = 14.4 / 2.4 = 6.00 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses static ratio R = V / I = 14.4 / 2.4 = 6.00 Ω (B).

items.stem: In a simple-pendulum experiment, the graph shows the steepest line of worst fit drawn from 1.0 m to 6.0 m. Calculate the gradient of this worst-fit line.
items.workedSolution: At x₁ = 1 m, y₁ = 3 s²; at x₂ = 6 m, y₂ = 26 s². Worst-fit gradient m_worst = (26 − 3) / (6 − 1) = 4.60 s² m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δy / Δx = (26 − 3) / (6 − 1) = 4.60 s² m⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: Red axis breaks allow both axes on a copper-wire graph to start away from zero. Why is a false origin chosen when all data points lie far from zero?
items.workedSolution: On a suppressed-origin NCUK graph, the procedure expands the plotted data to fill more than half of the grid improving reading precision.

markScheme.criterion: States accurately that the graphing technique expands the plotted data to fill more than half of the grid improving reading precision.

options.distractorRationale: A suppressed-origin line rarely passes through the false corner point.

items.stem: A class tests a trolley on a smooth inclined ramp (sin θ = 0.15, g = 9.8 m s⁻²) and plots v² versus s up to 4.0 m. Find the gradient of the line in m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: From v² = u₀² + (2g sin θ)s, the vertical intercept is u₀² = 2.6 m² s⁻² and at s = 4 m, v² = 14.36 m² s⁻². Gradient = (14.36 − 2.6) / 4 = 2(9.8)(0.15) = 2.94 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept u₀² = 2.6 m² s⁻² (or evaluates 2 × 9.8 × 0.15) to get 2.94 m s⁻² (B).

items.stem: Every voltage reading in a Paper 3A plot of potential difference $V$ against current $I$ carries an 8% uncertainty, whereas current has a fixed absolute uncertainty. How do the vertical error bars change across the graph?
items.workedSolution: Under AQA Paper 3A graphical rules: Vertical error bars grow proportionally with the dependent variable because percentage uncertainty is constant, whereas horizontal bars remain uniform.

markScheme.criterion: Vertical error bars grow proportionally with the dependent variable because percentage uncertainty is constant, whereas horizontal bars remain uniform.

options.label: A
options.text: Vertical error bars remain identical in length at every plotted point while horizontal bars shrink.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses fixed percentage uncertainty with a constant absolute uncertainty.

options.label: B
options.text: Vertical error bars grow proportionally with the dependent variable because percentage uncertainty is constant, whereas horizontal bars remain uniform.

options.label: C
options.text: Vertical error bars shrink at higher voltages because percentage uncertainty improves at larger readings.
options.distractorRationale: Applies constant-absolute-resolution reasoning to a fixed-percentage-uncertainty instrument.

options.label: D
options.text: Error bars disappear on the line of best fit once repeat readings are averaged.
options.distractorRationale: Misconception that repeating readings eliminates uncertainty completely.

items.stem: A student wants to light ten LEDs one at a time in order. Why is a 4017 Johnson decade counter preferred over a 4-bit BCD counter for this task?
items.workedSolution: For sequential 1-of-10 activation, a Johnson decade counter activates one decoded output at a time without extra decoding gates whereas a BCD counter outputs binary weights needing a decoder.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that Johnson decade counter activates one decoded output at a time without extra decoding gates whereas a BCD counter outputs binary weights needing a decoder.

options.label: A
options.text: Johnson counter outputs a weighted 4-bit binary code that directly drives seven-segment displays.
options.distractorRationale: A BCD counter outputs binary weights; a Johnson counter outputs 1-of-10 sequential decoded lines.

options.label: B
options.text: Johnson counter doubles the clock frequency on each of its ten outputs.
options.distractorRationale: Each decoded output pulses at $f_{\mathrm{clk}}/10$.

options.label: C
options.text: BCD counter cannot count past decimal 7 without a Johnson stage.
options.distractorRationale: A 4-bit BCD counter counts cleanly from 0 to 9.

options.label: D
options.text: Johnson decade counter activates one decoded output sequentially without extra decoding gates whereas a BCD counter outputs binary weights needing a decoder.

items.stem: The displacement–time graph shows the motion of a trolley moving along a straight track. Calculate its constant velocity between t = 0.0 s and t = 4.0 s.
items.workedSolution: At t = 0.0 s, s₀ = 14 m; at t = 4 s, s₁ = 42 m. Velocity v = Δs / Δt = (42 − 14) / 4 = 7.00 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts initial position s₀ = 14 m to obtain v = (42 − 14) / 4 = 7.00 m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: From the origin through (10.0 V, 0.500 A), the I (y-axis) against V (x-axis) line describes a uniform alloy-80 wire. Given length 1.40 m and cross-sectional area 7.70 × 10⁻⁸ m², find the resistivity of the alloy-80 wire.
items.workedSolution: Calculating the slope gives gradient m = ΔI / ΔV = 0.5000 A / 10.00 V = 0.05000 A V⁻¹. Since gradient = 1/R, R = 1/m = 20.00 Ω. Therefore ρ = R A / L = 1.100 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m ≈ 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses R = 1 / gradient and ρ = R A / L to obtain 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m.

items.stem: The graph shows the force–extension line for a light spring up to 0.8 m. The spring obeys Hooke's law. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored when it is extended by 0.8 m.
items.workedSolution: Elastic potential energy equals the triangular area under the F–x line: E_p = ½ F x = ½(68)(0.8) = 27.2 J.

markScheme.criterion: Computes triangular area ½(68)(0.8) = 27.2 J (D).

items.stem: A student measures the background-corrected count rate C from a radioactive sample using a Geiger–Müller tube over 50.0 s. The graph plots ln(C / s⁻¹) against time t, following ln C = ln C₀ − λt. Calculate the gradient of the best-fit line.
items.workedSolution: At t = 0.0 s, ln C₀ = 9; at t = 50 s, ln C = 4. Gradient = (4 − 9) / 50 = -0.100 s⁻¹.

items.stem: On a normal human ECG waveform, which electrical event in cardiac muscle produces the small initial upward P wave?
items.workedSolution: The sinoatrial node triggers atrial depolarisation, generating the small positive P wave ahead of atrial contraction.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies atrial depolarisation.

options.label: A
options.text: The wave of atrial depolarisation spreading across the upper chambers just before they contract.

options.label: B
options.text: Rapid ventricular depolarisation spreading down the thick ventricular walls.
options.distractorRationale: Rapid ventricular depolarisation produces the large sharp QRS complex, not the P wave.

options.label: C
options.text: Ventricular repolarisation as the lower chambers return to resting potential.
options.distractorRationale: Ventricular repolarisation produces the broader T wave following the QRS complex.

options.label: D
options.text: Closing of the semilunar valves after systole without electrical activity.
options.distractorRationale: Valve closure causes heart sounds rather than surface action-potential waves.

items.stem: Data for a trolley along a straight track produce the velocity–time plot below. Use the gradient between t = 6.0 s and t = 10.0 s to calculate its signed acceleration.
items.workedSolution: Between t = 6 s and t = 10 s, velocity changes from +9 m s⁻¹ to −3 m s⁻¹. Acceleration a = Δv / Δt = (−3 − 9) / (10 − 6) = -3.00 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δv / Δt = (−3 − 9) / (4) = -3.00 m s⁻² (D).

items.stem: Initially at momentum 12.0 kg m s⁻¹, a puck of mass 4.0 kg receives a forward force over 2.0 s as plotted below. Use the impulse area to calculate the mean force over 2.0 s.
items.workedSolution: Total impulse J = ½(2 + 1)(32) = 48.0 N s. Mean force F_mean = J / Δt = 48.0 / 2 = 24.0 N.

markScheme.criterion: Divides impulse (48.0 N s) by 2 s to obtain 24.0 N (B).

items.stem: A student records the I–V graph for a light-emitting diode (LED), placing current I vertically and potential difference V horizontally. What accounts for the shape shown?
items.workedSolution: On an I–V graph (I on the vertical axis, V on the horizontal axis), gradient equals reciprocal of resistance. For this light emitting diode, conducts sharply above the forward threshold voltage and has very high resistance in reverse bias.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that conducts sharply above the forward threshold voltage and has very high resistance in reverse bias.

items.stem: Shown below is a straight-line charging graph from the origin to Q = 7.20 mC and V = 24.0 V. Deduce the capacitance of this capacitor.
items.workedSolution: First convert charge to SI units: Q = 7.2 mC = 7.200 × 10⁻³ C. Capacitance C = Q / V = 3.000 × 10⁻⁴ F = 300 μF.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly converts mC to C and obtains 300 μF.

items.stem: A metal wire obeying Hooke's law stretches by $3.20\text{ mm}$ when the tension increases smoothly from zero to $64.0\text{ N}$. Calculate the elastic strain energy stored in the wire.
items.workedSolution: $E_{\text{el}} = \frac{1}{2}F\Delta L = 0.5 \times 64.0 \times 3.20 \times 10^{-3} = 0.102 J$. Option C (0.102 J) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Elastic strain energy $= 0.102 J$ (0.102 J, option C).

items.stem: Moving forward at 13.0 m s⁻¹ at t = 0.0 s, a train has the forward acceleration plotted over 16.0 s. Use the positive area to calculate the highest speed during the 16.0 s run.
items.workedSolution: Maximum speed is reached when a > 0 ends (from t = 0.0 s until a = 0 at t = 10 s). Positive area Δv_max = (4)(5) + ½(6)(5) = 35.0 m s⁻¹. Maximum speed = u₀ + Δv_max = 13 + 35.0 = 48.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Integrates positive acceleration up to t = 10 s (35.0 m s⁻¹) and adds 13 m s⁻¹ to get 48.0 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: For a dynamics cart rolling down a frictionless ramp at sin θ = 0.45 (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²), v² is plotted against s over 1.2 m. Use the graph to calculate its gradient.
items.workedSolution: From v² = u₀² + (2g sin θ)s, the vertical intercept is u₀² = 3.8 m² s⁻² and at s = 1.2 m, v² = 14.3948 m² s⁻². Gradient = (14.3948 − 3.8) / 1.2 = 2(9.81)(0.45) = 8.83 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept u₀² = 3.8 m² s⁻² (or evaluates 2 × 9.81 × 0.45) to get 8.83 m s⁻² (A).

items.stem: Over a 14.0 m distance, the plotted resultant force acts on a block (mass 3.2 kg) moving forward at 4.0 m s⁻¹. Use the work–energy theorem to calculate its speed at x = 14.0 m.
items.workedSolution: Area above the distance axis (0 to 11 m) = ½(11 + 6)(16) = 136 J. Resistive work (11 m to 14 m) = −½(3)(4) = −6.00 J. Net work W = 130 J. From ½mv² = ½mu₀² + W, v = √(4² + 2 × 130 / 3.2) = 9.86 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds net work W = 130 J and v = √(4² + 2W/3.2) = 9.86 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: Measurements on a silicon rod produce the straight-line R against L / A graph reaching 400.0 m⁻¹. Deduce the resistivity ρ using the line's gradient.
items.workedSolution: From the linear relation R = ρ(L / A) + R₀, subtracting the intercept gives ρ via ΔR / Δ(L / A) = (30 − 6) / 400 = 0.0600 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept R₀ = 6 Ω to obtain ρ = (30 − 6) / 400 = 0.0600 Ω m (D).

items.stem: A rechargeable battery is tested over current I between 0.0 A and 2.5 A, giving the downward linear V–I graph below. Use the linear graph to calculate the mean terminal potential difference.
items.workedSolution: Since the V–I plot is linear from 10 V at I = 0.0 A down to 4 V at I = 2.5 A, V_mean = ½(10 + 4) = 7.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Averages endpoint voltages ½(10 + 4) = 7.00 V (D).
